chapters.title: Vienna Gambit
chapters.subtitle: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4
chapters.intro:
With 3.f4 White plays a King's Gambit in which Black's knight is already on f6. That one detail changes everything: taking on f4 is bad because e4-e5 comes with tempo, and every quiet third move lets White play fxe5 followed by d4 and e5. Only 3...d5 holds the balance, and after 4.fxe5 Nxe4 the real opening begins: White has a pawn wedge on e5 and a half-open f-file, Black has a strong knight on e4 and free development.

Theory's verdict is that Black equalises with accurate play, and the sources agree on where the accuracy is needed. The classical 5.Nf3 is under a cloud because of 5...Bc5 (Finkel's survey in Yearbook 110, Tseitlin and Glazkov before him). 5.d3 is met by 5...Nxc3 6.bxc3 d4. That leaves Spielmann's 5.Qf3, which Goeller's survey of the literature, Breutigam's ChessBase Magazine article, the Sveshnikovs' repertoire book and Illingworth's guide all single out as White's best practical try. It is the main repertoire here; 5.Nf3 and 5.d3 follow as complete second weapons, because the traps and the plans in them are worth knowing even if you never switch.

The lines are short on forced wins and long on patterns. Learn which pawn takes back on c3 and why, what the queen does on e2, f3 and g3, and how the queenless ending is played, and most positions in the chapter can be handled by understanding.

sections.title: The position after 4...Nxe4
sections.body:
Black threatens ...Qh4+ and the knight on e4 stops White from developing normally (d4 would leave it a permanent outpost, Bc4 is not possible). White has to question the knight at once, and there are three ways.

- **5.Qf3** attacks it a second time and defuses the check: 5...Qh4+ 6.g3 Nxg3 7.Qxg3. The g1 knight goes to e2 later. Black chooses between 5...Nc6 (the forcing main line), 5...Nxc3 and 5...f5.
- **5.Nf3** develops and protects e5; the knight on e4 is then attacked by Qe2 or d3. Black's replies are 5...Be7, 5...Bc5, 5...Bg4, 5...Nc6 and 5...Bb4.
- **5.d3** hits it with a pawn and invites 5...Qh4+ and 5...Bb4, both of which are worse than they look.

5.Nxe4 is the move to avoid: after 5...dxe4 the pawn takes f3 from the knight, ...Qh4+ is still there and e5 becomes a target.

sections.title: The e5 wedge and the half-open f-file
sections.body:
Once the knights are exchanged on c3 the structure decides the plans. The e5 pawn takes f6 and d6 from Black's pieces, so the black king has few defenders, and it gives White's pieces the squares f4 and (after an exchange on d4 or e6) d4. The f-file points at f7.

- **White** castles long, puts the bishop on f4 and the queen on g3, and pushes the h-pawn. The standard attacking model is Paulsen-Schiffers 1889: Qg3, Bd3, Nf3-g5, h4 and the h-file opens.
- **Black** has two pawn breaks. ...f6 removes the wedge and is the equalising idea in most lines, so White wants to meet it with a piece on e5 or with the pin on the d-file. ...c5 gains space and prepares ...Nc6 and ...Qa5; White answers with c4, using the rook on d1 against d5.
- **Trades:** Black wants the f4 bishop off (it holds e5), which is the point of ...Bg5. White is happy to give the light-squared bishop for the c6 knight, because that knight is the piece that attacks e5.

sections.title: Which pawn takes back on c3
sections.body:
The recapture is the most important decision in the opening, and the rule is simple.

- **With the d-pawn** when it is still on d2: the c1 bishop and the a1 rook come out at once, the d-file bears on d5 and White castles long. This is Paulsen's recapture in the 5.Qf3 lines and the point of the Qe2 systems after 5.Nf3. In the main line 7.bxc3 is a known inaccuracy: the same ending arises with White's bishop shut in and Black slightly better.
- **With the b-pawn** when d3 has been played (5.Qf3 f5 6.d3, or 5.d3). Then White wants d3-d4 and the chain c3-d4-e5, and Black's standard antidote is ...d4 himself, giving a pawn back to stop it.
- **One exception:** after 5.Nf3 Bc5 6.Qe2 Bf2+ 7.Kd1 Nxc3+ White takes with the b-pawn, because 8.dxc3 lets the f2 bishop out via h4 with tempo.

sections.title: The queenless ending
sections.body:
About four in ten of the 5.Qf3 Nc6 games reach this ending, so it has to be played well. Black has the bishop pair; White has the healthier pawns and a knight that will sit on d4.

- **White's plan:** Be3 first (so that ...Bc5 does not take the g1-a7 diagonal), then Ne2-d4, O-O-O and a rook to e1 or f1. The targets are e4, which has lost the d-pawn that supported it, and the c-pawns. The f-file is useful: Rf1 often wins f7 or forces a concession.
- **Black's plan:** attack e5 with a rook (...Rb8-b5, ...Ra5 or ...Re8), open the h-file with ...h5-h4, and exchange a bishop for the d4 knight when it suits him.
- **Good trades for White:** the e-pawns (e5 for e4) and one pair of rooks. In the model game Lagarde-Bouget, White let e5 go, took e4 and was left with the better structure and a dominant knight.
- **Verdict:** equal with best play. Illingworth's description is the practical one: an equal position that the stronger player wins.

sections.title: Black keeps the knight: 5...f5
sections.body:
The Bardeleben Variation is the line that makes 5.Qf3 a practical weapon and not a refutation. Black supports the knight, and after 6.d3 Nxc3 7.bxc3 plays 7...d4, the same pawn offer as in the 5.d3 line, so that White never gets d3-d4.

White's answer is 8.Qg3 (Bangiev). The queen ties the f8 bishop to g7 and frees f3 and e2: Be2 comes with the threat of Bh5+, then Bf3 and Ne2. White gives up the c3 pawn and gets the bishops, the long light diagonal and castling; with 12.Bxc6 he removes the knight that could use b4 and d4 and has lasting compensation. Illingworth, who recommends 5.Qf3, rates this line as objectively equal and the one he would be least happy to face in a slow game, so it is the line to know best.

sections.title: The queen on e2 in the 5.Nf3 lines
sections.body:
"If in doubt, play Qe2" is Gary Lane's summary of White's play after 5.Nf3. The move does four things: it attacks the knight on e4 again and prepares d3, it lets White take back on c3 with the d-pawn and castle long, it sets up Qb5+ against an undefended b7 (a recurring trick after ...Bg4), and it keeps d2-d4 in reserve so that ...Bb4 has no target.

It works against 5...Be7 (Hector's and Adams's line), 5...Bg4 (Kaufmann's move, with two famous traps), 5...Bb4 and, after 6.Bb5 first, against 5...Nc6. Against 5...Bc5 it is White's best try as well, but there 6...Bf5 followed by ...d4 is the line that the surveys consider better for Black, which is why 5.Nf3 is the second choice in this chapter.

sections.title: Traps and standard tactics
sections.body:
- **6.Nxe4? Nd4!** (diagram). After 5.Qf3 Nc6 White must pin with 6.Bb5. Taking on e4 loses to the knight jump: 7.Qd3 dxe4 8.Qxe4 Bf5 and c2 falls with check.
- **The Würzburger Trap:** 5.d3 Qh4+? 6.g3 Nxg3 7.Nf3 Qh5 8.Nxd5!. If 8...Nxh1 then 9.Nxc7+ and 10.Nxa8, and the h1 knight does not get out. After 8...Bg4 White plays 9.Bg2, or goes for the old finish 9.Nf4 Bxf3 10.Nxh5 Bxd1 11.hxg3 Bxc2? 12.b3, trapping the bishop.
- **Euwe-Yates:** 5.Nf3 Bg4 6.Qe2 Nc6? 7.Nxe4 Nd4 8.Qd3 Bxf3 9.Ng3!. The quiet retreat leaves two black pieces attacked.
- **Spielmann-Flamberg:** 5.Nf3 Bg4 6.Qe2 Nc5?! 7.d4 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 Qh4+ 9.g3 Qxd4 10.Be3 Qxe5 11.O-O-O and 12.Nxd5!. Black's queen has eaten two pawns and the d-file opens on his king.
- **The pin on the d-file:** with a rook on d1 against a queen on d8, c4 attacks a d5 pawn that cannot take, and ...f6 fxe5 can be met by Rxd5 or even Qxe4 and Bc4+ (the 5...Bb4 line).
- **Bh5+ in the 5...f5 line:** once Black has played ...f5 the diagonal e8-h5 is weak. With the queen on g3 a bishop check on h5 forces ...g6 and a sacrifice on g6 follows.

sections.title: When Black does not play 3...d5
sections.body:
Most games below master level leave the main line on move three, and the punishment is always the same pawn move. After 3...exf4 4.e5 the knight has no square but g8 (e4 and d5 are covered by the c3 knight, g4 and h5 by the queen), and the attempt to pin with 4...Qe7 fails to 5.Qe2 and Nd5. After 3...Nc6 4.fxe5 Nxe5 5.d4 both knights are driven back in turn. After 3...Bb4 or 3...Bd6 White takes on e5 and wins material with Qg4 or with the fork e4-e5.

The only respectable alternative is 3...d6, which gives a King's Gambit Declined without the active bishop on c5. White keeps the tension with Nf3 and Bb5 and has a small, risk-free advantage.

sections.title: Sources
sections.body:
- Michael Goeller, annotated games of the Alrick H. Man Vienna Gambit theme tournament (New York 1924-25), "Vienna Gambit (C29) Bibliography" and "The Critical Line of the Vienna Gambit", The Kenilworthian, 2014, https://kenilworthian.blogspot.com/2014/05/vienna-gambit-c29-bibliography.html (the main source for the 5.Nf3, 5.d3 and 5...f5 lines)
- Analysis quoted and assessed in Goeller's notes, used through them and not read first hand: Alexander Bangiev, *White Repertoire 1.e4* (ChessBase, 2003); Alexander Finkel, "A Worthy Alternative", *New in Chess Yearbook 110* (2014); Gary Lane, *Vienna Game* (Everyman, 2000); John Emms, *Play the Open Games as Black* (Gambit, 2000); Igor Lysyj and Roman Ovetchkin, *The Open Games for Black* (Chess Stars, 2012); Gabriel Velasco, *The Life and Games of Carlos Torre* (Russell Enterprises, 2000)
- Max Illingworth, "Dangerous Chess Openings: The Vienna Gambit", Chess.com blog, https://www.chess.com/blog/Illingworth/dangerous-chess-openings-the-vienna-gambit-1 (the 5.Qf3 repertoire and its verdicts)
- Evgeny and Vladimir Sveshnikov, *A Chess Opening Repertoire for Blitz and Rapid* (New in Chess, 2015), chapter 21: table of contents and its recommendation of 5.Qf3 as reported by Goeller; the chapter itself was not available
- Andrew Martin, *The Vienna Game: Dynamic, Flexible and Deeply Underestimated* (ChessBase video course, 2026): list of lines and model games only
- "Vienna Game" and "Vienna Game, Würzburger Trap", Wikipedia (the second cites the *Encyclopaedia of Chess Openings*, volume C, and *Modern Chess Openings*)
- "Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Nf6/3. f4" and its sub-pages, Wikibooks
- "The Vienna Game: A How to Play Guide for White and Black", Chessable blog, https://www.chessable.com/blog/vienna-game/
- "Surprise Black With The Vienna Game", Wholesale Chess blog, https://www.wholesalechess.com/chess-blog/the-vienna-game/
- Vitualis, "How To Play The Vienna Gambit: A Complete Guide For Beginners", Chess.com blog
- Lichess studies "The Vienna Gambit" (dNYgykBC) and "Vienna Gambit" (mOYlmDuC), for the lines after 3...exf4
- The Lichess Elite Database (the app's own book of 2400+ games), for how often each move is played

lines.name: 5.Qf3 Nc6 6.Bb5: the queenless ending
lines.summary: Black's most popular defence forces the queens off. White gets the healthier pawns and a knight on d4 against the bishop pair; equal, but easier to play for White.

next.text: A King's Gambit in which Black's knight is already on f6, so that fxe5 and e4-e5 will come with tempo. That is why taking the pawn is a mistake here (see the line on 3...exf4) and why only one reply holds the balance.

The only move that equalises. Black answers the wing thrust in the centre and makes sure that after fxe5 the knight has e4 to go to and not g8. Every other third move lets White play fxe5 or e5 with gain of time.
This capture puts the pawn on e5, where it takes f6 and d6 from Black's pieces for the rest of the game, and half opens the f-file.

The position the chapter turns on. Black threatens ...Qh4+ and the knight on e4 cramps White; White has the e5 wedge and the f-file. The knight has to be questioned at once: by 5.Qf3 (this line and the next three), 5.Nf3 or 5.d3 (their own lines below).

Spielmann's move, and the choice of most current sources: the Sveshnikovs' repertoire book, Illingworth, and the first three model games of Andrew Martin's course.

**Why here:** the knight is attacked twice, so Black must decide about it now; the check has lost its sting (5...Qh4+ 6.g3 Nxg3 7.Qxg3); and the g1 knight is kept for e2, from where it reaches d4 or f4 without blocking the f-file.

**The price:** the natural square of the g1 knight is taken, which matters in the 5...f5 line.
The most popular reply and the most forcing: it attacks e5 and sets a trap based on ...Nd4.
The only good move. The pin removes the pressure on e5 and the ...Nd4 trick together, and Bxc6 will split Black's queenside.
The knight is attacked twice and cannot be supported, so Black cashes it in.

Paulsen's recapture, away from the centre. The c1 bishop and the queen's rook come into play at once (Bf4, O-O-O), the d-file bears on d5, and White's king will be safe on the queenside. The doubled pawns do not matter: they cannot be attacked.

Played in about seven games out of ten. The check provokes g3 so that ...Qe4+ forces the queens off, and Black gets an ending with the bishop pair. Keeping the queens on with 7...Be7 is the next line.
White has no reason to avoid the exchange: the ending is where the better structure counts.
Goeller's preferred order: take while Black has to recapture with the pawn.

The key ending.

**Structure:** Black has the bishop pair but three pawn islands. The e4 pawn has lost its supporting d-pawn and c6 and c7 are fixed targets. White's only weakness is e5.

**Plan:** Ne2-d4 (the knight cannot be driven away and eyes c6 and e6), O-O-O, a rook to e1 or f1, then c4 and the capture of e4.

**Why the bishop first:** after 11.Ne2 Black plays 11...Bc5 and takes the g1-a7 diagonal. Lysyj and Ovetchkin then give 12.Nd4 Bb6 13.a4 a5 14.Bf4 h6 15.h4 Bg4 with the initiative for Black.
Stops ...a3, which would loosen the king's cover.

Lagarde-Bouget, Avoine 2012. White has exchanged his weak pawn for Black's and keeps the better structure and the dominant knight; the bishops have nothing to attack, and c7 and a4 stay weak. White won.

**Verdict:** equal with best play, in Illingworth's words 'an equal position where the stronger player will win'. That is the fair summary of the whole 5...Nc6 line: no advantage, but a position where White knows what to do.
The most common move in recent elite games: Black wants ...h4 to open the h-file for the rook.
White simply finishes development. After 12...h4 13.gxh4 Rxh4 the file is open, but all of White's pieces are out and Ne2-d4 follows as usual.
Stops Ne2 and castling for a move.
The bishop has been driven to a square where it only defends e4, and Ne2 comes with a choice of d4 and f4.
The f-file at work. 13...Re8 14.Rxf7 Rxe5 15.Bd4 was unclear in Lederle-Pfuetzner 2007.

The other main move. Black avoids the split pawns but has to spend ...Bd7 on it, and White blockades with Nd4 and Be3. Illingworth quotes this as a balanced line from engine practice. Choose it if you prefer a firm blockade to a target on c6.
Putting the question to the bishop first.
The structure of the main line with queens on: Nd4 or Nf4, Be3 and castling follow. If Black now checks, 9...Qh4+ 10.g3 Qe4 11.Qxe4 dxe4 is the main-line ending with ...a6 thrown in.
The structural move, given by many older books, is worse here: the queen exchange follows all the same and the recapture has opened nothing.
The ending of the main line with the c1 bishop still shut in and a2, c3 and e5 all weak. Goeller rates it slightly better for Black.
What 5.Qf3 seemed to prepare, and a classic error.
The queen is hit and c2 would fall with check, so there is no time to save the knight on e4.
The queen must give up c2 and ...Nxc2+ wins a rook. Other queen moves avoid the worst, but the opening advantage has changed hands.

The obvious capture is the worst of the natural moves. The e4 pawn takes f3 from the knight, the d-pawn cannot advance without leaving something behind, ...Qh4+ is still in the air and e5 will be hit by ...Nc6.
Black has at least equalised.

Really a King's Gambit: 4...exf4 5.Nf3 is the Modern Defence by transposition, and 4...Nxd5 is simple and good. The independent try is the Falkbeer-style 4...e4. Payne and Read give 4.exd5 three chapters as a surprise weapon; it is not the repertoire because Black chooses the kind of game.
The point of Black's play: the pawn is returned to disturb White's development.
Sharp, with White's king in the middle for a while. Goeller's survey calls it generally favourable to White, but it has to be known by heart.

lines.name: 5.Qf3 Nc6 6.Bb5 Nxc3 7.dxc3 Be7: queens stay on
lines.summary: Black refuses the ending and castles short. White plays Bf4 and O-O-O; Black needs the accurate 9...Bg5 to equalise, otherwise the kingside attack plays itself.

next.text: Goeller's recommendation for Black, who 'should equalise' this way. Black keeps the queens on because White's king has not decided where to live either.
Overprotects e5 and clears the way for castling.
Castling on opposite sides with White's pieces already aimed at the king.
The equaliser. The f4 bishop is the piece that holds e5 and leads the attack, so Black exchanges it and follows with ...f6.
Removing the piece that attacks e5 before the bishops come off.
The freeing break.

The d-file pin again: the d5 pawn is attacked and exchanging on c4 is not attractive. Sofronie-Scetinin, Cappelle la Grande 2002, went 15...Bxf3 16.gxf3 Qf6 17.Qxf6 Rxf6 18.cxd5 cxd5 19.Rxd5 Rxf3 20.Rc5 and White's more active rooks won a long ending.

**Verdict:** equal. Black has solved his problems, but he had to find 9...Bg5 and is left with the worse pawns.
The natural developing move is too slow.
Threatening Bh6.
Paulsen-Schiffers, Breslau 1889. The h-file is open, the bishop on d3 aims at h7 and White won in 35 moves. The model attack for this structure, and still the plan.

lines.name: 5.Qf3 Nxc3 6.dxc3: development first
lines.summary: Black exchanges knights at once. White again takes away from the centre, plays Bf4 and O-O-O and uses the pin on the d-file; a sharp middlegame with castling on opposite sides.

next.text: As common as 5...Nc6. Black gives up the outpost at once so that nothing hangs and he can choose his set-up. Illingworth is 'not convinced' it is best: White gets his ideal recapture for nothing.
Illingworth's choice, and the same rule as in the main line: with the d-pawn, for the bishop, the d-file and queenside castling.
The most common move. Black covers d5 before a rook arrives on d1 and keeps ...c5 and ...Nc6 in reserve.
The active plan: space, ...Nc6 and ...Qa5, with the king staying in the centre or going long.

The tactical point of the whole set-up. The d5 pawn is attacked three times and defended twice, and it is pinned to the queen, so it cannot take the bishop. Black has to release the tension with 9...d4 (when Bxe6 damages his pawns) or defend passively with 9...Ne7.

**Verdict:** an unbalanced middlegame with no settled theory. In elite online games Black has scored well with the ...c5 plan, so do not play it on general principles: remember the pin on the d-file, Qg3 against g7, and that the e5 pawn must stay protected by the f4 bishop.
The standard follow-up in practice: the queen leaves the f-file to the rook, looks at g7 and the h-pawn starts to run.
Illingworth's move order. The queen ties the f8 bishop to g7 before Black has decided on ...Be7, so that normal kingside development costs something. It often transposes after Bf4 and O-O-O.
Trying for the ending of the first line.
A worse version for Black: White still has both bishops and e4 is attacked before Black has developed. Illingworth: a reliable advantage thanks to the more active pieces.
Illingworth's 'most solid' choice.
The set-up of the 7...Be7 line without having spent a move on Bb5. Qg3, Bd3 and h4 follow.
Transposes to the main line.
Transposes to the first line.

The classical recapture, a little more common in practice and fully playable. White wants d4, Bd3, Ne2 and O-O with a broad centre and a kingside attack. Its drawback is theoretical: Black can hit the centre at once with 6...c5, or follow the old equalising line given here.
Challenging the wedge before White has castled.
Theory gives a draw by perpetual check (Qh6+, Qg6+).

lines.name: 5.Qf3 f5: the Bardeleben Variation
lines.summary: Black supports the knight. After 6.d3 Nxc3 7.bxc3 d4 White plays 8.Qg3 and gives up the c3 pawn for the bishops and the light squares. Objectively equal and the line to know best.

next.text: The knight stays where it is. This is the one line where the queen on f3 is slightly in the way, because Nf3 is not available. Illingworth calls it the reply that would stop him from playing the gambit in slow games, while rating it only 'objectively equal'.
The only way to put the question to the knight. 6.exf6 Nxf6 just develops Black and gives up the wedge.
Forced this time, and it has a point: White threatens d4 with the ideal chain c3-d4-e5, followed by Bd3.

The thematic answer, the same as in the 5.d3 line. Black gives White no time for d3-d4, fixes the d3 pawn and attacks c3. Against anything slower (7...Be7, 7...Be6) White plays 8.d4 and has everything he wants.
Bangiev's move, the key to the line. The queen ties the f8 bishop to g7 and vacates f3: Be2 is coming with the threat of Bh5+, then Bf3 and Ne2. White is ready to give up c3.
The bishop takes the long diagonal that 7...d4 opened.
The critical test: Black takes the pawn before White can castle and play c4.
Goeller's improvement on Bangiev's 12.Be3, which runs into 12...Nb4! against c2 and d3. With the knight gone, ...Nb4 and ...Nd4 disappear and c3 is easy to collect.

White has full compensation for the pawn (Goeller). Nxc3 or Qxa7 comes next, the b-file is open against the king and the knight has d4 and f4, while Black's bishop is hemmed in by its own f5 pawn.

**Verdict:** balanced, and unexplored compared with the other lines. White must be willing to play a pawn down for a few moves; in return every one of his pieces has a job.
White has the centre he wanted from the start.

The old main line. White keeps the pawn, puts the knight on f4 and attacks down the b-file. 13...Bxc4 14.Nf4 led to great complications in Vorotnikov-Kapengut 1975 and Vankov-Angelov (corr. 1992), where the analysis of Bangiev and van der Tak favours White.
Offering to exchange White's best piece.
The bishop may be taken: White recaptures with the queen and the f5 pawn falls.
Clearly better for White (Goeller). The f-file is open against a king that cannot castle short, and 14...Qxe5 would have lost to 15.Qf7+ Kd8 16.Bf4.
Keeps the pawn but lets Black develop with check: 10...Bb4+ 11.Kd1 O-O. Illingworth finds the result chaotic and easier for Black to play, with White's king stuck in the centre.
Hromadka-Schreiber, Munich 1936. The king is safe on f2, Bf3 and Ne2 follow and the b-file belongs to White.
Taking at once.
Nothing is recaptured: the threat is Bh5+ and a sacrifice on g6.
Unclear according to Bangiev. White wins c3 back with the knight and owns the long diagonal; Black has had to fianchetto into the e5 pawn.
Defending the pawn loses time to a small combination.
The bishop cannot be taken for free: the check on h4 forks king and b4.
The bishop is regained and Black is better: White's king has lost its shelter and e5 is weak.

lines.name: 5.Nf3 Be7 6.Qe2: the Breyer line
lines.summary: The classical fifth move as a second weapon. Against the solid 5...Be7 White plays Qe2, takes on c3 with the d-pawn and castles long; the Adams-Anand line is level but full of play.

next.text:
The traditional main move. It stops ...Qh4+, protects e5 and keeps every option open. It gets full coverage here because the positions differ in kind from 5.Qf3: the queen goes to e2, the knight is already on its natural square, and there is no queenless ending.

**Its problem** is theoretical. 5...Bc5 (third line of this section) is the critical reply, and Finkel's survey in Yearbook 110 argues that it puts 5.Nf3 in doubt. Against everything else White is at least comfortable.
Breyer's quiet move: Black castles first and decides about the knight later.

'If in doubt, play Qe2' is Gary Lane's slogan for White in these lines, and Jonny Hector made the move his speciality. The queen attacks e4 a second time and prepares d3, it allows dxc3 and queenside castling, and Qb5+ is often available against an undefended b7. It also keeps the d-pawn at home, so ...Bb4 has no target.
The same rule as after 5.Qf3: open the bishop and the d-file, castle long.
Space on the queenside and a square for the knight. Black delays castling on purpose, as the next note shows.
Gains space and rules out ...g5 against the bishop; the pawn will go to h5 to fix g7.
The bishop is going to g2 (or h3) to press on d5 and e6.

Adams-Anand, Linares 1994, drawn after 13...Na5 14.b3 Nc6 15.Qf2 Qc7. Both kings are safe and the centre is fixed. White plays for Nh4 and Bh3 or for the c4 break, Black for ...d4.

**Verdict:** level, with all the pieces on. Goeller suggests 13.Qf1 intending Bh3 as another try.
The standard break when a rook on d1 faces the queen: the d5 pawn cannot take.
Janosevic-Gligoric, Belgrade 1964. The d-pawn is blocked, Bd3 comes with tempo against h7 and White is clearly better.
Exchanging the defender of the dark squares.
Slightly better for White, Janosevic-Reshevsky, Maribor 1967.
Here the structural recapture is simply slow.
Black opens the f-file first and is slightly better (Goeller).
Karpov's way: exchange the f3 knight.
Better than 8.Qf2 Nxf3+ 9.Qxf3 Qb6!, when Black had counterplay in Hellers-Karpov, Haninge 1990.
Adams-Xu Jun, Cap d'Agde 1994. The g-file is open and the pawns roll with f4 and h5; White has the initiative, though Black held the draw.
Supporting the knight, Bardeleben style.
Unclear. This is the one Qe2 line where the b-pawn takes back, because the d-pawn has already moved; White continues g3, Bg2 and later d4 or c4.

The natural move, building the centre, gives Black two good replies. The first is the old main line shown here, where taking twice on e4 runs into the pin ...Re8. The second is Goeller's point 6...Bb4!, which reaches the 5...Bc5 6.d4 Bb4 line, where in his view only Black can be better.

lines.name: 5.Nf3 Bc5: the critical test
lines.summary: The reason theory prefers other fifth moves. 6.Qe2 is the best try: after 6...Bf2+ the king stands well on d1, but 6...Bf5 followed by ...d4 is a real problem.

next.text: The move that Tseitlin and Glazkov, and later Finkel, single out as the challenge to 5.Nf3. Black threatens ...Bf2+ and ...Nf2 and makes White solve a problem before he has castled.
Goeller's choice after working through the literature. The queen attacks e4, and after a check on f2 the king is not badly placed on d1.
The forcing line, and the one a surprised opponent will choose.
The queen cannot take: the knight defends f2.
The exception to the recapture rule.
9.Qb5+ Nd7 10.d4 c6 11.Qb3 is Velasco's suggestion, about equal.
The queen clears e2 for the king's bishop and heads for g3.

Bangiev: slightly better for White. The king is safe on d1 behind the pawn centre, the kingside pawns have gained space with tempo and the queens come off on White's terms.

**Verdict:** the 6...Bf2+ line is fine for White. The whole variation stands or falls with 6...Bf5 and 7...d4, and there the published analysis favours Black.
A forced draw.
Marshall's attempt to save a tempo against d4.
Goeller's improvement on Torre's 9.d4. The bishop takes the diagonal that Black's has abandoned and Black cannot castle.
8...Bh4! brings the bishop out on the kingside with tempo, and Black is slightly better.
Mamedyarov's move against Jobava (Warsaw 2013) and the real test: Black just defends the knight and keeps his threats.
Covers f2 and frees the d-pawn: d3 will drive the e4 knight away, and the knight on d1 comes back via e3 or f2.
Jobava played 9.Ne3 and was gradually outplayed.
Benjamin and Finkel: slightly better for White, who has a piece for two pawns and is about to consolidate.
The critical move according to Finkel. It takes e3 from the knight and c3 from the pawn, so White cannot untangle normally.
White's only consistent plan (d3 comes next), but Finkel's analysis ends in Black's favour. This is the main reason the chapter prefers 5.Qf3.
Wins the exchange and loses the game.
The knight in the corner is lost. White will have two pieces for a rook and pawn, with the centre.

By far the most common move, and Lane's recommendation. After 6...Bb4 7.Bd2 the bishop has taken two moves to reach b4, but White's centre is under pressure from ...c5 and ...Bg4. Goeller thinks only Black can be better; this is the safest line he gives. In current practice Black more often plays 7...c5.

lines.name: 5.Nf3 Bg4 6.Qe2: the Kaufmann line
lines.summary: The pin invites two famous traps, Euwe-Yates and Spielmann-Flamberg. If Black avoids them with 6...Nxc3, White castles long with a pleasant game.

next.text: Natural, and a favourite at club level.
Arthur Kaufmann's move. Black has to decide about the e4 knight at once, and with the bishop gone from c8 the check on b5 picks up b7 in several lines.
The only move that keeps the balance.
7.bxc3 is playable too (Tholfsen-Torre 1925), but the d-pawn is consistent: Bf4 and O-O-O.
Discouraging O-O-O by looking at a2.
Asks the bishop where it is going before White commits his king.
Norwood's move in the model game. It hits f4 and stops c4, but it costs a tempo and White simply improves the bishop.
Torre's idea. The bishop keeps Black's king in the centre (no ...O-O-O, no ...Be7) and supports e5-e6.
The most solid reply according to Goeller.
Slightly better for White (Goeller): two bishops, and a black king that has to live on d7.
With h3 and Bb5 to come. Mallahi-Quintero, Yerevan 1999, was clearly better for White once the pin was broken and c4 was played.
The common error: it develops and seems to defend everything.

The quiet retreat that is easy to miss: Euwe-Yates, The Hague 1921. The bishop on f3 and the knight on d4 are both attacked and Black loses a piece. In the 1925 theme tournament Smirka played 9.gxf3 and Torre escaped.
White is a clean pawn up.
Keeps the knight but loses time.
Two pawns down, with every piece out and the black queen in the firing line.
The d-file is opened by force.
Spielmann-Flamberg, Mannheim 1914: 15...Qxf3 16.Re1+ and mate follows. Black should prefer 8...Ne6 9.Be3, when White is only much better.
Goeller thinks 7.h4 may be stronger still.
Barle-Pavasovic, Ljubljana 1994: a slightly better ending thanks to the centre and the open g-file.

lines.name: 5.Nf3 Nc6 6.Bb5, and 5...Bb4
lines.summary: Against the knight move White pins first and then plays Qe2; the knight is chased to e6 and White keeps a small plus. 5...Bb4 6.Qe2 can end in a queen sacrifice.

next.text: Development with an eye on e5.
The pin comes first: it secures e5 and makes ...Bc5 less effective. The immediate 6.Qe2 Bf5 gave White nothing in Berg-Spassky, Bundesliga 1987.
Yegiazarian-Estrada Nieto, Linares 1999: slightly better for White. Black has the bishops but no pawn break, while White can play c4 against d5 and use the f-file.
Bangiev's sharper recommendation: 10...h6 11.O-O-O Nb4 12.Qd2 c6 13.Be2 Re8 14.g4 with the initiative. The choice when a win is needed.
The familiar set-up. The break 9...f6 fails to 10.O-O-O fxe5 11.Rxd5!.
Turner-Motwani, British Championship 1994. White has the centre and castles long.
The most common move in practice.
Removing the bishop that presses on d4.
White has castled and ...Bxc3 only strengthens his centre.
Pinning the knight that attacks e4.
Once more. After the exchange on c3 the d-pawn recaptures and the bishop pair is White's.
The thematic break fails tactically here.
A queen sacrifice that Spielmann missed against Cohn in 1908 (he took on e5 and won anyway).
Nf7+ is threatened and Black cannot meet it properly; Goeller gives the position as winning.
Slightly better for White (Goeller): after 10...Qb6 11.Qe1 the knight on e4 is short of squares.

lines.name: 5.d3 Nxc3 6.bxc3 d4: the Oxford Variation
lines.summary: The direct challenge to the knight. Black's accurate 6...d4 stops White's centre and equalises; the variation is worth playing mainly for the two traps in the next lines.

next.text:
The most direct move: the knight must be exchanged, and White gets bxc3 and d3-d4 if he is allowed to. It also invites 5...Qh4+ and 5...Bb4, which look crushing and are not (the next two lines).

**The drawback:** the solid reply in this line equalises without risk, and 5...Bb4 can force a draw. Goeller is blunt that 5.d3 'cannot be White's best'. Use it as a surprise weapon against opponents who are likely to go for the check.
The key move, and one many opponents do not know. If White gets d3-d4 he has the chain c3-d4-e5 and a free attack; so Black puts his own pawn there, fixes d3 and attacks c3.
White ignores c3 and gets castled; the pawn on d4 is the one he wants to remove.
In practice 8...Bc5, keeping the pawn on d4, is played as often.
The centre is built after all, at the cost of a pawn.

Bronstein-Malaniuk, Hastings 1996.

**Verdict:** equal. White has the centre and the f-file for the pawn on c3, which is going nowhere; Black has a superb knight on d5 and no weaknesses.
The old main line simply liquidates, and the game is level and simplified.
Not 10.Ng5 Nxe5, as in Seret-Spassky, Angers 1990.
Equal.
What White is hoping for: Bd3, O-O and a kingside attack in the style of the French Advance, with the f-file thrown in.

lines.name: 5.d3 Bb4: the king walk to e3
lines.summary: Black sacrifices the knight for a check on h4. White's king marches to e3, and with exact play the game ends in a repetition.

next.text: Leaves the knight to be taken on purpose: the pin on c3 and the check on h4 are the compensation.
The only move.
The queen comes out with tempo against e4 and supports the king's walk.
Keeps the pin and makes room for ...Qg4.
The king steps out of the pin and attacks e4 itself. On 11.Kd2 Black has 11...Qg4.

Drawn by repetition, Nunn-Speelman, London 1980. Makarychev-Razuvaev, USSR Championship 1979, ended the same way after 11...exf3 12.gxf3 Qe1+ 13.Kf4.

**Verdict:** a draw whenever Black wants one, which Goeller counts as good evidence that 5.d3 is not White's most ambitious move.
The usual attempt to avoid the draw. After 12...c6 13.gxf3 the play is very sharp and theory has never given a clear verdict; only for those who have prepared it.
Blocks the check and loses a rook.
The c3 knight is pinned and cannot take the queen, so h1 falls.

lines.name: 5.d3 Qh4+: the Würzburger Trap
lines.summary: The check that 5.d3 invites. White gives up the h1 rook, wins it back on a8 and comes out on top; the famous finish with a trapped bishop on c2 is one version.

next.text: The move every opponent sees first, and the only real reason to play 5.d3.
Developing with tempo on the queen. The knight cannot be taken (7.hxg3 Qxh1), so White lets it take the rook and counts on what the c3 knight does next.
The point. Nxc7+ and Nf4 are both threatened, and Black cannot meet both and save the knight on g3.
The best practical try: a pin against the pin.
The recommendation of the Encyclopaedia, giving White the better game. The rook is defended, the pin on f3 is broken and both Nf4 and Nxc7+ are still in the air.
The move that gave the trap its name. If Black takes on c2 at the end, 12.b3 shuts the bishop in and Kd2 or Rh2 collects it. It works only if Black is greedy, which is why 9.Bg2 is preferred.
Taking the rook.
White collects the h1 knight as well and is winning (Dobosz-Ganev 1971).
Covers c7.
A discovered attack on the queen, and the g3 knight is lost.

lines.name: 3...exf4: the gambit accepted
lines.summary: The most common reply below master level, and simply bad: 4.e5 sends the knight home and White has a King's Gambit with two extra moves.

next.text: In the King's Gambit proper this is the main line. Here the knight on f6 turns it into a mistake.
The knight has no square: e4 and d5 are covered by the c3 knight, g4 and h5 by the queen.
Stops ...Qh4+, the only thing Black had gained. Compared with 1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3, White has e5 and Nc3 for nothing (Illingworth).
The pin on the e-file wins the pawn back with a lead in development, and is stronger than recapturing at once.
The knight is pinned, so the queen stays where it is.

White has regained both pawns, leads in development and has g7 and c7 to aim at.

**Verdict:** clearly better for White, which is Illingworth's judgement of the whole 3...exf4 line.
White has his pawn back and the better development; the queen exchange does not help Black.
The f4 pawn falls and Black's kingside is full of holes. Goeller gives 8...f3 9.gxf3 Be7 10.Bg5 as slightly better for White.
The pin is the only other try, and it fails to a pin in return.
Nd5 is coming with tempo on the queen.
The typical finish.
Discovered check, and the queen is lost.

lines.name: 3...d6: the solid decline
lines.summary: Black props up e5 and reaches a King's Gambit Declined without the active bishop on c5. White develops with Nf3 and Bb5 and keeps the tension.

next.text: The only sound alternative to 3...d5, but a passive one: the f8 bishop is shut in and White is not forced to do anything. Illingworth calls it too passive.
Keep the tension. Taking on e5 would free Black's game; as it is he has to worry about fxe5 and about d4 on every move.
The pressure on e5 becomes real: Bxc6 followed by fxe5 is a threat.

The usual continuation. White castles next and the f-file opens when he chooses.

**Verdict:** a small, risk-free advantage for White: more space, the f-file, and a black position with no active plan.
Again the centre is White's, and the f4 pawn will be collected by the bishop.
Giving up the centre.
The full centre and the f-file for nothing. White scores close to sixty per cent from here in elite games.
The Hanham set-up.
A Philidor in which White has already played f4.
The bishop pair and a lead in development. If the bishop retreats to h5 instead, g4 gains more time.

lines.name: 3...Nc6: both knights are driven back
lines.summary: Developing instead of fighting for the centre. After 4.fxe5 Nxe5 5.d4 and 6.e5 both black knights go home and White has a huge lead.

next.text: Natural, and already a serious mistake: the knight will be hit by the d-pawn and its colleague by the e-pawn.
Not 7.Bc4 at once because of 7...Nxe5!, when 8.dxe5 Qh4+ wins the bishop back.
White does not recapture. The target is f7, and Ng5 comes next with a strong attack (Goeller) against a king that is three moves from castling.
White is fully developed in three more moves, and Black has not started.
Clearly better for White. Hromadka-Jonet, Paris 1924, continued 8...Bb4 9.O-O Bg4 10.Ne2 and the kingside attack decided quickly.

lines.name: 3...Bb4 and 3...Bd6
lines.summary: Pinning the knight lets White take on e5 and recapture on c3 with the d-pawn, after which Qg4 wins material. 3...Bd6 loses a piece at once.

next.text: The pin does not stop fxe5, and the bishop will have to be given for the knight.
The d-pawn again, this time to open the queen's way to g4. After 5.exf6 or 5.bxc3 White is only slightly better.
A double attack on e4 and g7.
Not 8.g3, when 8...Qe4+ picks up the rook. On d1 the king is safe and h1 stays defended.
Deflects the queen. After the exchange on h5 the g7 knight is attacked by the bishop and cannot be held: if it moves the f8 rook falls, and ...Rg8 is met by Rg1.
Winning for White according to Goeller, who gives this as an improvement on Kornin-Frota, Fortaleza 1979: a pawn up with the bishops, and the g7 knight and f8 rook are both in trouble.
Defends e5 with a piece that is then forked.
Bishop and knight are attacked and one of them goes.

chapters.title: Vienna: 2...Nc6, 2...Bc5 and rare replies
chapters.subtitle: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3
chapters.intro:
This chapter covers everything Black can play on move two except 2...Nf6, which has its own chapters. The weight is on 2...Nc6, the most popular reply and a straight copy of White's move. Against it the main line is 3.Bc4: it keeps one set of ideas for both 2...Nc6 and 2...Nf6, because the natural 3...Nf6 transposes into the sibling chapter on 3.Bc4, and every other third move runs into a queen raid on g4 or a quick f-pawn break. The Vienna Gambit 3.f4 is the second weapon, with its own lines for 3...exf4 and for the three ways of declining.

Against 2...Bc5 the main line is 3.f4 d6 4.Nf3, with the bishop pair won by Na4, and 3.Na4 is the quiet alternative. Against 2...Bb4 the main line is the direct 3.d4. The remaining second moves (2...d6, 2...f5, 2...g6, 2...c6) all fail to develop a piece, and White's answer is the same each time: strike with d4, take on d4 with the queen and pick up the tactics that follow.

The chapter is built from popular Lichess studies, mainly anomality's "Vienna Repertoire" and the studies by Bosburp, Chessmate_0204 and ST123_stsoham_Chess listed below. They disagree in places, for example on 2...Bc5 and 2...Bb4, and the notes say where. The studies stop where the plans take over, and the notes say so where a line is left without a verdict.

sections.title: The map: two roads against 2...Nc6
sections.body:
White has two good third moves and the choice is between a safer and a sharper game.

- **3.Bc4** aims at f7 and keeps the g1 knight at home so that the queen can reach g4 at once. Black's sensible answers are 3...Nf6 (transposes to the sibling chapter), 3...Bc5 4.Qg4, and the quiet 3...d6 4.a3 and 3...h6.
- **3.f4** is the Vienna Gambit against the copycat knight. After 3...exf4 4.Nf3 White gets a pawn centre with d4 and the pawn comes back with Bxf4. The three ways of declining (3...d6, 3...Nf6, 3...Bc5) are all covered.

Note that the stock reply to 3.Bc4, 3...Nf6, is not part of this chapter. Everything that follows 3...Nf6 4.d3 is in the sibling chapter "Vienna with 3.Bc4".

sections.title: The copycat 3...Bc5 and the Qg4 raid
sections.body:
Black copies White and puts the bishop on c5, but a bishop that leaves f8 stops guarding g7. The queen goes to g4 straight away and the pawn is attacked together with the rook on h8. This is why the knight stays on g1: Nf3 would sit on the queen's diagonal and spoil the idea.

Black has four tries and White has an answer ready for each.

- **4...g6** defends the pawn with a pawn and gives up the dark squares. White retreats 5.Qf3, threatening mate on f7, and builds Nge2, d3 and Qg3.
- **4...Kf8** keeps the pawn with the king and gives up castling. The plans are the same as against ...g6; the studies point to it as Black's best try.
- **4...Qf6** defends g7 and attacks f2, but 5.Nd5 gives the pawn for an attack: after 5...Qxf2+ 6.Kd1 the black queen is nearly trapped.
- **4...Nd4** takes the initiative, but 5.Qxg7 ignores the fork: if Black takes on c2, Qxf7 is mate.

The quiet 4.Nf3 is possible and equal. The point of 3.Bc4 is to play for more than that.

sections.title: The set-up against ...g6: Qf3, Nge2, d3
sections.body:
Once the queen is on f3 the pieces have fixed jobs.

- **The queen on f3** pins down f7 with the bishop, which forces Black to block with ...Nf6 at once. 5...Nd4 loses to Qxf7#.
- **The knight goes to e2, not f3.** From e2 it covers d4, so that ...Nd4 (which attacks the queen and c2) can be met by Nxd4, and it can go to g3 later. The pawn on d3 then frees the c1 bishop.
- **The bishop and the queen on the dark squares.** After ...Bg4 the queen steps to g3, from where Bg5, Qh4 and Nd5 pile up on the f6 knight. Black has holes on f6 and h6 and no safe home for the king: short castling walks into the dark-square weaknesses, long castling is stopped by the queen on h4 looking at d8.
- **Bosburp's move order** plays 7.h3 first to stop ...Bg4 and ...Ng4. After 7...Be6 8.d3 the capture ...Bxc4? loses to Bg5.

sections.title: The f2 pawn: sacrifices and king walks
sections.body:
The Qg4 lines are full of the same few tactics, and it is worth knowing them as patterns.

- **Qxf7 mate.** Queen and bishop both attack f7 and the king is the only defender. Any move that neither blocks the f-file nor defends f7 (...Nd4, ...Nge7) loses at once.
- **The poisoned f2 pawn.** After 4...Qf6 5.Nd5 Qxf2+ 6.Kd1 White has two threats, Qxg7 and Nxc7+, and Black has one move that deals with both: ...Kf8. Every other reply loses material. If Black plays 6...g6, Nh3 traps the queen on d4.
- **The ignored fork.** After 4...Nd4 White takes g7 and does not mind ...Nxc2+, because Qxf7 is mate. Queen and bishop beat a fork.
- **The king on d1.** The walk ...Qxf2+ Kd1 looks frightening, but Black's queen is alone and short of squares, and White's threats (Qxg7, Nxc7+) come first.

sections.title: The Vienna Gambit against 2...Nc6
sections.body:
With 3.f4 White sacrifices a pawn for the centre, as in the King's Gambit but with the knight on c3 already.

- **4.Nf3** is the point: the knight stops ...Qh4+ and prepares d4. Black can only keep the pawn with ...g5.
- **5.d4 Bb4 6.Bd3** is the main structure. The bishop guards e4 so that the pin on c3 does nothing, Bxf4 regains the pawn with a gain of time, and White castles. Black's natural castling is a mistake because White simply plays Bxf4, O-O and answers ...Nxe4 with d5.
- **The pawn recapture on c3 is bxc3** after ...Bxc3+: the chain c3-d4-e4 stays solid and the b-file opens for the rook.
- **4...g5 5.Bc4 g4 6.O-O** is the speculative branch. White gives the knight on f3 for a Muzio-type attack on f4 and f7. It is playable and the study shows strong attacking ideas, but it is the least tested line in the chapter, and the same studies warn that the knight on f3 is in danger after ...g5.
- **4...d6, 4...Bb4 and 4...Bc5** are all met by 5.d4: the centre first, the pawn back with Bxf4, and an attack on the queen side or on the g-file.

sections.title: When Black declines the gambit
sections.body:
Over half the players at club level decline the pawn, and each of the three ways has a plan.

- **3...d6 4.Nf3 Bg4 5.Bb5.** The bishops pin each other's knights. Black plays ...a6, and after 6.Bxc6+ bxc6 7.fxe5 dxe5 8.h3 and recaptures on f3 with the queen. Black's pawns on c6, c7 and e5 are loose, and White has the f-file, d3 and the plan of long castling.
- **3...Nf6 4.fxe5 Nxe5 5.d4.** The Corell Variation. The knights are driven back by d4 and e5, and Black must find 7...d5! after 6.e5 Ng8 7.Nf3. Everything else loses a pawn or worse: 7...d6? 8.Bb5, 7...Bb4? 8.d5. The same position arises from 2...Nf6 3.f4 Nc6.
- **3...Bc5 4.Nf3 d6 5.Na4.** The Quelle Variation. The knight takes the bishop pair, the bishop on b5 cannot be kicked after Nxb6 axb6 because the a-pawn is no longer on a6, and f5 gains space.

sections.title: 2...Bc5: the bishop pair and the f-pawn
sections.body:
With the bishop on c5 the f-pawn needs support. The bishop eyes f2 and g1, so 3.f4 is only safe if White covers g1 and h4 at once with 4.Nf3 and is ready to castle quickly. Two of the larger studies recommend 3.f4 here, and the biggest (anomality) gives it as the accepted Jeanisch Gambit next to its main chapter on 3.Na4.

- **Na4 for the bishop pair.** With no knight on c6 Black has no ...Nd4 resource, so White can spend time on Na4 and Nxb6, which gives him the bishop pair and doubles Black's b-pawns. This is the same idea as in the Quelle line of 2...Nc6.
- **f5.** The pawn blocks the c8-h3 diagonal, cages a bishop on c8 and prepares Bg5 and Qh5 or Qh3.
- **The king-side attack.** With the bishop pair and the pawns on f5 and e4, the plan is h3 (forcing the bishop to decide), Bxf3, Qxf3, Bg5, Qh3 or Qh4, and a rook lift Rf3-h3.
- **3.Na4** is the quiet alternative: the knight attacks the bishop at once, and after 3...Bb6 4.Nxb6 axb6 5.d4 the bishop pair and the structure are White's, with no risk.

sections.title: 2...Bb4: the quick centre
sections.body:
After 2...Bb4 White gives up no time and takes the centre with 3.d4. After ...Bxc3+ and bxc3 White has the bishop pair and the pawn centre, and the plan is plain: Bd3, Ne2, O-O and c3, then a4, Ba3 and f4 with the pieces aimed at the king side. The b-file is half open and Rab1 limits the black bishop.

- **3...exd4 4.Qxd4** Bxc3+ 5.Qxc3 Nf6 6.Be3: the e4 pawn is not hanging, because ...Nxe4 runs into Qxg7.
- **3...Nc6 4.dxe5 Nxe5 5.Qd4:** the queen forces ...Bxc3+ and after the right recapture after 7.Nf3 Nxf3+ is 8.gxf3 (not Qxf3), which opens the g-file.
- **3.f4!?** is a trap line (...Bxc3 bxc3 exf4 Qg4 Qf6 Ne2 g5? h4 wins). It is not the main line.

A warning. The app's book of elite games contains 133 games from this position and not one continues with 3.d4: they play 3.Bc4, 3.Nd5 (the Nikolic Variation, the main line of anomality's study), 3.Nf3 and 3.Nge2. The move comes from one study with 519 likes and a sideline of another, so it is the least tested choice in this chapter.

sections.title: Rare second moves: strike with d4
sections.body:
Moves like 2...d6, 2...g6 and 2...c6 do not develop a piece, and the answer is always the same: 3.d4. Black either takes (3...exd4 4.Qxd4) and the queen develops with tempo, or he holds with ...d5 and loses the right to castle after the queen trade.

- **2...d6 3.d4** is the Cenni Variation: Qxd4, Qd3, Be3 and f4. The sharper 3.f4 exf4 4.Qf3 (the Omaha Gambit) is a second option, and 4...g5? 5.h4 f6? 6.Qh5+ wins material.
- **2...f5** is a Latvian Gambit without the f3 knight: 3.exf5 Nf6 4.g4 d5 5.g5 Ne4 6.Qh5+ Ke7 7.f6+ wins material.
- **2...g6 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4** attacks g7, and 4...Qf6 5.Qxf6 Nxf6 6.e5 Ng4 7.Nd5 wins material in the study's line. The study does not cover 4...Nc6.
- **2...c6 3.d4 d5 4.dxe5 dxe4 5.Qxd8+ Kxd8 6.Bg5+** leaves Black without castling and a pawn down. After 3...exd4 4.Qxd4 Nf6 5.e5 White wins time on the knight.
- **Typical tactics:** a knight jump to d5, e4 or d6 forking king and rook, a bishop on g5 that pins the queen to the king, and smothered mate on e8 after Nd6.

sections.title: Sources
sections.body:
- anomality, "Vienna Repertoire" (Lichess study), https://lichess.org/study/ePMOV5k4, 4132 likes (the copycat lines 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Qg4, the 3...d6 4.a3 and 3...h6 chapters, 2...Bc5 3.Na4, the Burden, Cenni, Omaha and Nikolic variations)
- Bosburp, "CRUSH with the Vienna!" (Lichess study), https://lichess.org/study/nq1GGbNO, 1208 likes (the copycat 4...g6 and 4...Qf6 lines, and the lines against 2...f5, 2...g6, 2...c6, 2...Bb4 and 2...Bc5 3.f4)
- Chessmate_0204, "Vince With The Vienna Gambit! | Part 1: Crush The Copycat Move 2...Nc6" (Lichess study), https://lichess.org/study/2jzZEwlz, 538 likes (all of 3.f4 against 2...Nc6, accepted and declined)
- ST123_stsoham_Chess, "WIN with 1. e4 | The Vienna Game" (Lichess study), https://lichess.org/study/GsgWTTgK, 519 likes (3.Bc4 Bc5 4.Qg4, 2...Bc5 3.f4, 2...Bb4 3.d4)
- raeyment, "Vienna System" (Lichess study), https://lichess.org/study/UPHk9bvW, 2669 likes (the Copycat Variation, used as a cross-check)
- "Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4", Wikibooks (the map of the copycat line and the verdicts on 4.Qg4)
- The Lichess Elite Database (the app's own book of 2400+ games), used by the checker to see which moves are really played
- Not used: Phil224, "The Vienna Gambit Nc6" (Lichess study, 1199 likes) could not be loaded when this chapter was written (the site refused the request)

lines.name: 3...Bc5 4.Qg4 g6 5.Qf3: the copycat reply
lines.summary: Black copies White and puts the bishop on c5, leaving g7 undefended. 4.Qg4 hits it; after 4...g6 the queen retreats to f3 with the threat of Qxf7 and White builds Nge2, d3, Qg3 and Bg5 against a loosened king side.

next.text: The most popular reply, which simply copies White. White has two serious answers: 3.Bc4 (the main line of this chapter) and 3.f4, the Vienna Gambit proper, which gets its own lines further on. The choice of 3.Bc4 is practical: it keeps one set of ideas for both 2...Nf6 and 2...Nc6, because the natural 3...Nf6 simply transposes into the sibling chapter on 3.Bc4, while every other third move allows a queen raid or a quick f4.

The bishop eyes f7, the one square that only the king guards while Black is uncastled. The g1 knight stays at home on purpose: Nf3 would sit on the d1-g4 diagonal and block the queen from reaching g4, and the knight is better placed on e2 anyway, where it does not stand in front of the f-pawn.
The copycat. The bishop eyes f2, but it has left f8 and with it the last defender of g7. That is the whole point of White's next move.

The point of the setup. The queen attacks g7 and with it the rook on h8, and Black has no way to keep both his pawn and his development in order. Every sensible reply weakens something: ...g6 loosens the dark squares, ...Kf8 gives up castling, ...Qf6 walks into a knight jump and ...Nd4 loses a tempo to a queen trade.
The solid-looking reply: the pawn move itself defends g7. What it costs is the dark squares: f6 and h6 are now permanent holes and the bishop on c5 no longer guards anything on that side.

The queen retreats with a mate threat: f7 is attacked twice and defended only by the king, so Qxf7# is on. Black must block the f-file or defend f7 at once, which gives White a free move to develop. Note that the queen now stands in the way of the g1 knight, which is another reason Ne2 is the right square for it.
Blocks the f-file.

Prevents ...Nd4. After 6...Nd4 White simply takes, and the knight on e2 also keeps c2 safe, which matters because ...Nd4 would otherwise fork the queen and attack c2. The knight can later go to g3, from where it supports the pressure on the king side.
Opens the diagonal for the c1 bishop. Bg5 pins the f6 knight against the queen and Black's king side has no pieces to answer it.
Attacks the queen and prepares ...Qd7 and long castling.

The queen steps out of the attack with tempo and keeps an eye on e5. If Black takes on e2, the knight recaptures and keeps d4 covered. The threat now is Bg5, Qh4 and Nd5 winning the pinned knight, so Black has to spend moves on it.

Pins the knight again and stops long castling: if the knight ever leaves f6, the queen looks straight at d8. Short castling means putting the king on a weakened g-file, so Black's king has no good home. Next come Bd2, O-O-O and f4, with the usual Vienna attack on a king that has not found a place.

**Verdict:** White is clearly the one with the easier game here. The line is a model for the dark-square weaknesses after ...g6; the practical risk for White is small as long as the queen is not trapped by ...h5-h4 or ...Nd4.
Bosburp's preference: h3 takes g4 away from the bishop and the knight in advance, so that the queen never has to leave f3.
Not 8.Bxe6, which hands Black the half-open f-file after ...fxe6.
The most popular reply and a blunder.
The knight on f6 is attacked twice and defended once.
White comes out a full rook up.
The knight attacks the queen but unblocks the f-file. A very common mistake in this line.
Stopping Qxf7 by offering a queen trade, but White does not have to accept it passively.
The knight hits the queen and c7 at once.
The exchange has not removed the problems: Nxc7+ is threatened and the pawn on g6 leaves f6 and h6 weak.
Black's structure is wrecked: pawns on b6, b7, d4 and d7 are all weak and f7 is under the bishop's eye. White's task in the ending is to collect them.

The studies single this out as Black's most accurate reply: the king guards g7 and Black gives up castling. They treat the plans against ...g6 and ...Kf8 as the same, because the queen goes back to f3 in each case.
Mate threat on f7, again. 5...Nd4 would lose at once to Qxf7#.

The same set-up as in the main line. The h-pawn is stopped: ...h4 would have chased the queen off g3. Black has no castling rights and a bishop that is shut out of the kingside by its own pawns, while White plays Bg5 or Nd5, then Bd2 and O-O-O.

The quiet alternative. It is perfectly playable and gives an Italian-style game, but Black equalises without difficulty: 4...Nf6 5.d3 d6 6.Bg5 h6 is the standard picture, and the Vienna sting is gone. Qg4 is the reason to put the bishop on c4 and keep the knight on g1.
Level.
By far Black's soundest and most common reply. After 4.d3 we are in the sibling chapter "Vienna with 3.Bc4", so the lines stop here.

lines.name: 4.Qg4 Qf6?! 5.Nd5: the poisoned f2 pawn
lines.summary: Black defends g7 with the queen and threatens f2. White offers the pawn: 5.Nd5 Qxf2+ 6.Kd1 and the king survives while the queen is nearly trapped and both g7 and c7 are loose.

next.text: The most natural-looking defence: the queen guards g7 and adds to the pressure on f2 (bishop, queen) at once. It is the move that costs the most at club level, but it is not refuted by force: the Wikibooks table gives White only a slight edge here, so it is a trap, not a refutation.
A counter-sacrifice. The knight attacks the queen and the c7 pawn (a fork of king and rook is in the air after Nxc7+), and White does not care about f2.
The only move. The king is exposed, but White now threatens two things at once: Qxg7, attacking the rook on h8, and Nxc7+, forking king and rook on a8. Black has one move to meet both.
The only move that meets both threats: the king guards g7 and leaves the e-file, so that Nxc7 is no longer check.
The knight comes to the f2 square, attacking the queen and giving the rook the f-file.
Attacks the queen.
The queen goes to g5, from where it attacks h5 and covers e7 and d8.
The only safe square.
The queen on d4 is short of squares: c3 or Be3 will harass her.
The bishop attacks the queen on g5 and gives the black queen the c5 square.

The queen retreats and again looks at g7 and e5. The Vienna System study continues 10...b5 or 10...Nf6 11.c3, when the black queen is short of room.

**Verdict:** White has the initiative in return for one pawn, and the black king is stuck on f8. The Wikibooks table marks this as a slight advantage (+/=), which is the fair summary: a good line to play against a player who will walk into 5...Qxf2+ without knowing the follow-up, but not a forced win.
Loses the queen's retreat: she gets trapped on d4.
The knight hits the queen and f2 is covered twice, so the queen has one square left: d4.
The queen is almost trapped: c3 and Be3 are coming.
White wins the rook on a8 and comes out well ahead.
Defends neither g7 nor c7.
Takes g7 with an attack on the rook h8, and the fork on c7 is still on the board. Black cannot meet both threats.
White has won g7 back for the f2 pawn and the rook on h8 is still attacked.
Develops, but g7 is simply lost.
The knight on f6 is attacked and the rook is hit.
White has won the rook for a knight and the queen on h8 attacks the bishop, though it is far from its own king.

lines.name: 4.Qg4 Nd4 5.Qxg7: the queen trade
lines.summary: Black attacks c2 with the knight. White ignores the fork and takes g7, because Qxf7 is mate; after 5...Qf6 the queens come off and White is a pawn up in an open position.

next.text: Black counter-attacks: the knight eyes c2 and f3. A natural idea, since Nxc2+ would fork king and rook.
Ignores the threat. The queen attacks the rook on h8 and, with the bishop on c4, the f7 pawn. If Black takes on c2 now, Qxf7# is mate.
Black has to defend f7 and meet the threat on h8 with one move; the queen trade does both.
The bishop guards c2 against the fork. White is a pawn up and has to consolidate.
The rook uses the open g-file at once; Black's compensation is activity and the g2 pawn.
Closes the file.
The knight heads for d4, where it can swap the strongest black piece, and c3 can follow.

With the strong knight gone, White has a pawn more, a solid position and a bishop on d3 against a bishop on d4 that still hits b2 and f2.

**Verdict:** White is a pawn up and has the easier game, but Black has the g-file and the bishop pair for a while, so the extra pawn must be converted with care. The studies stop at this point.
The other way to meet ...Nxc2+: trade the bishop for the knight.
The structure is a little worse, and the bishop pair is gone, but the a-file is open. Bd3 is more natural because it keeps the bishop.
Black has no time to take the rook.

lines.name: 3...d6 4.a3: a quiet set-up
lines.summary: After the passive 3...d6 White takes b4 away from Black's pieces and keeps the bishop with Ba2, then d3 and f4 in the Vienna manner.

next.text: A cautious reply that does not threaten anything. Black avoids the Qg4 idea, but he has given up the chance to develop the bishop actively and the c8 bishop is now free to be exchanged on c4 or e6.

A prophylactic move that sounds slow and has three jobs: it stops ...Nb4 and ...Bb4 with a pin or an attack on c2, it gives the bishop the a2 square if Black plays ...Na5, and it prepares b4 for a queen-side advance.
The most natural development.
The central pawn structure for the Vienna: d3, e4 and f4 later. White has the plan Nf3, Be3 and a break with f4 or d4.
The most active reply: the knight uses d4 before White can control it.
Challenges the knight at once and keeps the bishop on c4.
The queen recaptures, not the knight: the c3 knight stays on its good square and the queen supports e4 and the coming f-pawn break.
With the knights traded the f-pawn can challenge e5 at once; the queen on e2 backs the advance and the f-file opens for White's rooks.
The queen steps out of the attack onto the open f-file, with the bishop on c4 behind her.
With ...c5 played, no black pawn watches d5 any more and the knight takes the outpost.

The bishop on d5 hits the rook on a8; White has the more active pieces and the f-file.

**Verdict:** roughly level, but with the easier plans for White. The studies end here; the position is typical for the 3...d6 line: White uses the f-pawn and the central squares, while Black's pieces are passive.
A typical structure for the Bxc4 lines: White has a half-open d-file and the bishop pair is gone. The knight on a5 is badly placed, and c4 is weak but defended.
The bishop keeps the diagonal; without a3 White would have to trade on a5.

A fully playable second choice: after 4...Nf6 5.f4 we reach the structure of the sibling chapter on 3.Bc4 by transposition, so one may prefer it if one wants to avoid learning anything new against 3...d6.

lines.name: 3...h6 4.d3: a waiting move
lines.summary: 3...h6 prepares to meet Qg4 with ...Qf6, but the queen goes to g3 and a messy fight on the queen-side follows.

next.text: Black prepares the copycat set-up without the g7 weakness: if the bishop goes to c5, ...Qf6 or ...g5 follows. The move is a slight loss of time.
Prepares Be3 and avoids the knight jump to d4 for a while.
The same idea as in the main line, only now g7 is undefended even without the bishop leaving f8.
Defends g7 and eyes f2.
The queen steps out of the way, still attacking g7 and e5. The sacrifice 6.Nd5 Qxf2+ is not the same trick as in the 4...Qf6 line, and the study avoids it.
Counter-attacks: the knight eyes c7 and d4 and ignores the fork on c2.

A mutual rook swap: both kings are exposed and both sides have a knight on the edge, the one on a1 and the one on a8. The line is a coin-flip melee and I would only enter it with preparation.

**Verdict:** unclear. The study shows how rich the position is but does not give a clear assessment; the safer course against 3...h6 is the plain development with Nf3 or Nge2, d3 and Be3, keeping the Qg4 idea in reserve.
A calm position in which White has the half-open f-file and a firm centre.
A tactical line in which White comes out ahead: the rook on h8 falls.

lines.name: 3.f4 exf4 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.d4: the Fozo Defence
lines.summary: The Vienna Gambit against the copycat knight. After 4.Nf3 and 5.d4 White owns the centre and recovers the f4 pawn with Bxf4 and a lead in development.

next.text: The Vienna Gambit against 2...Nc6, the second weapon of this chapter. It is a King's Gambit with the knight already on c3: White builds a pawn centre and opens the f-file, and the f4 pawn is a loan that is nearly always repaid by Bxf4. Compared with 3.Bc4 it is more direct and demands more precise knowledge of the lines.
Black takes. In practice most players decline, with ...d6, ...Nf6 or ...Bc5 (see the next file).
The knight stops ...Qh4+ before it starts and prepares d4. Black can now keep the pawn only at the price of ...g5, or develop and let White take it back.
The Fozo Defence, by far Black's most common reply. It hits e4 and invites ...Bb4.
White takes the whole centre: pawns on d4 and e4 control c5, e5, d5 and f5, and the f4 pawn will be recovered by Bxf4 with a gain of time.
Pins the knight, so that ...Nxe4 is a threat.
A second guard for e4. The study rates 6.Qe2 and 6.Bxf4 as mistakes and 6.Qd3 as inferior.
The study's verdict is that castling here is an error, because White recovers the pawn with gain of time.
The bishop returns with an attack on c7 and the f-pawn is back.
Not a defence of e4 but an invitation to take it: White completes development and the capture on e4 turns out to cost Black more than it wins.
Takes the bait.
A double attack: d5 attacks the knight on c6 and the bishop on d3 attacks the knight on e4, so Black cannot save both.

The queen attacks the c3 knight and the pawn on d5 attacks c6. If Black takes on d5, Bxh7+ wins another piece.

**Verdict:** a clear edge for White according to the study. Black's mistake was to castle before the centre was settled, so the lesson is to meet the pin with Bd3, regain the pawn and keep the lead in development.
Gives up the centre pawn for a flank pawn.
The e4 pawn falls, because the c3 knight is pinned and cannot help.
Strikes at once in the centre.
Do not trade on d5: the pawn thrust kicks the knight and the e5 pawn cramps Black.
Pins the knight, but the bishop has left c8 and b7 is loose.
The knight on c6 is pinned, White has the centre and the open b-file, and the pawn structure on c3 gives no target.
Passive.
The knight is driven back at once.
The queen guards the bishop on f4 against the pin and prepares Rae1 or Rf1. White has more space and a firm centre.

The Steinitz Gambit, 4...Qh4+ 5.Ke2, is a real alternative, but it leaves the king in the middle and none of the studies used for this chapter recommend it. 4.Nf3 gets the same centre without the check.

lines.name: 3.f4 exf4 4.Nf3 g5 5.Bc4: the Muzio structure
lines.summary: Black holds the f4 pawn with ...g5 and ...g4. White castles into a Muzio-style attack, a risky gambit of a knight for the f-file and the f7 square.

next.text: Black clings to the pawn. It is the most testing reply and it makes 4.Nf3 a real decision: the knight will be attacked after ...g4 and cannot retreat without handing Black the initiative. The Vienna System study calls the line problematic for exactly this reason and says the knight will probably have to be sacrificed.

The usual choice of the studies. The other classical route, the Hamppe-Allgaier with 5.h4 g4 6.Ng5, is a different gambit that none of the studies used for this chapter treat, so it is not given here. The bishop eyes f7 and White will castle at once.
Attacks the knight.
The same idea as in the Muzio Gambit of the King's Gambit: White does not move the attacked knight but castles. If Black takes on f3, the queen recaptures with a strong attack on f4 and f7.
The queen hits f4 and f7 (together with the bishop and the rook behind it), and White has a lead in development in return for a knight.
The best defence according to the study: an in-between check that prepares ...Qh4, defending f4 from the other side.
Black defends f4 and starts an attack of his own on h2.
Kicks the bishop and opens the c1 bishop.
The queen leaves the knight's attack and White threatens Rxf4 or Bxf4.
A counter-blow: the pawn goes forward and threatens ...Qxh2#.

The study continues 12.Rxf3!? Nxf3 13.Qxf3, a rook sacrifice with White's pieces aimed at f7 and d5.

**Verdict:** speculative. The study treats this as promising for White, but it is the least explored line of the chapter, with few games behind it, and White is a knight and a pawn down before the final sacrifice. If you do not want to gamble a knight on move 6, the whole 3.f4 branch is optional: 3.Bc4 is the main line of the chapter.
The most popular move and a mistake.
The knight hits the queen and c7.
The queen is attacked again and the fork on c7 follows.
Wins the rook on a8.

lines.name: 3.f4 exf4 4.Nf3 d6 5.d4: the Triscow Defence
lines.summary: Black develops quietly. White takes the centre, wins the f4 pawn back and gets the bishop pair with a half-open g-file.

next.text: The Triscow Defence. It prepares ...Bg4 and ...Nf6 without giving White a target, but it leaves the f4 pawn to its fate.
The centre again.
The pin is the usual idea.
The pawn is back and the bishop eyes c7.
Black gives the bishop for the knight to stop White's attack.

The recapture with the pawn. White gets the half-open g-file and keeps the centre. The study's plan is to castle long, put the king on b1 and push the h-pawn, with rooks on the g-file, e5 and d5 thrusts and Bd3 or Bh3 as needed.
Black counts on a check.
Blocks the check and attacks the queen.
The queen moves again but runs into a knight jump.
The knight attacks the queen again, with a fork on c7 in the air.

White has a strong knight on d5, a solid centre and the bishop pair, and the g-file is half-open for the rooks.

**Verdict:** a plus for White and an easy plan: O-O-O, Kb1, rooks to the g-file, h4-h5 and the central thrusts e5 or d5.
Also fine, but the pawn recapture gives White more play against g7.
Tries to keep the pawn, but the knight on c6 is loose.
The knight must move before the g5 pawn can be defended.
Black cannot reply 7...c6 because of dxc6.
The g5 pawn was left without a guard.
White has regained the pawn and has the better centre.

lines.name: 3.f4 exf4 4.Nf3 Bb4 5.d4
lines.summary: Black develops the bishop before taking back the centre. After 5.d4 Bxc3+ 6.bxc3 White has the centre and the open b-file, and the f4 pawn comes back.

next.text: The Westraller Variation, a bishop move that ignores the centre.
Always towards the centre: the chain c3-d4-e4 stays solid and the b-file is open for the rook.
Hits e4.
Defends e4 before ...Nxe4.
Taking on e4 at once is bad, and castling is the natural reply.
The right way to challenge White: the pawn hits e4.
Gains a tempo on the knight.
An annoying knight, but White has a resource.
Defends the pawn on c3 in advance, so that ...Nxc3 can be met by Qxc3, and keeps Bxf4 for later.
Not the best move, but the natural one.

The pawn is back. White's plans are Rb1 and c4 against the d5 pawn, with a4-a5 on the queen-side, and Nh4 to trade off the bishop on f5.

**Verdict:** a pleasant advantage for White in the study's view, with the more flexible pawn structure.
Strikes at once.
Looks like a blunder but it is not.
The black queen is pinned to the king, so she cannot take on f4.
White has the centre and the more active pieces.
Transposes to the 4...Bc5 line above.
The Gusten-Vignok Variation: the bishop is attacked at once by d4.
The bishop pins the knight and White threatens d5.
Takes g4 away.
The plan is an attack on the queen-side, where Black's pieces are.

lines.name: 3.f4 d6 4.Nf3 Bg4 5.Bb5: the Stington Variation
lines.summary: Black supports e5 with ...d6 and pins the knight. White pins back, takes on c6 to wreck the pawn structure, trades on e5 and gets the f-file and the better pawns.

next.text: The Stington Variation, the most common way of declining. The pawn on e5 is held, the c8 bishop is freed, and f4 has not been taken, so White's f-pawn has not yet been used.
Puts pressure on e5 and prepares Bb5.
The most natural developing move: it pins the knight, so that fxe5 dxe5 Nxe5 is not yet a threat.
Pins the knight in turn. Both pins are real, but White's is the more useful one: the c6 knight is the only guard of the e5 pawn and it is now tied to the king.
Asks the bishop what it intends.
The right moment to trade: after 6.Ba4 b5 the bishop is out of play, and 6.Bc4 runs into ...Nd4, which hits the queen and f3. Taking on c6 wrecks Black's pawns for good.
Exchanges the f-pawn for the d-pawn and opens the f-file.
Forces the bishop to decide.

The f-file is White's. The plan is Rf1 doubling against f7, d3 and Be3 or Bd2, then O-O-O, with a king-side attack against a pawn structure that has a weak c6, c7 and e5.

**Verdict:** a small but lasting edge for White: better pawns, the f-file and the more harmonious pieces.
Not Bxc6+: after ...Nxc6 the knight is improved and no longer pinned.
The a-file is open for White, the pawn structure is a little worse, but the queen on f2 and the pressure on f7 give White the better game.
A typical structure: Black's pawns on c6, c7 and e5 are loose and White has the f-file.
Stops the bishop being driven back and prepares fxe5 with a strong pawn chain. Bc4 would run into ...Nd4 with a fork.
The Knight Variation, nearly as common as 4...Bg4.
The same pin against the c6 knight.
A mistake; 8...Ng4!? is better, offering the pawn for activity.
The pawn is won and the knight moves to the queen-side.
White has the better hand: a centre, the open f-file and open lines for the bishop and queen against a damaged pawn structure.

lines.name: 3.f4 Nf6?! 4.fxe5 Nxe5 5.d4: the Corell Variation
lines.summary: Taking the pawn with the knight loses time: the knights are driven back by d4 and e5, and Black has to find 7...d5 to stay in the game.

next.text: The Corell Variation. The knight attacks e4, but after fxe5 it has no good square and White gains time on it.
The knight takes the pawn and centralises.
Kicks the knight at once while building the centre.
The knight retreats. Alternatively the other knight goes to g6.
Drives the other knight back too.
The only move that holds the balance: it attacks e5 and keeps the c8 bishop in play. 7...d6 and 7...Bb4 both fail, as the variations show.
Pins the c6 knight (d7 is empty) and adds a second attacker to d5. Black can answer with 8...Bd7, 8...a6, 8...Bg4, 8...Bb4 or 8...Be6; the study analyses 8...Bd7 and gives short lines for the others.
The main line of the study.
The bishop on d7 blocked the queen's defence of d5, so the pawn simply falls.
Keeps the pressure on d5 and avoids the exchange on c6.
White has more space in the centre and the e5 pawn cramps the black pieces.

The study stops here.

**Verdict:** a small space advantage for White, with the e5 pawn cramping Black. The study gives no clear verdict at this point and I would call it a pleasant but not decisive edge.
White comes out a bishop up.
White has the initiative against the king.
Ignores the centre.
Gains a tempo: the knight on c6 is attacked.
Supports e5 and attacks the bishop.
White is far ahead in development and space, and the b-file is open.
Defends e5 with a pawn, but it cannot hold.
Pins the knight; the d6 pawn cannot hold.
White wins the exchange and more.
Black's pieces are back where they started, with the knight on g6 misplaced.
Attacks the e5 pawn.
Ignores the pawn and aims at f7.
Ignores it again: a lead in development against an uncastled king is worth a pawn.
Takes the pawn and walks into the knight jump.
Threatens Nxf7 forking queen and rook.
A king hunt that ends in mate.

lines.name: 3.f4 Bc5 4.Nf3 d6 5.Na4: the Quelle Variation
lines.summary: Black puts the bishop on c5 and White chases it with Na4, gets the bishop pair, pins on b5 and then expands with f5.

next.text: The Quelle Variation. The bishop eyes f2 and g1, and White must not leave the king uncovered.
Puts pressure on e5 and covers g1, which neutralises the bishop's pressure for the time being.
Attacks the bishop and gets the bishop pair.
Keeps the bishop; 5...Bd4 and 5...Bb4 lose time.
Pins the knight on c6 (d7 is empty) and develops with an eye on the king.
The bishop pair is White's, and the a-pawn has left its file.
Builds a pawn chain and opens the bishop's diagonal. The bishop on b5 cannot be kicked: the a-pawn is no longer on the a-file.
Protects the knight.

Gains space on the king-side: the f5 pawn takes e6 and g6 from the black pieces, and there is an outpost for the dark-squared bishop on g5 or h6. White can castle soon.

**Verdict:** a small edge for White, with the bishop pair and the f-pawn thrust.
Also good, and it reaches the same position by another move order: taking at once and then playing Bb5 gives Black no additional options.
Gives up the bishop's retreat but grabs the pawn.
The pin against the c6 knight is what makes d4 possible.
Now ...Nxd4 runs into Bxd7+ and Nxd4, winning a piece, because the queen no longer has ...Qh4+ once it has recaptured on d7.

lines.name: 2...Bc5 3.f4 d6 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bc4: the main line
lines.summary: Black puts the bishop on c5 at once. White plays the Vienna Gambit anyway, covers g1 with Nf3 and, after 5.Bc4 O-O 6.d3 Bg4, takes the bishop pair with Na4 and plays for the king side.

next.text: Black develops the bishop before the knight, which keeps ...Nc6 in reserve and aims at f2 at once. White has several playable answers (3.Nf3, 3.Na4, 3.Qg4, 3.Bc4); the studies behind this chapter prefer 3.f4, with 3.Na4 as a second weapon, and 3.Bc4 Nc6 simply transposes to the copycat line 4.Qg4 of the first file.

The Vienna Gambit with Black's bishop on c5. The bishop eyes f2 and g1, so the move needs care: every line below starts with Nf3 to cover g1 and h4, and the king should be ready to castle quickly. The bishop is also exposed to a gain of time by d4 or Na4.
The solid reply: it supports e5 and does not take the pawn.
The knight covers h4 and g1 and attacks e5.
The flexible developing move.
The bishop develops with an eye on f7. After 5...Nc6 6.d3 the game transposes to the Vienna with 3.Bc4 (see the sibling chapter).
A solid pawn move that prepares Bg5 and Na4.
Pins the f3 knight.
Takes the bishop pair. With no knight on c6 Black has no ...Nd4 to worry about, so White can afford this knight move that costs time.

Black's pawn structure is a little worse (doubled b-pawns), and White has the natural plan: h3, forcing the bishop to decide, then Bxf3 and Qxf3; f5, Bg5 and the queen on h3 or h4, with Rf3-h3 as an attacking manoeuvre. Do not be afraid of pushing the pawns: the pieces that attack the king can return to defend.

**Verdict:** a pleasant game for White with the bishop pair and attacking chances, though not more than a small edge.
Cages the c8 bishop: the pawn blocks the diagonal c8-h3.
A complicated position in which the plan is Qf3 and Qg3, with Bg5 and Bf6 or Bh6 ideas.
Transposes to the Quelle Variation in the previous file, where the idea is explained.
Takes the pawn and hands White the whole centre. White plays Nf3 first, to prevent ...Qh4+, then d4 and Bxf4.
White has the centre and the lead in development. Grabbing the d4 pawn runs into a pin on the d-file.
Grabs a pawn that is not free.
Falls into the pin.
The queen on d8 is pinned by the rook and e5 attacks the knight.

lines.name: 2...Bc5 3.f4 exf4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Bc4 Nd4 6.Na4
lines.summary: Black takes the pawn and uses the c6 knight at once. White plays 5.Bc4 instead of 5.d4, because d4 allows ...Nxd4, and meets ...Nd4 with Na4 against the bishop.

next.text: The most natural way to defend: the knight eyes d4 in advance.
Not 5.d4: Black replies 5...Nxd4 6.Nxd4 Qh4+ and White's king is in trouble. After 5.Bc4 the plan is d3 and Bxf4, the same set-up as in the other 3.f4 lines.
Black takes the initiative: the knight eyes f3 and c2.
The knight hits the bishop on c5. White does not mind ...Nxf3+, because the queen recaptures and the bishop on c4 is aimed at f7.
Black takes the knight first.
The pawn on f4 is Black's extra pawn, but the bishop on c5 is hanging.
Black strikes in the centre, attacking the c4 bishop and giving the c5 bishop the d6 square.

Attacks the bishop; the knight on a4 attacks the bishop on c5.

**Verdict:** unclear and very sharp. The study stops here with both bishops attacked, and I have no published source for the best continuation, so this is a line to prepare before using it.
