The study stops here without a verdict: the queen on e7 recaptures on c5 and Black's king is still in the centre.

lines.name: 2...Bc5 3.Na4: the second weapon
lines.summary: The Hamppe-Meitner move: the knight asks the bishop to leave or be exchanged. After 3...Bb6 4.Nxb6 axb6 White has the bishop pair and an easy game.

next.text: The Hamppe-Meitner Variation. The knight looks misplaced on the rim, but it asks the bishop on c5, the piece that eyes f2, to leave or be exchanged.
The bishop retreats, but White exchanges it.
The a-pawn leaves the a-file and Black's pawns are doubled. White has the bishop pair.

**Verdict:** a quiet, risk-free edge for White: the bishop pair and a better pawn structure against a king that has lost the right to castle. The edge is small and the game is long.
White has the bishop pair.

The study calls this the Immortal Draw: Black gives the bishop for a perpetual check, and some masters play it when a draw has been agreed in advance. The study gives no further moves, so I do not analyse it.

lines.name: 2...Bb4 3.d4: the main answer
lines.summary: After 2...Bb4 White takes the centre at once. After ...Bxc3+ and bxc3 White has the bishop pair, a mass of central pawns and an easy attack.

next.text: Pins the c3 knight and threatens to double the pawns.
The principled reply: White takes the centre and lets Black give up the bishop pair.
The most natural reply.
Always towards the centre: the c3 pawn supports d4, the b-file is open for the rook, and the bishop on c1 can go to a3.
The plan is simple: Ne2, castle, c3.

White has the bishop pair and a strong centre. In this structure the plan is a4, Ba3 and f4, with an attack on the king side where all of White's pieces are aimed. Rab1 is also an option, to limit the development of Black's light-squared bishop.

**Verdict:** a pleasant advantage for White. The pawn centre is strong, the bishop pair gives long-term chances, and Black's position offers little counterplay.
There is no need to protect e4: after 6...Nxe4 7.Qxg7 White wins a pawn and attacks the rook on h8.
Breaks the pin and prepares long castling.
Black cannot castle and White has the better development.
The only move: Qxf3 loses the advantage. The pawn recapture opens the g-file for the rook, and White has the bishop pair.
A gambit given by one of the studies mainly as a trap: 3...Bxc3 4.bxc3 exf4 5.Qg4. It is not the main line.

The Nikolic Variation. It is the main line of the largest study behind this chapter and the second most played move in the elite games, so it deserves a mention, but the study offers only short lines and no verdict.
Each side has won a pawn and the position is open; the study stops here.

lines.name: 2...d6 3.d4: the Cenni Variation
lines.summary: Against the passive 2...d6 White opens the centre at once with 3.d4, keeps the queen active on d3 and e2 and gains space with the f-pawn.

next.text: A solid but passive reply: Black rules out any tactics on f7 and keeps the centre intact, but he gives White a free hand in the centre.
The Cenni Variation: White opens the centre at once, before Black has developed a piece.
The natural capture.
The queen takes the pawn and eyes g7.

The queen retreats along the d-file and still covers e4.

**Verdict:** White has the space and the more harmonious development, and Black's knights have been pushed around. The edge is small, but Black has no real counterplay.
White has the more harmonious pieces and the centre.
The Omaha Gambit, covered by two of the studies: after 3...exf4 the queen comes to f3 and regains the pawn. A second weapon, not the main line.
The sound reply.

lines.name: 2...f5? 3.exf5 Nf6 4.g4: the Latvian shot
lines.summary: 2...f5 is a Latvian Gambit without a knight on f3 to harass, so White simply takes and uses g4 to drive the f6 knight away, with Qh5+ and the fork on c7 to follow.

next.text: Black borrows the Latvian Gambit. In the real Latvian White has a knight on f3, which ...e4 kicks away with tempo; here there is no such knight, so the idea simply loses a pawn.
Takes the pawn.
Develops and eyes e4 and g4.
Drives the knight away and prepares Qh5+.

The knight jumps into the centre.

A pawn check that opens the g-file and the diagonal.
Opens the centre and threatens Nxe4 and dxe5.

White wins the rook and has a decisive material advantage.

**Verdict:** White is clearly better. The pin on the e8-h5 diagonal and the fork on c7 decide.
Counterattacks the knight on c3 and ignores the knight on f6.
White is a knight up for a pawn, and the simplification helps him.

lines.name: 2...g6 3.d4: the fianchetto is not ready
lines.summary: The fianchetto is not possible without a pawn on d4: White opens the centre and the queen takes on d4 with tempo, hitting g7.

Opens the centre at once.
The queen takes the pawn and attacks g7 and the rook behind it.
The most popular reply. It defends g7, but it leads into a queen trade that favours White.
The knight attacks e5 and gets out of the pawn's way.

chapters.title: Advance Variation
chapters.subtitle: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5
chapters.intro:
The Advance is the principled answer to the Caro-Kann: White takes the space on offer and keeps every piece on the board. The price is that Black gets what the French player never gets, the queen's bishop outside the pawn chain. The whole opening is an argument about whether that bishop on f5 is an asset or a target, and whether Black can break with ...c5 or ...f6 before the lack of space tells.

The repertoire has three parts. Against 3...Bf5 the main weapon is the **Short System**, 4.Nf3 e6 5.Be2: quiet development, then c4 or dxc5 to open the centre the moment Black plays ...c5 with the king still on e8. The second weapon, in its own lines, is the **Tal Variation** 4.h4, which goes straight for the bishop and gives sharper, less symmetrical play. Against 3...c5 White takes, 4.dxc5, and makes Black spend time winning the pawn back.

Be honest about what it asks for. The forcing lines after 5...c5 6.Be3 are deeply analysed, and a fully prepared opponent can steer the 6...Qb6 line into a drawn ending. Everyone else gets a hard defensive task.

sections.title: Choosing between the Advance, the Fantasy and the Exchange
sections.body:
- **The Advance** suits a player who is happy to sit on a space advantage, manoeuvre on both wings and wait for the right moment to open the game. Nothing is exchanged early, so the stronger player has time to outplay the weaker one. It needs the most theory of the three, almost all of it in the 5...c5 lines.
- **The Fantasy** (3.f3) is the choice when you want an open fight and a surprised opponent at once, and accept some structural risk for it.
- **The Exchange with 4.Bd3** gives a healthy, risk-free game with a clear plan, but Black is never in danger of being worse out of the opening.

If the complaint about the old Exchange lines was "equal and nothing to play for", the Advance is the direct cure: the pawn on e5 takes f6 from Black's knight, the kingside pieces have to queue for e7, and Black cannot castle quickly.

sections.title: The structure: a French with the bishop outside
sections.body:
Black has the French pawn chain without the French bishop. Three things are paid for it.

- **A tempo.** The c-pawn reaches c5 in two moves. That is why White can afford the modest Be2 and still be ahead in development when the centre opens.
- **The queenside light squares.** With the bishop on f5 nobody guards b7, and once the c-pawn moves, b5, c6 and the a4-e8 diagonal are soft. Bb5, Qb3, Qa4 and Nb5 keep turning up for that reason.
- **The bishop itself is a target.** Nh4 wins the bishop pair if the bishop has no retreat, and g4 gains time when the centre is closed.

Black's breaks are ...c5 against d4 and ...f6 against e5. White's levers are c4, opening the centre before Black has castled, and on the kingside f4-f5 after Ne1 or Nh4.

sections.title: Short's idea: develop, then punish ...c5
sections.body:
Nigel Short's discovery was that White does not need to chase the bishop. Black's kingside is hard to develop (the knight wants e7, the bishop wants e7, f6 is unavailable), so ...c5 always comes with the king in the centre.

- **6.Be3, not 6.c3.** Supporting d4 with the pawn gives a French where Black's extra piece on f5 outweighs the lost tempo. The bishop on e3 lets White recapture on d4 with a knight, which then hits f5 and b5, and it prepares dxc5.
- **When to take on c5.** Take when Black cannot recapture at once with the bishop: when a knight on e7 blocks it, or when ...Nc6 has been played against a bishop on e3 (then ...Bxc5 runs into Bxc5, ...Qa5+ and b4, winning a piece). White then holds the pawn with Be3 and b4 for as long as it is convenient and gives it back for a lead in development.
- **When to play c4.** Play it when Black's king is still on e8 and a knight on e7 or d7 blocks the f8-bishop. After ...dxc4 a knight recaptures (Na3 or Nd2) and looks at d6.

sections.title: The b2-pawn
sections.body:
After 6...Qb6 the b-pawn cannot be defended comfortably, so White gives it up twice, on move 7 and again on move 8. The compensation is concrete: the queen on b2 is short of squares and the knight jumps to b5 with threats on c7.

- If Black takes at once, 7...Qxb2, then 8.Qb1 forces the queens off and the rook lands on b7.
- In the main line the knight on c3 hangs, and 9.Qe1 is the move: it defends the knight so that Rb1 becomes possible (9.Rb1 would simply lose the knight).
- The standard punishment for a careless move is Rb1, Nb5 and Nc7+, winning the rook on a8. It works after 9...c4 because the queen has to go to a3 and a4.

sections.title: The slow set-ups: Nbd2-b3 and play on both wings
sections.body:
When Black holds back ...c5 with ...Nd7, ...Ne7 and ...h6 in some order, White builds the same set-up every time. The knight on b3 controls c5 and a5, so ...c5 costs a pawn or hands White the d4-square. Then:

- **Queenside:** a4-a5 gains space and fixes b7; if Black stops it with ...a5, the pawn on a5 is a target for Bd2 and b5 belongs to White.
- **Kingside:** Ne1-d3 frees the f-pawn; f4, and g4 once the bishop has gone to h7, start the pawn storm.
- **Centre:** c4 is held back until Black commits the king.

Black's counterplay is ...g5 with ...Bg7 and ...f6, or ...Nf5 and ...Be7 with a late ...c5. White's king is the safer one, and the bishop on h7 can end up shut out by its own pawns.

sections.title: Good and bad trades
sections.body:
- **Light-squared bishops:** in the Short System do not offer the trade with Bd3. Black's bishop is the piece that is short of a future; White's is the one that will use the weak light squares.
- **Knight for the f5-bishop:** Nxf5 is good when Black must retake with the e-pawn. The pawns on d5 and f5 are then fixed, d4 is a permanent square for a White piece, and White has the bishops. It is less good when a knight recaptures and sits on f5 attacking e3 and d4.
- **The double exchange** in the diagram, Bxc6+ and Nxf5, breaks both of Black's pawn groups before c4 opens the centre.
- **Dark-squared bishops:** their exchange suits White, because d6 and c5 lose their defender.
- **Endings:** space and the bishop pair make most of them pleasant, with one exception to know: the pawn-down ending of the 6...Qb6 main line, which is level.

sections.title: The second weapon: the Tal Variation 4.h4
sections.body:
4.h4 threatens to trap the bishop (4...e6 loses it to g4, f3 and h5), so Black has to move the h-pawn. After the usual 4...h5 two things have changed for good: g5 is an outpost that no pawn can attack, and h5 is a weakness. That turns the normally harmless exchange Bd3 into a serious plan. The queen recaptures on d3, the bishop goes to g5 where it paralyses the kingside, and c4 opens the game.

After 4...h6 White plays g4 and Black must choose between a passive retreat to d7 and allowing the pawn sacrifice e6, which shuts in the f8-bishop.

Compared with the Short System the positions are less worked out to a draw, and White's own king is a little airier.

sections.title: 3...c5: why it is not a French a tempo down
sections.body:
Black attacks d4 at once and keeps the bishop at home, hoping to bring it out to g4 later. Against the French recipe, 4.c3, that works well: Black has lost a move but has the good bishop. So White changes the structure with 4.dxc5.

The tempo count now favours White. Black needs ...e6 and ...Bxc5 to regain the pawn, the bishop on c8 is shut in after all, and 5.a3 prepares b4 with a further gain of time. White's set-up is b4, Bb2, Nf3, Bd3 and castles, with the e5-pawn overprotected and c4 in reserve. Black plays against e5 with ...Ne7-g6 and ...f6, and against the queenside pawns with ...a5.

sections.body:
- Alexey Dreev, *Attacking the Caro-Kann: A Repertoire for White* (Chess Stars, 2015): the choice of systems and the chapter structure
- John Shaw, *Playing 1.e4: Caro-Kann, 1...e5 & Minor Lines* (Quality Chess, 2016): 4.h4 as a repertoire
- Leonid Kritz, "The advance variation Nf3-Be2; Black plays 5...c5", ChessBase Magazine 138 (2010), summarised at https://en.chessbase.com/post/opening-surveys-in-cbm-138
- Zahar Efimenko, *Ambitious Repertoire against the Caro-Kann* (Modern Chess, 2020), course outline, https://www.modern-chess.com/course/ambitious-repertoire-against-the-caro-kann/30404/
- Pavel Eljanov, *My Caro-Kann, Part 2* (Modern Chess), course outline: Black's best defences to 4.h4, https://www.modern-chess.com/course/my-caro-kann-part-2/48951/
- Alexey Dreev and Pier Luigi Basso, *Dreev Deep Caro-Kann, Part 3* (Modern Chess), course outline: the 5...h6 and ...g5 set-ups

- Jeremy Silman, "Kt Maneuvers Against the Advance Caro-Kann" and "Caro-Kann Advance Variation", Chess.com (2010)
- Bryan Smith, "More Ways To Battle The Caro-Kann", Chess.com (2015)

lines.name: Short System: 6...Qb6 7.Nc3 Nc6, the b2-pawn main line
lines.summary: White gives up b2 for a lead in development. Exact play by Black leads to a level ending a pawn down; anything less is punished quickly.

next.text: White takes space and denies f6 to the knight. In return Black's bishop gets out, and the base of the chain on d4 will be attacked by ...c5.
The bishop comes out before ...e6 shuts it in. 3...c5 and the rare third moves have their own lines.
The Short System. White does not chase the bishop: the plan is Be2, castle, and open the centre when Black plays ...c5. The sharper 4.h4 is the second weapon and has its own lines.
The modest square is chosen on purpose. On e2 the bishop stays on the board, covers g4 and h5 so that Nh4 becomes an idea, and can go to b5 or g4 later.
The critical move, and Black's strongest according to Kritz: d4 is attacked before the kingside is developed. The set-ups that keep the centre closed (5...Nd7, 5...Ne7, 5...h6) are in the slow lines.
The key move of the system. The bishop defends d4, so that ...cxd4 can be answered by Nxd4 with a knight hitting f5 and b5, and after dxc5 the pawn on c5 is protected.
The most testing reply: the queen attacks b2, adds to the pressure on d4 and takes the sting out of dxc5. 6...cxd4 and the knight moves are separate lines.
The pawn has to be given up. 7.b3 and 7.Qc1 hold it but are too passive (Kritz). Nc3 develops with Na4 and Nb5 in the air, and 7...Qxb2 is answered by 8.Qb1 (next line).
Black brings a third attacker to d4 before deciding about b2.
White offers the pawn a second time. Castling is worth more than any defensive move, and the knight on c6 has made the fork on c7 a real threat after Nb5.
The critical test, and the only way to justify the queen's sortie.
The knight on c3 is attacked. The queen defends it from a square where it is not in the way, and now Rb1 followed by Nb5 is the threat.
The only good move. Black must open the game for the f8-bishop at once; everything slower runs into Rb1 and Nb5.
The bishop takes, so that after the exchange a knight stands on d4, attacking f5 and ready for b5.
Development first. Black has no time to save the bishop on f5 (Kritz); the counterattack on c3 is what holds the position together.
The main move and Kritz's recommendation. White forces a queenless position in which Black's extra pawn is no comfort.
Forced: there is no other way to meet both Rxb7 and Nxf5 (Kritz).

**Verdict:** White is a pawn down with full compensation. The c- and d-files open for the rooks, d5 falls or becomes weak, and the rook on h8 needs several moves to get into play. Kritz: only two results are possible.

Against exact defence it is a draw, and modern practice (often with 15.h4 h5 inserted first) confirms it. That is the price of the main line: White risks nothing and the opponent has to know all of this.
Efimenko's recommendation for players who want to keep more tension: the knight heads for d6 and c7 and Rb1 follows.
White can repeat with Rb1 or play on with Na4 or Nd6+. Black should hold with exact defence, but has to find a string of only moves.
Natural, shutting in the e2-bishop and keeping d4 closed, but now the queen is cut off.
White has won the exchange. Even if the knight is eventually lost in the corner, Black's king is stranded in the centre. Practice is heavily in White's favour.
Running with the king.
Very good compensation (Kritz, citing Kamsky-Morozevich): the king has castled into the line of fire of the rooks and the bishop.
The rook move needs the knight to be protected first.
The older try, threatening Nc7+. After 9...c4 the complications are unclear at best: Kritz concludes that it gives no clear advantage, and in practice Black has scored well.
Black declines and closes the centre, still eyeing b2. But d4 is now safe, so White has a free hand on the wings.
Covers b2 for good and prepares b3, opening the b-file against the queen.
Stops ...Bb4 and slows down ...b5-b4, Black's only active plan. White continues with Nh4 (or Ne1 and g4) and f4-f5 on the kingside and b3 on the queenside.
The French reflex is the wrong one here.
Black has an Advance French with the bishop already on f5, which is worth more than the tempo spent on ...c6-c5 (Kritz). The knight goes to c8-b6 or g6 and Black has no problems.
The exchange helps only Black, whose bishop is the one without a future.
Capablanca's manoeuvre. Without queens White's space means little and every remaining black piece is good: an ideal French.

The other sharp try, the Bayonet or Van der Wiel Attack: after 4...e6 White hunts the bishop with g4, Nge2, h4 and Nf4. It was the fashion of the 1990s. Black's antidote is the immediate counterblow in the centre.
White has won a pawn, but the kingside is full of holes and d4 is collapsing. Eljanov's repertoire for Black is built on this position. Not our line.

A quieter route to the same set-up: Nb3 comes first, to hold c5, and Nf3 and Be2 follow. It usually transposes to the slow lines of the Short System, but it gives up the option of meeting ...c5 with Be3.
Opens the c-file at once. Black develops with ...Ne7 and takes on c4 at a good moment, when the d5-square and the knight route b6-d5 give easy play.
Kasparov's move, keeping the knight's options open. The drawback is 4...Qb6, when b2 is awkward to defend and White's queen has to go to c1.

lines.name: Short System: 6...Qb6 7.Nc3 c4 and 7...Qxb2
lines.summary: Black closes the centre or takes b2 a move early. Against the first White covers b2 with Rb1 and plays on the wings; the early capture is met by 8.Qb1.

next.text: Black keeps the threat to b2 but releases d4. That is a real concession: with the centre closed White no longer has to hurry and can attack on either wing.
The simplest answer to the threat. The rook will be well placed when b3 opens the file.
Pinning the knight to renew the pressure, and developing the bishop before the knight takes e7.
The standard reaction once the centre is closed. The bishop cannot avoid the exchange (h7 is occupied), so White collects the bishop pair when it suits and frees the f-pawn.

A regrouping taken from practice: the bishop clears e2 for the knight (11...Nc6 12.Ne2, heading for f4) and aims at e6, the point that f4-f5 will attack.

**Plan:** Nxg6 at a moment when ...hxg6 does not help Black, then f4-f5; on the queenside b3 opens the b-file. **Verdict:** White has the initiative on both wings and will have the bishops, and Black still has to find a home for the king.
Taking at once is worse than taking a move later, because the queens can be forced off.
Kritz prefers this to the wild 8.Nb5 c4 9.Nc7+ Kd7 10.Nxa8 Bxc2, which nobody can calculate. The rook takes the b-file with tempo, and b7 and c7 cannot both be held.
Threatening the fork on c7.
Material is level, Black's kingside is still at home, and White's king and rook reach the queenside first. Kritz gives this (Bologan-Palo) as a clear advantage.
The sacrifice opens everything while Black has only the bishop on f5 in play.
White is a piece down for a pawn, but Black is tied hand and foot: Baklan-Rasmussen was won by White (Kritz).

lines.name: Short System: 6...cxd4 7.Nxd4 Ne7 8.O-O
lines.summary: Black releases the tension and develops. White pins on b5, breaks up the pawns with Bxc6 and Nxf5 and opens the centre with c4.

next.text: The solid choice: Black removes the tension before White can use it and aims simply for ...Ne7 and ...Nbc6.
The knight covers f5 and makes room for the other one on c6. Black is not afraid of Nxf5 here: a knight recaptures, the closed centre blunts the bishop pair, and e5 needs watching (Kritz).
The modern main move, keeping both c4 and Bb5 available. Dreev covers all three of White's options.
A pin with a positional point, and Efimenko's recommendation: White will take on c6 and on f5 and leave Black with broken pawns on both wings.
Black asks the question at once. 9...Bg6 saves the f-pawns from being doubled but leaves the pin, and 10.c4 opens the centre in the same way.
Black keeps d5 covered and gets the b-file.
The point of the whole operation. Black's king is two moves from castling and the queenside pawns are broken: now the centre is opened.
The queen guards c6 and d5 and prepares ...dxc4 followed by ...Nd5. The alternatives 11...c5 and 11...dxc4 open the position while Black is still undeveloped.
The pawn on c4 will not run away. The knight heads for b6 and c5, the squares that the exchange on c6 created.
The pawn could not be held, so Black returns it in the way that damages White's structure most.
Keeping the queens on: 16.Nxc3 Nxe3 would allow the exchange on d1.

**Verdict:** roughly level, and easier for White. Black has a bishop against a knight but weak pawns on a6, c6 and f5 and an uncastled king; White has the open d- and f-files and a lead in development to set against the doubled e-pawns. Top-level games usually end in draws, but Black has to be accurate for some time yet.
Keeps the queenside intact but allows the other half of the plan.
The d-pawn is isolated, the f-pawns are doubled, and the knight comes to f3 or b3 and then d4. A pleasant edge without risk.

The sharp alternative, which Kritz calls the only way to fight for an advantage. It leads by force to a queenless middlegame in which White has the bishops and the initiative; g4 comes next (Caruana's treatment). More forcing than the main line, and a good second string.
The quiet treatment: the knight supports its colleague from f3 and White simply completes development. Black usually answers ...Bg4 or ...Be4 and exchanges a pair of minor pieces.

lines.name: Short System: 6...Nd7, 6...Nc6 and 6...Ne7
lines.summary: Black develops a knight before resolving the centre. White answers with c4 or dxc5 and opens the game while the f8-bishop is still blocked.

next.text: A developing move that supports c5 and keeps the tension. Its defects (Kritz): the knight is passive on d7 and takes the queen's eye off d5.

Kritz's recommendation; he judges White's position excellent (Haslinger-Strating). The knights on d7 and e7 are in each other's way and block the f8-bishop, so Black is at least three moves from castling: the moment to open the centre. Efimenko prefers to prepare it with 8.Nbd2.

The knight, not the bishop, will take on c4, because from there or from b5 it reaches d6. With both black knights blocking the queen and the bishop, d6 is unguarded and the king has no square: a knight landing there is mate.
Returning the pawn to spoil White's structure after 10.bxc3.
White ignores the pawn: the threat is Nd6 mate.
The most active way to open the bishop's view of d6: the knight also attacks e3 and supports the pawn on c3.
**Verdict:** White has regained the pawn with a lead in development. After 11...Nxe3 12.fxe3 the open f-file and the central pawn mass make up for the doubled pawns, and Black still has to castle.
The most natural square, but the pawn on c5 is simply hanging.
The bishop cannot recapture: 7...Bxc5? 8.Bxc5 Qa5+ 9.b4! costs Black a piece, because the bishop on c5 covers b4 (9...Nxb4 10.Bxb4). So the pawn has to be won back slowly.
8...Nxe5 9.Nxe5 Qxe5 10.Bb5+ costs Black the right to castle.
White opens the centre before Black has castled and keeps the extra pawn for the time being: a clear advantage (Kritz, citing Edouard-Reinhart).
Prepares ...Nec6 or ...Nf5 and keeps ...Nbc6 for later, but blocks the bishop again.
Dreev's choice. The pawn is held by the e3-bishop, and Black gets it back only by spending several moves on the knights.
The same recipe: the centre is opened against the uncastled king.

lines.name: Slow set-up: 5...Nd7 6.O-O Ne7 7.Nbd2 h6 8.Nb3 g5
lines.summary: Black keeps the centre closed and expands on the kingside. White holds c5 with the knight on b3, regroups with Ne1-d3 and is ready for f4 or for play on the queenside.

next.text: Black postpones ...c5 until the pieces are out. The knight supports both breaks, ...c5 and ...f6, and leaves e7 for the other knight. 5...Ne7 and 5...h6 usually reach the same positions.
The knight is heading for g6 or f5, or will make room for the bishop by going on to c8.

Dreev's set-up. The knight goes to b3, where it stops ...c5 and looks at a5, the c-pawn stays flexible, and the c1-bishop keeps its diagonal. 7.c3 and 7.a4 are the other popular moves, and Efimenko recommends 7.Nh4 to take the bishop pair at once.
A retreat for the bishop against Nh4, and the first step of ...g5.
Now ...c5 loses a pawn or, after exchanges on c5, hands White the d4-square for a knight. Black has to look for play elsewhere.
The most ambitious plan, and the one Dreev and Basso recommend for Black: space on the kingside, ...Bg7 and ...f6 against e5, with the king often going to the queenside.
The knight is not needed on f3 any more. From d3 it covers c5, b4 and f4, and it gets out of the way of the f-pawn before ...g4 can gain time.
10.f4 at once is the other move Dreev and Basso analyse. With the knight on d3 first, White keeps the choice between f4 and the queenside.

**Plan:** Black usually castles long now. White then has a ready-made attack with a4-a5 and c4, while f4 is played at a moment when ...gxf4 does not hand Black the g-file. Bg4 or Bh5 are typical ways to exchange or disturb Black's active pieces.

**Verdict:** a full-blooded middlegame with chances for both sides. White has more space and the safer king; Black has the breaks ...f6 and ...c5 and must time them well.

Equally popular: White gains space on the other wing first and keeps the knight on f3 until Black shows his hand. The pawn goes on to a5 and threatens a6, loosening the light squares where Black's king may want to live.
Premature with the king in the centre.
The knight on d2 is ready to recapture on c4 and head for d6, and the position opens before Black can castle.
Clearing f5 for the knight. This reaches the position of the ...Nh6-f5 line below, where g4 and f4 follow.
Only a different move order.

lines.name: Slow set-up: 8.Nb3 against 8...Bh7 and 8...Qc7
lines.summary: Black waits. White gains space with a4 and prepares Ne1-d3 and the advance of the kingside pawns; stopping the a-pawn with ...a5 leaves a target.

next.text: A prophylactic retreat: the bishop is out of the way of g4 and Nh4, and f5 is free for the knight.
With the centre closed White gains space where Black cannot answer. A pawn on a5 cramps the whole queenside, and a6 would break up the light squares.
Stops the pawn at the cost of the b5-square and of a pawn that needs defending.

**Plan:** the bishop attacks a5 and makes ...c5 harder still. White continues with Ne1-d3 and f4, and g4 gains time whenever a knight lands on f5.

**Verdict:** White is a little better: more space on both wings and no weaknesses, while Black still has to find work for the h7-bishop and a safe place for the king.
Black develops and lets the pawn run.
With the queenside fixed the central break comes with more force: Black's pawns are fixed on a6 and b7, the c-file is about to open against them, and the bishop on h7 is a spectator.
Keeps ...c5, ...g5 and long castling all open.
The natural square: the bishop supports a4-a5, and it meets ...a5 by attacking the pawn.
The plans of the 8...g5 line with the a-pawns fixed, which helps White: b5 is his, and the pawn on a5 ties a black piece down.

lines.name: 5...Ne7 6.O-O c5 7.c4
lines.summary: Black breaks with ...c5 behind a knight on e7. White strikes back with c4 and takes on c5, because the f8-bishop is blocked.

next.text: A flexible move order: the knight can go to g6, f5 or c8, and ...c5 can be supported by either knight on c6. Its drawback is that the f8-bishop is shut in for the moment.
The independent try. 6...h6 also transposes to the slow lines, and against 6...Bg6, 6...Ng6 and 6...Nc8 White uses the same Nbd2-b3 set-up.
Recommended by both Dreev and Efimenko. Black has two central pawns under attack and a king that cannot castle for at least two moves, so White wants the files open now.
The rule from the 6.Be3 lines: take when the bishop cannot recapture.
Black gets a passed pawn and the d5-square for the pawn, and hopes to round up c5 later with ...Ng6 and ...Bxc5.
The absent bishop again: b7 is attacked, and the queen steps off the d-file so that a rook can go to d1 against the d-pawn.

**Verdict:** White is a pawn up and attacks d4. Black can win a pawn back with ...Ng6, but has to spend time on it while White finishes development with Na3 or Nbd2. Efimenko judges White's chances preferable; the position is sharp and far less explored than 5...c5.
Here the bishop recaptures: it looks at e6, and after 8...Nbc6 White takes on c5, when the knight on e7 again prevents ...Bxc5.
Back in the main slow line.

lines.name: Slow set-up: ...Bg6 with ...Nh6-f5, and the fifth-move sidelines
lines.summary: Black brings the knight to f5 through h6. White lets it come, drives it off with g4 and gains space with f4. The rare fifth moves transpose or lose time.

next.text: Black clears f5 for the king's knight, which will travel h6-f5, leaving e7 for the bishop: the most harmonious way to develop the kingside without ...c5.
8.Bxh6 is possible at any moment, but it gives up the bishop that guards the dark squares and opens the g-file. White prefers to keep the tension.
A useful waiting move: the bishop looks at a5 and the queen's rook is free, before White decides about g4.
The knight has no comfortable retreat: h6 is passive, and after ...Nh4 the exchange leaves White free to play f4.

**Verdict:** White has a large space advantage on the kingside and threatens f5. Black has to stop it with ...f5 himself, and White then keeps the choice between opening lines and playing g5, which cuts the bishop on h4 off from its camp. White is better.
Dreev and Basso's move order for Black; it reaches the main slow line.
A waiting move that prepares ...c5 by ruling out Bb5 and Nb5. White develops in the usual way.
Now 8...c5 is met by 9.dxc5, and the move ...a6 has changed little.
Tried by Carlsen: the check provokes c3, so that a later c4 costs a move.
The bishop is a long way from the kingside, and b4 will gain time on it.
Prevents the Nb3 and a4-a5 clamp in advance.
Fixing the pawn and taking b5 for good. Black's usual follow-up is 7...f6, which White answers in the centre with 8.c4.

lines.name: Tal Variation: 4.h4 h5 5.Bd3
lines.summary: After ...h5 White exchanges bishops after all, puts the other bishop on g5 and opens the centre with c4. The g5-square and the pawn on h5 are permanent assets.

next.text: The Tal Variation, and Shaw's repertoire choice. The threat is g4 followed by h5, winning the bishop, so Black must do something about the h-pawn at once.
The main move: it stops g4 for good. The price is the g5-square and a target on h5.

In the Short System this exchange was a mistake. Here it is the modern main line, because the pawn moves have changed the balance: Black can never play ...h6, so g5 belongs to White's bishop, the pawn on h5 needs constant protection, and the queen on d3 looks at g6.

The point of exchanging on d3. The bishop sits outside its pawn chain on a square from which no pawn can drive it, and it cramps the whole kingside: ...Ne7 walks into a pin, ...Be7 offers Black's better bishop for exchange, and ...f6 weakens e6 and g6.
The main reply: the queen leaves the bishop's diagonal, attacks b2 and prepares ...Qa6.

The b-pawn is offered: after 8...Qxb2 9.Rb1 and 10.Rxb7 the rook is on the seventh rank before Black has developed a kingside piece. The knight supports c4 and will be followed by the other one on f3.
Black offers queens to get rid of the pressure on the light squares.
White refuses, since after Qxa6 Nxa6 Black's game is easy, and uses the queen's position to open the centre. If Black takes, Nxc4 brings the knight towards d6.

**Plan:** rooks to the c- and d-files, then cxd5 or c5 according to where Black's king goes. A knight heading for f4 attacks h5 and e6.

**Verdict:** White is the more comfortable: more space, the better minor pieces, and a weakness on h5 that will still be there in the ending. This is the line that has made 4.h4 the most popular fourth move in elite online play.
The other main move.
The same break. With both c-pawns advanced the centre is blown open while Black's kingside is still at home. The usual reply, 9...Qxb2, leads to wild play after 10.Rd1 or 10.Rb1.
Black accepts the exchange of dark-squared bishops to free the position.
White does not hurry to take on e7. After the exchange the d6-square and the pawn on h5 stay weak, and Bxh6 is an extra option now that the knight has gone there.
The move Eljanov's repertoire for Black calls essential: before ...e6 the queen checks and heads for a6 to offer an exchange.
7.b4 is a serious pawn sacrifice (7...Qxb4+ 8.Nd2 e6 9.Rb1 Qe7 10.c4), for those who want more.

White keeps the queens on. Eljanov considers 11...b6 followed by ...c5 satisfactory for Black. The position is balanced, but Black still has to solve the problem of the king: castling short leaves h5 weak, and Bg5 is always available.

The older main line, and the one Shaw gives in Playing 1.e4: White keeps the bishops and opens the c-file. Black chooses between 6...Ne7 followed by ...Nd7, and 6...dxc4 7.Bxc4 Nd7 (Eljanov), playing for the d5-square. A good alternative if you prefer more pieces on the board.
The natural developing move loses a piece.
The bishop has no square: h7 is occupied, and g4 and f3 cover the rest.

lines.name: Tal Variation: 4.h4 h6 5.g4
lines.summary: Black keeps g5 covered but lets White gain space with tempo. The bishop either retreats to d7, with a French where White owns the kingside, or allows the pawn sacrifice e6.

next.text: Black gives the bishop a retreat on h7 and keeps g5 under control. The cost is that g4 now comes with tempo.
White takes the space for nothing. The bishop has three squares, and only the most modest one avoids the e6 sacrifice.
Played by Leko and Ivanchuk (Silman). Black admits that the bishop went to f5 for nothing and plays a French with ...c5, counting on White's advanced kingside pawns to become targets.
Fixes the kingside pawns and, above all, stops Black from ever undermining g4 with ...h5. The same move is right against 4...Qb6 for the same reason.

**Plan:** a French Advance in which Black's bishop is back on d7 and White has been given g4, h5 and f4 for nothing. White defends d4 (Na3-c2, with Rh2 to cover b2 after ...Qb6), puts the king on f2 and prepares f5.

**Verdict:** more space and the initiative for White. The thing to respect is White's own king, which has no pawn cover: do not let ...Qb6 and ...cxd4 open the centre before the queenside is developed.
Provoking f3 first, which takes that square from the knight.
The thematic sacrifice. If Black takes, the e6-pawn blocks the f8-bishop and the whole kingside, and Bd3 exchanges the only piece that covers g6.
The usual reply, attacking the pawn and threatening ...Qg3+.
Closes the diagonal to g3 and takes e5 for the knight. Material is level, Black's king has lost the right to castle and the bishop on h7 is shut out; Nf3-e5+ and Bd3 follow.
The retreat the bishop was given h7 for.
The same idea without f3 included.
White is a pawn down for a lasting bind: after the exchange of bishops the queen comes to g6 with check, the king has to stay in the centre, and Nf3-e5 follows.

lines.name: Tal Variation: 4...Qb6, 4...a6 and 4...c5
lines.summary: Black sidesteps the h-pawn question with a useful move. White plays g4 and h5 anyway and reaches the French structure with extra space, or takes on c5.

next.text: The queen eyes b2 and d4. The idea is to answer g4 with ...Bd7 and then hit the pawn chain with ...h5 and ...c5, arguing that White's pawns have gone too far.
The bishop must go all the way back: 5...Be4 6.f3 Bg6 7.h5 traps it, as after 4...e6.
Stops ...h5, which would undermine g4 and win f5 for a knight.

**Plan:** the structure of the 4...h6 line, with one difference in White's favour: the h-pawn can go on to h6. White continues Nf3 and Na3-c2, covering d4 and b2.

**Verdict:** White has the space, and the queen's sortie has not changed the assessment.
The third most popular move in elite online games: a pure waiting move that prepares ...c5 and keeps the bishop's options.
Again the French structure with extra space. Black continues ...c5, and ...a6 turns out to be only moderately useful.
Striking at d4 with the bishop already out.
5...e6 still loses the bishop to g4.
White pins the knight, holds the pawn with Be3 or b4 and keeps g4 in reserve to gain more time. The main reply is 6...Qc7, when 7.Nf3 e6 follows.

lines.name: 3...c5 4.dxc5 e6 5.a3: main line
lines.summary: White takes on c5 and uses a3 and b4 to gain time on the bishop. The set-up Bb2, Bd3, castles and Re1 overprotects e5 against ...f6 and ...Ng6.

next.text: Black hits d4 before White has developed and keeps the bishop flexible: if allowed, it goes to g4, a better square than f5. Botvinnik used the move against Tal in 1961; Arkell and Khenkin made it respectable.

The critical move and by far the most popular. White gives up the pawn that supports e5 but wins time: Black has to spend moves regaining c5, and with ...e6 the c8-bishop is shut in after all. 4.Nf3 is the main alternative, which Johnsen and Hansen consider the most critical; it is sharper and needs more theory.
Black shuts the bishop in voluntarily in order to win the pawn back with the other one. 4...Nc6 is the next line.

Dreev's choice, and the most popular move in practice. It prepares b4, which hits the bishop as soon as it arrives on c5, and the bishop on b2 then protects e5. The obvious 5.Be3 holds the pawn for a while (Efimenko recommends it) but the bishop gets in the way there; 5.Nf3 Bxc5 6.a3 comes to the same thing.
6.b4 first is more common and usually transposes. 6.Qg4 is an independent and sharper try, attacking g7 before Black has castled; Idani's repertoire for Black gives it a chapter of its own.
With tempo: the queenside pawns gain space and b2 is cleared for the bishop.
The active square, aiming at f2 and at d4 once e5 comes under fire.
The bishop takes the b1-h7 diagonal unopposed, a small echo of the 3...Bf5 lines, where Black would exchange it.
The standard manoeuvre: the knight attacks e5 and can jump to f4.

**Plan:** e5 is overprotected, so ...f6 only opens lines for White's pieces. Nbd2 and c4 come next, opening the long diagonal and the c-file, and g3 keeps the knight out of f4 if necessary.

**Verdict:** a normal, healthy edge: more space, the wedge on e5, and Black's c8-bishop is still a problem piece. Black's counterplay is ...f6 and ...a5; neither should be ignored, and neither equalises on its own.
Black can also attack the pawn at once.
White develops and lets Black take: after ...fxe5 the knight recaptures and e5 becomes a square for the pieces.
The same plan from e7.
The knight goes to f7 to attack e5 a third time. White holds the pawn with Re1 and Qe2; if Black ever takes on e5, a piece recaptures and the e5-square belongs to White.
The immediate attack on e5, the main line of Idani's repertoire for Black.

White keeps e5 overprotected and does not take on f6 voluntarily, and the pawn on b5 takes c6 from Black's knight. Black usually continues ...Nh6-f7 to add pressure; White castles and supports the pawn with Re1 and Qe2.
Developing first changes nothing.
The French move is what Black hopes for.
A French Advance with the bishop outside the chain and pinning the defender of d4: the lost tempo does not matter (Silman, quoting Houska).

lines.name: 3...c5 4.dxc5 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bg4
lines.summary: Black develops the bishop to g4 before ...e6 and wins the e5-pawn. White keeps c5 with c3 and Be3 and gets the bishop pair and a queenside majority.

next.text: Black develops first and wants the bishop on g4 before playing ...e6: the pawn on e5 is then attacked twice and its defender pinned. Efimenko calls the move dubious and answers 5.f4; the natural 5.Nf3 is Dreev's repertoire and is followed here.
The point. If Black now gets ...e6 and ...Bxc5 in, it is a French with the good bishop outside, so White has to do something about c5.
The solid way to keep the pawn: Be3 and b4 will defend c5. White accepts that e5 will fall and takes the bishop pair and the queenside majority for it.
Protects c5; 7.b4 is the alternative. Black now chooses how to win e5.
A check that gains time: the knight has to go back to block.

White strikes at d5 while the pin on c6 lasts. 10...dxc4 11.Bxc6+ bxc6 12.Qxc6+ drives the king to e7.

**Verdict:** White has the two bishops, the more active pieces and a mobile queenside majority led by the c5-pawn. Black has an extra centre pawn and needs two more moves to castle. Practice favours White.
Ruling out the check on b5 before taking.
The pin is broken and White castles next. Material is level; the c5-pawn cramps Black and b4 will support it.
Aiming at the bishop on e3 before taking the pawn.
The bishop keeps both c5 and e5 covered, and Black has to exchange the knight to make progress.
The sharp alternative, covered at length by Johnsen and Hansen. White keeps the pawn with b4, but after ...Bxf3 gxf3 the structure is ragged and both kings are exposed. Rich, and much more to learn.
Black changes his mind about the bishop.
Back in the main line with 5.a3, since 6...Bxc5 7.b4 follows.

lines.name: 3...g6
lines.summary: Black prepares ...Bg7 with ...f6 or ...c5 and keeps the bishop for g4. White develops simply, takes g4 away with h3 and keeps e5 supported.

next.text: A Gurgenidze-style set-up: the bishop goes to g7 to attack e5 with ...f6 (or d4 with ...c5), the knight to h6, and the c8-bishop is kept for g4. Wikibooks gives Short-Spassky 2001 as the reference game. Black's pieces come out slowly, so nothing sharp is needed.
Natural development; e5 will need this knight.
The key move of the set-up. Without g4 the bishop on c8 has no good square at all: on f5 it is hit by g4 or exchanged by Bd3, and after ...e6 it is a French bishop behind a French chain.
Heading for f5 or, after ...f6, for f7.
Controls f5, so the knight has to go the long way round. 6.Bxh6 is not necessary.

**Plan:** against 7...f6 White keeps the pawn on e5 as long as possible with Re1 and Bf4, or exchanges on f6 at a moment when the e-file and the e5-square fall to the knights. c3 keeps d4 solid if Black adds ...c5.

**Verdict:** White has more space and the easier development, and the bishop on c8 is Black's lasting problem.

lines.name: 3...Na6, 3...e6, 3...a6 and 3...Qb6
lines.summary: Slow or eccentric third moves. White does not take on a6, meets 3...e6 with a French a full tempo up and answers 3...a6 by taking f5 away from the bishop.

next.text: The knight is going to c7, which keeps the c8-bishop's diagonal open; then ...Bf5 or ...g6 and ...Ne6 put pressure on d4. It is slow, and White should simply develop.
Development first; where the f1-bishop belongs is decided later.

As against 3...g6: the bishop is denied g4, and after ...Nc7-e6 and ...Bg7 White plays c3, Bd3 and castles with a solid space advantage.

**Verdict:** White is comfortably better. Black has spent three moves on the knight and still has to solve the bishop.
Tempting, to double the pawns, but it does not even do that.
Black has the bishop pair with intact pawns, and the queen on a6 stops White from castling.
A French Defence in which Black has spent a move on ...c6.

Now it really is the Advance French with an extra move for White. Note that 5.dxc5 Bxc5 6.a3 would transpose to the 3...c5 main line, where Black has lost nothing; 5.c3 is the way to make the tempo count.
A waiting move with the idea of 3...c5: the pawn goes to c5 next, and the bishop stays at home for the moment.
Since the bishop has not come out, White takes f5 away from it.
The knight goes to e2 so that ...Bg4 can be met by f3, and f4 is prepared. A French Advance where ...a6 is of little use and Black has still lost a tempo with the c-pawn.
Marked dubious by Wikibooks: the queen is committed before Black knows where it belongs.
Simple development gives a pleasant edge, and the queen will lose time to c4 or to Nbd2-b3.

chapters.title: Fantasy Variation
chapters.subtitle: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.f3
chapters.intro:
The Fantasy is the Caro-Kann answer for a player who likes what the Vienna Game with f4 gives: a pawn centre, a half-open f-file and a bishop on c4 aiming at f7. After 3.f3 dxe4 4.fxe4 White owns e4 and d4 for a single tempo and every piece development points at f7. Compared with the Exchange (the symmetrical position with nothing to play for) this is a real fight in which Black has to know several things at once.

It is a weapon and not an advantage. In the Lichess elite database (2400+, about 7,200 games after 3.f3) White scores about 54%, an ordinary first-move result, and in the main lines Black can equalise. The pay-off is practical: the lines are rich in traps, most of which punish natural moves (6...Nf6?, 8...Nxe4? and 8...O-O? in the gambit line), and the positions are easy for White to understand. The risks are real too: f3 takes the knight's square and the pawn that shields the king, so the e1-h4 and a7-g1 diagonals are the targets (...Qh4+, ...Bc5, ...Qb6 and ...Bxg1 ideas), and in the Qb6, g6 and e6 lines White gets no more than equality.

The repertoire in this chapter: against 3...dxe4 play 4.fxe4 e5 5.Nf3, then 6.Bc4 against 5...Bg4, the gambit 6.Bc4 against 5...exd4 and 6.c3 against 5...Be6; against 3...e6 play 4.Nc3; against 3...Qb6 play 4.Nc3 dxe4 5.Bc4; against 3...g6 play 4.Nc3 Bg7 5.Be3 and meet ...Qb6 with b3. Rare tries are met by 4.Nc3 or 4.dxe5. The Advance (3.e5) has its own chapter.

sections.title: What 3.f3 is for, and what it costs
sections.body:
The pawn guards e4, so after ...dxe4 the f-pawn recaptures: White gets e4 and d4 without moving a piece, and the f-file points at f7. If Black does not take, e5 followed by f4 gives a French-type structure and the f3 pawn gets a purpose.

- **Gains:** the centre, the half-open f-file, quick development with Bc4 and castling.
- **Costs:** the g1 knight cannot use f3, so it goes to f3 only after the pawn has left (or to e2 or h3); the diagonals e1-h4 and a7-g1 have no pawn on them, so ...Qh4+, ...Bc5 and ...Bxg1 are always in the air; castling short can run into ...Bc5 and ...Qb6 pressure on g1, which is why the king so often steps to h1.
- **What kind of game:** open and tactical after 3...dxe4, a French or a Steinitz after 3...e6, a guarded fight for the dark squares after 3...g6 and 3...Qb6.

sections.title: The position after 5.Nf3
sections.body:
After 3...dxe4 4.fxe4 Black has one move to fight the centre, 4...e5, and then White develops with 5.Nf3. The three replies to know are 5...Bg4 (about half of the games), 5...Be6 (29%) and 5...exd4 (16%). 5.dxe5? loses the plot: after 5...Qxd1+ or 5...Qh4+ the pawn is a liability, the king is stuck and White has nothing for it.

- **5...Bg4** pins the knight so that ...exd4 wins a pawn: answer 6.Bc4 and castle.
- **5...exd4** takes the pawn: answer 6.Bc4 and play the gambit (Ng5 and Nxf7 tricks).
- **5...Be6** keeps the pawn centre and stops Bc4: answer 6.c3 and Bd3.
- **5...Nd7 and 5...Nf6** are rare and transpose or lose time.

sections.title: 5...Bg4 6.Bc4: the pin and the fork on f7
sections.body:
The knight on f3 is pinned, so Black seems to threaten ...exd4. White does not defend: 6.Bc4 attacks f7, and the pin is not a real pin because Bxf7+ and Nxe5+ fork the king and the bishop. That is why Black has only one useful sixth move.

- **6...Nd7** defends e5 and prepares ...Ngf6 and ...Bd6. This is the only move that keeps everything together.
- **6...Nf6?** loses a pawn to 7.Bxf7+ Kxf7 8.Nxe5+ (a fork) 8...Kg8 9.Nxg4 Nxg4 10.Qxg4: in the elite database White won 28 of 35.
- **6...exd4** gives White a free development after 7.Qxd4 Qxd4 8.Nxd4, with Black's bishop loose and f7 soft.
- **Why castle and play c3 and not defend d4 directly:** the pin makes Black's ...exd4 look strong, but once the king is on g1 and c3 is played the knight is no longer needed on the d1-h5 diagonal, and ...exd4 is simply met by cxd4.

sections.title: The main-line set-up: c3, Bg5, Nbd2
sections.body:
After 7.O-O Ngf6 8.c3 the d4 pawn is fully supported, ...exd4 stops being a threat, and the pawn on e4 is bait: 8...Nxe4? 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Ng5+ is a double check (knight and f1 rook) and the g4 bishop falls. Black plays 8...Bd6 and White develops with 9.Bg5 (pinning the f6 knight) and 10.Nbd2.

- **White's plans:** Qe1 and Qh4 to hit the pinned f6 knight and the g4 bishop; Bb3 so that ...b5 loses its point; the break e4-e5 when it hits both Bd6 and Nf6; Rae1 and Nh4 towards the f-file.
- **Black's plans:** ...Qc7 and ...Rae8 against e4 and d4; ...b5 to drive the bishop away; ...h6 followed by ...Bh5-g6 to hit e4; ...exd4 once the pin on f3 has done its job.
- **Verdict:** equal. The studies stop at move ten and call the position attractive for White because Black has no clear plan. The elite results after 10...Qc7 11.Qe1 are not kind to White, so treat this as a line to understand and to win on traps, not as a forced edge.

sections.title: 5...exd4 and the pinned knight on f6
sections.body:
This is the line with the best results in the chapter (65% for White in elite games). The idea: do not recapture on d4, develop with tempo against f7 (Bc4, O-O, Ng5), and let Black's king pay for the extra pawn. After 6...Nf6 7.O-O Bc5 8.Ng5 Black castles into the combination: 9.Nxf7 Rxf7 10.Bxf7+ Kxf7 leaves his king on the f-file with the f6 knight pinned in front of the rook on f1.

- **With Bc5:** 11.Qh5+ Kg8 12.Qxc5 wins the bishop (the pinned knight cannot take the queen).
- **With Be7 or no bishop on c5:** 11.e5 wins the pinned knight; the elite score of 11.e5 is 20 wins in 31 games.
- **The gambit's price:** if Black avoids the trap (7...Be6 8.Bxe6 fxe6 9.e5), White regains d4 with a small initiative. The line works because Black's natural moves (castling and developing) fall into it.
- **Alternatives for Black:** 6...Bg4 7.Bxf7+ and 6...Bb4+ 7.c3 dxc3 8.Bxf7+ lead to sharp but unclear play; 7...Nbd7 and 6...Nd7 are playable.

sections.title: 5...Be6: the quiet way and the king on h1
sections.body:
Black keeps the e5 pawn and the bishop covers c4, so Bc4 is pointless. White plays 6.c3 (supports d4, allows Qb3 against b7 and e6) and 7.Bd3 (supports e4, eyes h7), castles and takes the king off the a7-g1 diagonal with 9.Kh1. This is a manoeuvring game; the elite database gives White 63% with 9.Kh1.

- **White's plans:** Bg5 or Ng5, Qe1-h4, Rae1 and a later dxe5 to open the f-file; a4 to fix the queenside.
- **Black's plans:** ...exd4 cxd4 to free the pieces and put a knight on b4; ...Qc7 and ...Rae8; ...Bg4 to bring the last piece out.
- **6.Bg5** (the other study line) leads to a level position by trades and is mainly a pattern.

sections.title: 3...e6: the Fantasy as a French
sections.body:
Black declines the pawn and builds a French. Then f3 is a plain extra move, so White's best plan is to use it: after 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.e5 the pawn goes to f4 and the position is the Steinitz Variation of the French, with an extra move for each side. The study says Black is "down in development", but the count shows both sides have used one extra pawn move, so the position is an ordinary Steinitz French: equal with correct play, and rich in attacking chances for White if you know the French.

- **4...Bb4** pins the knight: 5.Bf4 (the study's choice) Ne7 6.Qd3 b6 7.Nge2 and White has the centre; 5.Bd2 and 5.a3 are more common and score about the same.
- **4.Be3** is the alternative fourth move: 4...Nf6 5.e5 Nfd7 6.f4 transposes; 4...dxe4 5.fxe4 Qh4+ 6.g3 Qxe4 7.Qe2 is a pawn sacrifice with good elite results but no explanation I found.
- **The French plans:** White keeps the chain e5-f4, supports d4 and aims at the kingside; Black hits d4 with ...cxd4 and ...Qb6, and undermines e5 with ...f6.

sections.title: Black's anti-Fantasy systems: 3...Qb6, 3...g6, 3...e5
sections.body:
These lines work because they use the weaknesses that f3 creates, and they are why the Fantasy is not an advantage for White.

- **3...Qb6** hits b2 and d4. 4.Nc3 dxe4 and now 5.Bc4: if 5...exf3 6.Nxf3 is a gambit for development; if 5...Nf6 6.fxe4 e5 7.dxe5 Ng4 8.Qe2 Nxe5 9.Bb3 is level. Do not play 5.fxe4 e5 6.dxe5?: after 6...Be6 Black's pieces develop with tempo and the extra pawn falls. The quiet 4.a4 a5 5.exd5 cxd5 6.Nc3 Nf6 7.Nb5 is a good practical try.
- **3...g6** 4.Nc3 Bg7 5.Be3: the bishop fianchetto aims at the dark squares around the king. 5...Qb6 6.b3 (not the study's 6.Qd2 Qxb2) keeps the pawn; 5...dxe4 6.fxe4 Nf6 7.Nf3 Ng4 8.Bg1 is awkward but playable.
- **3...e5** 4.dxe5 Bc5 5.Nc3 Qb6 6.Na4 Qa5+ 7.c3 Bxg1 8.Rxg1 dxe4: White's king has lost castling rights but Black's pressure is spent. Level.

sections.title: Safety rules and typical mistakes
sections.body:
The same few mistakes recur, and they are the reason this is a weapon you can win with.

- **Never take on e5 early.** 5.dxe5? gives Black the d-file (Qxd1+) or a check on h4 followed by ...Qxe4+; the extra pawn is not worth the king's safety.
- **Taking on e4 with the knight** (5.Nxe4 against 3...Qb6) is playable but makes the f3 pawn pointless: its whole job was to recapture there.
- **Watch the a7-g1 diagonal.** Whenever a black bishop reaches c5 or a queen reaches b6, ask what happens after ...Bxg1 or ...Qxb2. Kh1 solves most of these questions, which is why it is such a common move.
- **Bxf7+ only with a follow-up.** The sacrifice works when Nxe5+ forks (after ...Nf6?) or when the f-file pins a knight on f6 (after Nxf7). Otherwise it loses a bishop.
- **Do not hurry e4-e5.** The thematic break needs Bd6 and Nf6 to be in the line of fire; against a prepared Black it only opens the long diagonal.

sections.title: Sources
sections.body:
- "Caro-Kann: Fantasy Variation", FatPigz69, https://lichess.org/study/mfsCPcxi, 304 likes (the lines after 3...dxe4, 3...e6, 3...g6 and 3...Qb6)
- "Caro-kann: fantasy variation", SovietRaven, https://lichess.org/study/KIL5Z4Dq, 251 likes (the 5...Be6 6.Bg5 line, the 5...exd4 6.Bc4 Nf6 7.O-O Bc5 8.Ng5 trap, and the 3...e6 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.e5 transposition)
- "1. e4 Repertoire for White", Green_Frog96, https://lichess.org/study/L1jb6bbg, 651 likes (chapter "Caro-Kann: Fantasy Variation": the main line 5...Bg4 6.Bc4 Nd7 7.O-O Ngf6 8.c3 Bd6 9.Bg5 O-O 10.Nbd2 and the poisoned e4 pawn)
- "Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. f3", Wikibooks (the map of the replies 3...dxe4, 3...e6, 3...g6 and 3...Qb6, and the tactic Bxf7+ and Nxe5+)
- The Lichess Elite Database (the app's own book of 2400+ games), used for how often each move is played and its results, and to confirm moves in lines the studies do not cover (3...e6 4.Nc3 Bb4 5.Bf4 Ne7 6.Qd3 b6, 3...g6 5.Be3 Qb6 6.b3, 3...Qb6 5.Bc4 Nf6, 3...e5 4.dxe5 Bc5, 4.a4, 5...Be6 6.c3 Nd7 7.Bd3 Ngf6 8.O-O Bd6 9.Kh1, 5...Nd7 6.Bc4, 4.Be3 and the 5...exd4 6.Bc4 sub-lines)

lines.name: Main line: 5...Bg4 6.Bc4 Nd7 7.O-O Ngf6 8.c3 Bd6 9.Bg5 O-O 10.Nbd2
lines.summary: Black takes on e4, strikes at d4 and pins the f3 knight; White develops with tempo against f7, castles and builds c3, Bg5, Nbd2. Balanced, with a pawn centre and the f-file to play with.

next.text:
**Idea:** the pawn guards e4. If Black takes, the f-pawn recaptures and White owns e4 and d4 without having moved a piece, with the f-file half open towards f7. If Black does not take, White can still build with Nc3 and Be3 or push e5 and f4.

**The price:** f3 takes the natural square of the g1 knight and removes the pawn that shields the king, so the e1-h4 and a7-g1 diagonals become Black's targets (...Qh4+, ...Bc5, ...Bg4). It is a practical surprise weapon and not a refutation: in the elite database White scores an ordinary first-move result, a little over half, after 3.f3.
The principled reply and the main line of the studies. Black's other thirds are 3...e6 (the most common in elite games), 3...Qb6, 3...g6, 3...e5 and 3...Nf6; each has a line of its own further on.
A big centre and an open f-file for nothing but a tempo. Black has to hit it now or White will simply play Nc3, Bc4 and Nf3 with a free hand.
The only way to fight the centre. Anything slower lets White have e4, d4 and a lead in development.
Attacks e5 and adds a second guard to d4.
The most popular fifth move (about half of the games). The bishop pins the knight to the queen, so ...exd4 threatens to win a pawn: Nxd4 is impossible, and Qxd4 is met by ...Bxf3.

Ignores the threat and aims at f7, which has only the king to protect it. The pin is not a real one yet: if Black takes on d4 or plays a careless developing move, Bxf7+ and Nxe5+ come with a fork on the king and the g4 bishop.
The only move that keeps everything together. It guards e5, so the fork is gone, and makes room for ...Ngf6.
Gets the king out of the e-file before ...exd4 and ...Qe7 ideas begin, and puts the rook on the open f-file behind the f7 target.
Develops the second knight, attacks the e4 pawn and prepares ...Bd6 and ...O-O.
Shores up d4 so that ...exd4 is no longer a threat, and keeps the d1-a4 diagonal free for the queen. The e4 pawn is left "en prise" on purpose.
Natural: Black prepares ...O-O and supports e5.
Pins the f6 knight to the queen. The key move of the line: the knight that guards e4 and h5 is under pressure, Bxf6 and e5 would hit Bd6, and the queen heads for h4 via e1.

**Position:** the standard Fantasy middlegame. White has the centre pawns on d4 and e4, every piece developed and a bishop on c4 that bears on f7. Black has no weaknesses but also little space.

**Plans for White:** (a) Qe1 and Qh4, using the Bg5 pin to win the g4 bishop's support or to force ...Bxf3; (b) Bb3, to keep the bishop safe from ...b5 and keep f7 under fire; (c) the break e4-e5, which hits Bd6 and Nf6 together; (d) Rae1 and Nh4, to swing a knight towards the f-file.

**Plans for Black:** ...Qc7 and ...Rae8 against e4 and d4; ...b5 to drive the bishop away; ...h6 followed by ...Bh5-g6 to hit e4 from behind. Black can also take on d4 once the pin on f3 has done its job.

**Verdict:** balanced. The studies end here and describe the positions as pleasant for White because Black has no obvious plan, but elite results are even, so this is a line for understanding and for the traps, not for a forced edge.
The sharpest reply: Black asks the bishop what it wants.

Black weakens his king to unpin and prepares ...Nxe4. The elite results here (4 wins for White in 14) show that White has to know exactly what he is doing; 10.Bxf6 Nxf6 gives up the bishop for a knight and the pin.
Hits b7 and f7 at once. Played in about 7% of elite games, with an even score; it is a reasonable alternative if you do not want the pin.
Goes for Qh4 at once, without the pin on f6. Also about 9% of the games and also even.
The bait.
**Trap:** a double check, by the knight and by the f1 rook down the open f-file. The king has to move and White then collects the g4 bishop and keeps the e4 knight under fire.
Opens the centre and hands Black easy development with ...Nxe5, hitting the bishop. Elite results with 8.dxe5 were poor for White (4 wins in 21).
The same position arrives by transposition: 7...Ngf6 8.O-O Bd6. About 40% of the games went this way; castling first keeps Qe1 and Qb3 available, so it is a matter of taste.
The tempting developing move loses a pawn at once to the tactic on f7.
The knight lands on e5 with check and attacks the g4 bishop as well. White is a pawn up and Black cannot castle. In 35 elite games White won 28.
Takes the pawn, but the pin is not worth it.

The bishop on g4 is now simply loose, f7 is soft, and White is ahead in development with an isolated but healthy e-pawn. After 8...Bxf3 9.Qxd8+ Kxd8 10.gxf3 would be the pawn-centre version; Black has lost the right to castle.
Gives up the bishop pair to remove the pin.
Bc4 and Qf3 both bear on f7, White has the bishop pair and the centre is intact. Black has to spend a tempo on ...Qf6 or ...Qh4+ before getting on with development.

Tempting because it wins a pawn, but after 5...Qxd1+ 6.Kxd1 the king is stuck on d1, the e-file is open and White's e-pawns are the targets; one study calls the position easier to play for Black, and 5...Qh4+ 6.g3 Qxe4+ is no better for White. Develop, do not grab.
Your usual Exchange: symmetrical, safe, and equal with little to play for unless Black errs. 3.f3 trades that security for an unbalanced game in which you have the initiative and carry the risks.

lines.name: Main line continued: 10...Qc7 11.Qe1
lines.summary: Black's most popular tenth move, taken from elite games: White swings the queen to h4 and keeps the pin on f6 until Black decides about the g4 bishop. Elite results are not kind to White here, so know the plan.

next.text: The most popular reply (about half of the elite games). The queen and the bishop look at h2, which White's king has to remember, and the queen backs up ...exd4.
Heads for h4, where it attacks the pinned f6 knight and the g4 bishop's support. With the queen off d1 the g4 bishop no longer pins the knight, and ...exd4 can be met by cxd4 with a safe centre.
Doubles the pressure on e4 and gets the rook off the a8-h1 diagonal.

The idea. Black's bishop is attacked and the f6 knight is pinned twice. Black has to choose between ...Bxf3 (giving up the bishop pair) and keeping the bishop with ...Bh5.

**What to know:** do not rush e4-e5. The break only works when the Bd6 is loose; with ...Qc7 and ...Rae8 Black meets e5 with ...Bxe5 and the pinned pieces slip away. Keep the position tense and wait for the bishop to give up the pin.

**Verdict:** a balanced middlegame with the safer king for White and the easier moves for Black. In the elite database White scored only 6 wins in 20 games with 11.Qe1, so this position is a warning that the line is a way to get a game and not an edge: understand the plan (Qh4, Bb3, Rae1, Nh4) and choose it when you are the better-prepared player.
Keeps the bishop; the queen goes to h4 anyway.
Gains space against the bishop.
The bishop retreats to the safest diagonal; ...b5 has weakened c5 and c6, but Black has gained space.
Asks the bishop what it wants right away, but 11...Bh5 and the pin on f6 is worth less once the bishop is on h5. This also scored poorly (3 wins for White in 12).

lines.name: Black changes his set-up: 8...Bh5 and 8...b5
lines.summary: Black keeps the bishop for ...Bg6 or breaks with ...b5 before developing the dark bishop. The same Bg5 and Nbd2 set-up works.

next.text: Avoids the pin and heads for g6 to hit e4. It costs a tempo, and the f3 knight is free to move: the second most popular eighth move (about one game in eight).
Back to the same plan. The pin on f6 is still there, and the h5 bishop has no way to attack e4 while the f6 knight is pinned.
The main-line position, with the bishop on h5 instead of g4. Black has avoided the pin on f3, but also the chance of ...Bxf3 followed by a bishop pair; both sides have fewer options.
Again the plan of Qh4, now against the h5 bishop. Compare the previous line: the position is the same except for the bishop's square.
Same idea as in the main line, played first.
Hits the bishop at once.
Black gains queenside space, but the c6 pawn and the c5 square are weaker, and the bishop on b3 stays on the a2-g8 diagonal against f7.

lines.name: 5...exd4 6.Bc4 Nf6 7.O-O Bc5 8.Ng5 O-O 9.Nxf7: the pinned knight
lines.summary: Black grabs d4, White develops instead of recapturing. If Black castles into Ng5 and Nxf7, the knight on f6 is pinned along the f-file and White wins material.

next.text: Black takes the pawn (about one game in six). The pawn on d4 is not going anywhere, so White does not recapture at once.

**Idea:** the Fantasy gambit. White ignores the pawn and develops with tempo: bishop to c4, castle, the rook on the f-file, a knight to g5, so that f7 is attacked three times before Black has castled. The pawn on d4 can be taken back with Nxd4 or Qxd4 whenever it suits.

**Why it works:** Black's king is still in the middle and only his pawns are developed. In elite games White scores about 65% after 6.Bc4, the best result of any line in this chapter. The quiet 6.Nxd4 is possible but gives Black time for ...Bc5 and ...Nf6.
The most popular reply (about 40%). It develops and attacks the e4 pawn.
Castling instead of defending e4: every tempo goes into development, and the rook joins the f-file behind the f7 target.
Defends d4 and eyes g1, but leaves f7 to the king alone.
Doubles on f7. Black's natural move now loses.
Castles into the combination. The king arrives on the f-file just in time for the pin.
The knight sacrifice that makes the pin work. Black has to take it, and did so in 15 of 15 elite games.
The bishop sacrifice pulls the king onto f7.

**The point:** the king now stands on f7 with the rook on f1 behind the f6 knight. The knight is pinned, so it cannot take anything and it cannot move.

Material is roughly level (two minor pieces for a rook and a pawn), but the pin decides the rest.
The queen checks on the diagonal that the pinned knight cannot cover, and then takes the c5 bishop along the fifth rank.
Kg8 or ...g6 makes no difference: the c5 bishop falls either way.
White is the exchange up with a safe king; the black king is bare and the queenside undeveloped.

**Verdict:** White wins material by force. Black's last resource is to take the e4 pawn, but the knight and the d4 pawn are loose and White has the exchange. In elite games this sequence won 14 of 18, and the study files it under the worst moves Black can make.
Also strong: the pawn attacks the pinned knight. With the bishop on c5 the queen move wins more, but e5 is the way to win the knight when there is nothing to capture on c5 (see the next line).
Grabs a pawn and leaves f7 to its fate.
The study's picture of how fast Black's position falls apart.
The king is dragged up the board and cannot get back; the finish is a mating attack.

lines.name: 7...Be7 8.Ng5 O-O 9.Nxf7 and 11.e5
lines.summary: The same sacrifice against the quieter bishop move. With nothing on c5 to win, White wins the pinned knight with e5.

next.text: The second most popular seventh move (about a third of the games). The bishop covers f6 and the king's squares, so Black thinks he is safe from Ng5.
The same idea. Playing 8.e5 first is the alternative and it scores poorly (2 wins in 11).
There is no bishop on c5 to win, but the f6 knight is pinned to the king and the pawn attacks it. The knight cannot move without exposing the king to the rook, so it is lost.
Gives the king a square and offers a pawn back.

**Verdict:** White has the exchange for a pawn, a safe king and the d4 pawn to take back. In the 31 elite games with 11.e5 White won 20 and lost 9. Every one of the 40 players who reached this position castled on move 8, so the line has not been tested against a Black who finds something else.

lines.name: 7...Be6 8.Bxe6 fxe6 9.e5: kicking the knight
lines.summary: Black challenges the bishop at once. After the exchange on e6 White kicks the knight with e5 and the Ng5 jump hits e6; the d4 pawn is regained with interest.

next.text: Challenges the bishop before it can do any harm. Played in about one game in eight.
Gives up the bishop pair for a pawn structure.
Black's pawns are now e6, c6, d4: the e6 pawn is isolated once the e-file opens, and the f-file is open for White's rook.
Attacks the knight. The e5 pawn cramps Black and takes d5 and f6 from his pieces.
The knight goes to d5, where it blocks the d-file and covers f4 and b4.
Attacks the e6 pawn and threatens to take on d4. Black has to answer both. Elite games: 11 games, 10 wins for White.

**Verdict:** a very small sample, but White has the easier game: the d4 pawn will be regained (Qxd4), e6 is a weakness and f7 and the f-file belong to White. The risk is the same as everywhere else in this chapter: the king on g1 faces the a7-g1 diagonal if a dark-squared bishop reaches it.
Keeps the knight active on e4, and the elite results favour Black (8 wins for Black in 16).
Also possible: Ng5 hits e6 and h7. In elite games it scored worse than e5 (one win in three).

lines.name: 6...Bg4 and 6...Bb4+: the early sixth moves
lines.summary: 6...Bg4 walks into Bxf7+ and Ne5+; 6...Bb4+ forces White to give another pawn but gets a strong attack.

next.text: Pins the knight again and wants to take on f3.
The same tactic as in the 5...Bg4 line.
A fork of the king and the bishop on g4, which is also attacked by the queen.
**Verdict:** White has regained the sacrificed pawn and taken away the black king's right to castle; the elite results in this line (7 games) were 6 wins for White.
Black interposes the check.
The move played in 19 of the 23 elite games.
The elite choice (12 of 14 games). Black has taken two pawns, White has taken one and dragged the king out.

**Verdict:** a real gambit. White is a pawn down and has open lines against the king. Four elite games reached 9.Qb3, which is far too few to call it theory. It is a sharp side branch; if you want to avoid it, recapture 6.Nxd4 against 5...exd4.

lines.name: 5...Be6 6.c3 Nd7 7.Bd3 Ngf6 8.O-O Bd6 9.Kh1
lines.summary: Black declines the pin and keeps the e5 pawn with the bishop on e6. White builds the centre with c3 and Bd3, castles and tucks the king away on h1.

next.text: Declines the pin. The bishop covers c4, so Bc4 would be met by ...Bxc4, and it guards d5. The second most popular fifth move (about 29%) and the quieter way to fight the centre.

Supports d4 so that ...exd4 can be answered by cxd4, and keeps Qb3 in reserve against b7. The most played move by far (about two thirds of the games). Bc4 is pointless here because the e6 bishop trades it off.
Guards e5, leaves the c-pawn alone and prepares ...Ngf6 and ...Bd6.
The bishop backs e4 and eyes h7. About 80% of the games.

**Idea:** the standard Fantasy waiting move. The king leaves the g1-a7 diagonal, so ...Bc5 and ...Bxg1 tricks stop mattering, and White prepares Bg5, Ng5 or Qe1-h4 without worrying about a check on g1. In elite games White scored 63% with 9.Kh1 (84 games), clearly more than with the other ninth moves.
Takes g5 away from the bishop and the knight.
The bishop steps aside from the ...h6 kick and eyes the c5 and a7 squares. Elite results here: 24 wins, 2 draws and 15 losses in 41 games.

**Position:** a manoeuvring game. White has the pair d4/e4 and the half-open f-file; Black has a solid centre and the bishops pointed at the king.

**Plans for White:** Nbd2 and Qe2 (or Qe1), Rae1 and a later dxe5 to open the f-file; Ng5 when the bishop on e6 can be traded; a4 to fix the queenside. **Plans for Black:** ...Qc7 and ...Rae8; ...exd4 cxd4 to free the pieces and put a knight on b4; ...Bg4 to bring the last piece into play.

**Verdict:** balanced, with White a little freer. The book stops here and the choice is yours.
Also possible: the knight supports e4 and frees the queen's rook for e1.
Another way to keep the pieces flexible.
59% for White in 32 elite games.

lines.name: 5...Be6 6.Bg5: the d5 break (study line)
lines.summary: A rare alternative from a Lichess study: Bg5 and the pawn break d5 force a series of trades that end level. Included for the pattern, not as the main weapon.

next.text: An alternative to 6.c3 given by a Lichess study: the bishop develops with the idea of the pawn break d5. It is rare (nine elite games).
Counterattacks b2 and takes the queen out of the centre.
**Idea:** the pawn break clears d4 and gives the knight a route. After 7...Bg4 White ignores the pawn on b2 and plays Nbd2-c4, using the tempo gained on the black queen.
Hits the queen at once and prepares the pawn push.
The pawn attacks the queen and cramps Black.
Takes the pawn with a tempo on the g4 bishop.

**Verdict:** a level position. The sequence is a series of trades that give back the extra pawns, and White's lead is better development with the king on the queenside. Interesting as a pattern, but 6.c3 is easier to play and scored better.

lines.name: 5...Nd7 6.Bc4: the knight steps in
lines.summary: Black defends e5 with the b8 knight and keeps the bishop home. White takes on the gambit idea with 6.Bc4 exd4 7.O-O, or meets 6...Bd6 with the main-line set-up.

next.text: Defends e5 without committing the c8 bishop, but blocks its own bishop and queen. Rare (about 2% of the games).
The usual developing move, aimed at f7.
The pawn grab: about 60% of Black's replies.
The same gambit idea as against 5...exd4: develop, castle, and wait for Black to run out of useful moves.
Gains space with tempo. The knight must go to d5 or e4.

The same king move as in the 5...Be6 line: the knight on d5 and a bishop on c5 would bear on g1, so the king steps off the diagonal. Elite games with 9.Kh1: 6 games, 4 wins for White, so the sample is small.

**Verdict:** unclear but easy for White: the bishop sits on b3, the d4 pawn will fall to Nxd4 or Qxd4, and Black is cramped by the pawn on e5. The sample is only a few games, and the position is playable for both sides.
Simplifies, but gives up the bishop and leaves Black a healthy d-pawn after ...cxd5. Elite results with this: 4 wins, 1 draw and 4 losses in 9 games.
Keeps the pawn centre and the bishop.

The main-line structure, but Black's c8 bishop has not committed, so there is no pin and the Bg5 plan is less pointed. The elite results were poor for White (6 wins in 18), which is why 5...Nd7 is a line to treat with respect.

lines.name: 3...e6 4.Nc3 Bb4 5.Bf4 Ne7 6.Qd3 b6 7.Nge2 Ba6
lines.summary: Black builds a French-style position and pins the knight. White develops with Bf4 and Qd3, aiming at e5 and queenside castling while Black tries to free his bad bishop.

next.text: The most common reply in elite games (about a third). It does not take on e4, so White has played f3 for a move that does little, and the position is a French Defence in which the c8 bishop is buried behind ...e6 and waits for a square. The f3 pawn is no longer a recapturing pawn: it will go to f4 after e5, which is the usual plan.
The main move (about two thirds of the games): the knight adds a defender to e4 and a second attacker on d5. Black's choices are 4...Bb4 (the pin), 4...Nf6 (the next game), 4...Qb6 and 4...Nd7.
Pins the knight and takes the pressure off e4. Almost half of the games.

The study's choice, in about 12% of elite games: the bishop eyes c7 and the b8-h2 diagonal and gets out before ...Nf6-e4 or ...Bxc3 bxc3 spoils the structure. The more common alternatives are 5.Bd2 (a third of the games) and 5.a3 (a quarter), which both score around 54% for White.
The knight heads for f5 or g6 to challenge the f4 bishop.
Backs up the pinned knight (so that ...Bxc3+ can be recaptured with the queen), eyes the b1-h7 diagonal and leaves d1 for the rook.
Prepares ...Ba6 to hit the queen and bring the bishop out. Black's whole problem in this line is the c8 bishop, and the b6-a6 plan solves it.
Develops the last piece so that ...Bxc3 can be met by Nxc3 and the structure stays healthy, and clears the way for long castling.
**Verdict:** balanced. Black has freed his bishop; White has the centre and the queen has to step aside from d3. Aim for e5 followed by f4 once Black's pieces are committed, and castle long.
Rare in elite play.
Black plays ...e5 anyway, two moves later than in the main line.
The centre is still White's, the knight is on f3 at last and Black has no developed piece.
The queen hits b2 and d4.

By far the most played reply (168 elite games), but the sample is a warning: 5...Nf6 6.Be3 won for White 16 times in 26 games, while 5...Nd7 won for Black 41 times in 59. If Black finds ...Nd7 you are not getting an advantage.

lines.name: 3...e6 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.e5 Nfd7 6.f4 c5 7.Nf3 Nc6 8.Be3: a Steinitz French
lines.summary: After 4...Nf6 5.e5 the Fantasy turns into the Steinitz Variation of the French Defence, with an extra move for each side. The chain e5-f4 gives White space and a kingside attack.

next.text: Challenges e4 at once.
Gains a tempo on the knight and prepares f4: the f3 pawn becomes the support of the e5 pawn, a better use of it than in any other line.

White now has the Steinitz chain e5-f4. The study says Black is "down in development" here; in fact each side has used one extra pawn move (f2-f3-f4 against c7-c6-c5), so the position is the French Steinitz Variation with the same player to move.
The French break against the base of the chain.
Develops and guards d4.
Black adds a second attacker to d4.

**Position:** the main-line position of the French Steinitz (it arises in some 15,000 elite games). White supports d4 with the bishop and Qd2, castles long or short, and keeps a space advantage.

**Plans for White:** Qd2 and O-O-O (or Be2 and O-O), then g4 and f5 or a kingside storm; keep d4 supported and answer ...cxd4 with Nxd4. **Plans for Black:** pressure on d4 with ...cxd4 Nxd4 and ...Qb6 (or ...Bc5, ...O-O); ...f6 to undermine the e5 pawn; ...a6, ...Be7 and ...Rb8 on the queenside.

**Verdict:** equal with accurate play; the main French theory applies. The Fantasy move order suits players who like these positions and know the French well, and it is no better than a normal French for White.
The study's move order.
The exchange on d4 hands Black the c-file, but gives White an outpost and quick development.
Gives up the tension. Black regains the pawn at once with ...Nxc5 or ...Bxc5, and the chain loses its point.

lines.name: 4.Be3: an alternative fourth move
lines.summary: The bishop move keeps the c3 square free and meets 4...Nf6 5.e5 with the same Steinitz set-up. 4...dxe4 is the sharp reply.

next.text: The second most popular fourth move (15%): the bishop supports d4 and keeps c3 free, so ...Bb4 has no pin. The price is that ...Qb6 hits b2 and the bishop is exposed to ...Nf6-g4 ideas.
**Verdict:** the same Steinitz position as in the previous line. Prefer 4.Nc3 unless you like the gambit.
The sharp reply.
Black gets in the check at once.

A pawn sacrifice: Qe2 prepares Bg2 against the queen on e4, and the greedy 7...Qxh1 8.Bg2 Qxh2 keeps Black's queen alive.
