The elite results are very good for White (36 wins in 54 games), but this is the one line in the chapter for which I found no published explanation, so learn it only if you want to risk it.

lines.name: 3...Qb6 4.Nc3 dxe4 5.Bc4 Nf6 6.fxe4 e5 7.dxe5 Ng4 8.Qe2
lines.summary: The queen sortie is Black's most awkward way to meet the Fantasy. White develops with Bc4 instead of recapturing, then regains the pawn and meets ...e5 with dxe5 and Qe2. Roughly equal.

next.text: The queen hits b2 and d4 at once and stops White from simply recapturing and enjoying the big centre. The third most popular reply (16%) and Black's best practical try.
Develops and keeps the knight flexible. Black's choices are 4...dxe4 (70%), 4...e6 and 4...e5.
Takes the pawn so that White's pieces cannot use the e4 square.

**Idea:** the study's choice (27% of the games). Instead of recapturing with the f-pawn, White develops with tempo against f7 and keeps the option of taking on e4 with the knight. If Black takes on f3, the knight recaptures with a lead in development. The main alternative is 5.fxe4 (56%), but it leaves b2 and d4 as targets and 5...e5 is awkward.
The most popular reply (two thirds). It defends the e4 pawn, develops and keeps the choice of ...exf3 or ...e5.
Now the pawn is regained.
Hits the centre before White consolidates.
Takes the pawn; Black will win it back with ...Ng4 and ...Nxe5, but White gains the tempo Qe2 and Bb3.
Attacks e5 and f2.
Defends e5 and eyes the knight; 57 elite games with this move.

**Position:** Black has regained the pawn; the bishop on c4 and the queen on e2 are both active, and the knight on e5 hits the bishop, so White plays Bb3.

**Plan:** Bb3 and Nf3; the knights exchange on e5 or Black answers with ...Nbd7 and ...Bg4. The c4/b3 bishop keeps f7 under pressure and the e-file pins are in the air for both sides.

**Verdict:** equal. Elite results are even (24 wins for White, 4 draws, 22 for Black).
The natural recapture and the most played move.
The right way to meet ...e5: develop and keep the tension.
Equal in elite games (about 50%). Black has ...Nf6, ...h5 or ...Bc5; the Bc5 line (8.Na4) scored badly for White (12 wins in 29 elite games), so know it before you walk in.
A mistake: the pawn grab hands the initiative to Black, who develops with tempo. Black's bishop comes to e6 with ideas of ...Bc4 (stopping White from castling) and ...Bc5 against g1.
The extra pawn on e5 will fall, and the elite results favour Black (44 wins for Black, 34 for White).

lines.name: 3...Qb6 4.Nc3 dxe4 5.Bc4 exf3 6.Nxf3 Nf6 7.O-O
lines.summary: Black grabs the second pawn. White is a pawn down but develops a bishop and a knight with tempo and castles.

next.text: Black accepts the second pawn. White is now a pawn down.

A real gambit: White has developed the knight and bishop with a lead on the king, and Black's queen is the one piece that has moved. Elite games show an even result (10 wins for White, 9 for Black in 20 games).
The king gets out and the rook stands behind the f7 target. **Verdict:** a gambit for development: White has two pieces out and the f-file; Black has the extra pawn and an undeveloped queenside.

lines.name: 3...Qb6 4.a4 a5 5.exd5 cxd5 6.Nc3 Nf6 7.Nb5
lines.summary: A quiet way to meet the queen: a4 stops ...Qb4+ and ...Qxb2 ideas, and after ...a5 the knight lands on b5. Rare, but it scores well.

next.text: Threatens a5, gaining time on the queen and taking b4 and b6 away. It also supports a knight on b5. Played in only 5% of the games, but White scored 65% in them.
Stops a4-a5. The pawn on a5 weakens b5, which cannot be defended by a pawn any more.
Removes Black's central pawn and lets the knight come to c3 and b5 at once.
**Idea:** the outpost on b5 is protected by the a4 pawn and Black has no pawn to chase it. It hits c7 and d6 and ties Black's queen to c7.
**Verdict:** pleasant for White. The sample is small (nine games after 6...Nf6, with 7 wins for White), but the structure favours the knight on b5 and White has a lead in development.
Black hits the centre.

lines.name: 3...g6 4.Nc3 Bg7 5.Be3 Qb6 6.b3
lines.summary: Black fianchettoes and goes for the dark squares. White guards d4 with Be3, then stops the ...Qxb2 grab with b3.

next.text: A Modern-style reply (9%): the fianchettoed bishop attacks the centre from the long diagonal. Combined with ...Qb6 it makes the f3 pawn a liability, because the dark squares around the white king are weak.
Natural development; the pawn on d4 needs support.
The main move (83%): the bishop guards d4 and prepares Qd2 and O-O-O.
The most popular reply (36%) hits b2 and d4 together.

Closes the diagonal so the b2 pawn is no longer a target. The best-scoring reply in the elite sample (21 wins, 2 draws and 8 losses in 31 games). The price is a weakened c3 and the long diagonal that Black's Bg7 eyes.
Black's main reply (about 57%): he breaks the centre before White consolidates.

**Verdict:** the knight comes out and covers g3, c3 and d4. White gets a playable position with an extra tempo in the centre, but it is no better than equal, and the Bg7 on the long diagonal is a constant reminder of what the f3 pawn costs.
The study's move.

A pawn is sacrificed for activity: the black queen on a3 is out of play for a while, but White cannot castle short, the dark squares around the king are weak and the f3 pawn is badly placed. The study's author did not like it, and the elite results agree: 43 wins for White, 54 for Black in 103 games.
Another way to cover b2.
Also good for Black.
The bishop has to retreat to g1. It looks awkward, but 8.Bg1 is the book move (33 of 38 elite games) and scores about even (14 wins, 3 draws, 16 losses).
The French structure again, with the extra Bg7 for Black. Slightly worse for White in the sample (15 wins in 39 games).

lines.name: 3...e5 4.dxe5 Bc5 5.Nc3 Qb6 6.Na4 Qa5+ 7.c3 Bxg1 8.Rxg1 dxe4
lines.summary: Black offers a pawn to open the diagonal to g1. White takes it, answers ...Bc5-Qb6 with Na4, and stands up fine after the trade of bishop for knight.

next.text: A pawn offer (5%): Black opens lines against the weakened diagonal.
Takes the pawn. 4.exd5 is the alternative but scores worse.
Aims at g1 and f2: the pawn on f3 has left the knight's guard.
Develops and eyes d5.
Doubles on f2 and hits b2.
The only move: it attacks the queen and the bishop at once.
The queen checks and keeps an eye on the knight.
Blocks the check.
Black takes the knight, since White cannot castle short anyway.

**Verdict:** equal, with 9.f4 to support the e5 pawn. White has lost the right to castle, but Black has lost his dark-squared bishop and his queen is placed on a5; elite results are about level (52 wins for White, 40 for Black in 100 games).
Black cashes in the bishop sacrifice first.

The king steps to e2 and Black swaps queens. Elite results are level (43 wins for Black, 39 for White in 84 games), and the endgame is not a simple one. You are better off steering the game to the 6...Qa5+ line.

lines.name: 3...Nf6 and the rare third moves
lines.summary: 3...Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4 is the Steinitz French again. Rare replies like ...a6, ...Nd7, ...h5 and ...Qa5+ are met by 4.Nc3.

next.text: Challenges e4 at once (3% of the games).
Gains a tempo, and the f3 pawn gets to move to f4.
Attacks the e5 pawn.
Supports e5 and sets up the Steinitz chain.
**Verdict:** a Steinitz French again; after 6...c5 7.Nf3 Nc6 8.Be3 the position is the one of the 4...Nf6 line. 4...Ng8 is also played (a third of the games) and loses time: White keeps the space.
A waiting move.
The most natural: develop and keep the centre.
Prepares ...e5 and ...Ngf6.
A French structure with the knight on d7: the Bb4 line is Black's best, but White is happy with the extra tempo of f3.
A strange move.
Black wants ...h4.
A sortie before ...dxe4.

chapters.title: Classical Variation and the Mar del Plata
chapters.subtitle: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.e4 d6 5.Nf3 O-O 6.Be2 e5
chapters.intro:
The Classical is the main road of the King's Indian. White develops without committing anything, and after 6...e5 he has to decide what to do with the centre. The repertoire answers 7.O-O with 7...Nc6, which forces that decision at once: after 8.d5 Ne7 the centre is closed and the game becomes the Mar del Plata, a race between White's queenside (c4-c5, the c-file, the squares c7 and d6) and Black's kingside (...f5-f4, ...g5-g4).

White is usually faster and Black plays for higher stakes. That is the whole character of the line: Black has to spend exactly as many moves on defence as the position demands and not one more, and he has to know the standard regrouping and the standard sacrifices by heart, because they are too slow to work out at the board.

The chapter also covers the ways White avoids the race: the Bayonet (9.b4), which fights on both wings, the Petrosian (7.d5), the Gligoric (7.Be3) and the Exchange (7.dxe5). Against all of them the same pieces go to the same kinds of squares, and the notes say where the differences lie.

sections.title: Why 7...Nc6, and the other seventh moves
sections.body:
7...Nc6 attacks d4 a second time, so White cannot go on making useful moves and keep the tension. 8.d5 gains a tempo on the knight, but it also gives Black what he wants: a fixed centre, a clear plan and a king's knight that can leave f6 without e4 becoming a target. 8.Be3 and 8.dxe5 are the only ways to avoid this and both are harmless.

The other seventh moves are respectable and are not the repertoire:

- **7...Na6** keeps everything flexible (the knight goes to c5 after d5) and avoids the heaviest theory, but it puts no pressure on d4, so White chooses the structure.
- **7...Nbd7** is the old main line: solid, with ...c6, ...Re8 and ...exd4 in reserve. It blocks the c8-bishop and leaves White a free hand with Re1, Bf1 and Rb1.
- **7...exd4** 8.Nxd4 Re8 9.f3 gives up the centre for piece play against e4 and d4. White keeps more space and a small pull if he knows what he is doing.

sections.title: The Mar del Plata structure
sections.body:
The pawn chains point in opposite directions and each side attacks the base of the other's chain. White wants c4-c5 and cxd6, then the c-file, a knight on b5 and an entry on c7; the pawn on d6 and the squares c7 and a7 are his targets. Black wants ...f5-f4, ...g5-g4 and then ...g3 or ...gxf3, and his target is g2 and the king behind it.

Three things decide the race:

- **The f6-knight must get out of the f-pawn's way.** After 9.Ne1 it goes to d7, where it also holds up c5; after 9.b4 it goes to h5, because c5 can no longer be held up and the knight is better aimed at f4.
- **Black never plays ...fxe4.** It gives White the e4-square and the open diagonal for nothing. The pawn goes to f4 as soon as White has played f3 or Be3.
- **White's dark-squared bishop decides which line it is.** On e3-f2 it eyes a7 and defends the king but loses a tempo to ...f4; on d2 it supports the queenside from a distance and keeps e1 for retreat.

sections.title: The attacking set-up
sections.body:
This is the formation Gligoric worked out, and every piece in it does two jobs:

- **...Rf7** covers c7 along the rank, so that the c-file leads nowhere, and frees f8.
- **...Bf8** covers d6, the base of the chain, and frees g7.
- **...Rg7** puts the rook behind the g-pawn, where ...g4 opens its file.
- **...Ng6** and then **...Nh4** bring the knight to the square that attacks g2 and f3.
- **...h5** supports ...g4. When White has played h3, ...g4 comes as a pawn sacrifice and the knight returns from e8 to f6 to recapture or to jump to h5 and g3.
- **...Ne8** is the one purely defensive move: it guards c7 and d6 while the others are regrouping, and it comes back to f6 as soon as the queenside is under control.

The order depends on what White threatens. A knight on b5 means ...Rf7 at once; pressure on d6 means ...Bf8; if White is slow, ...h5 and ...g4 come first.

sections.title: The c8-bishop and the sacrifices
sections.body:
The bishop on c8 looks undeveloped for twenty moves and is the most important attacking piece on the board. From its original square it supports ...g4 and it is the piece that sacrifices itself on h3 when White has answered ...g3 or ...g4 with h3. Black therefore avoids exchanging it: he does not put it on d7 unless that gains time against a knight on b5, he answers Bg4 ideas by keeping the diagonal closed, and in Korchnoi-Kasparov he even played ...Bb7-c8 to bring it home. White, for his part, will give a lot to exchange it, with Nb5-c7-e6 or Na7xc8.

The standard blows:

- **...g3** as a pawn sacrifice (the diagram, from Taimanov-Najdorf, 1953): after hxg3 fxg3 Bxg3 Black has ...Nh5, ...Bh6 or ...Be7-g5, the f4-square and the dark squares around the king. If White ignores the pawn it sits on g3 and the queen comes to h4.
- **...Bxh3** when a pawn stands on g3 and White has played h3: gxh3 Qd7 or ...Qc8 and the queen arrives on h3. Kotronias's rule of thumb: once a pawn has reached g3, the d8-h4 diagonal is what matters, and clearing it by sacrifice is often correct.
- **...g4 with h3 already played**: fxg4 hxg4 hxg4 (or Nxg4) and Black uses the h-file, h4 for the knight and g5 for the bishop.
- **...Nxg3** in the 9.Nd2 lines, where White has played g3 against a knight on h5.

sections.title: Holding the queenside
sections.body:
Black cannot stop c5; he can only make it cost something. With the knight on d7, c5 needs b4 or Nd3 first, and in the modern main line (the diagram) White gives the pawn up to save the time. Black takes it.

The rules for the defence:

- **Nb5 aims at c7 and at a7.** Against c7 the answer is ...Rf7, never a panicky ...Ne8 unless d6 needs it as well. Against a7, with White's bishop on f2, the answer is ...b6 and not ...a6, which runs into Na7! and the loss of the c8-bishop.
- **...a6** is right when the knight simply has to go back (with the bishop on d2, or after a4) and the hole on b6 cannot be used.
- **After cxd6, recapture with the c-pawn.** The chain stays intact and the c-file is covered by ...Rf7.
- **A pawn on a7 can be left hanging** when the knight that takes it is stranded there, or when ...Rc7 hits a queen on c2. Count the tempi: a knight on a7 is three moves from the kingside.
- **Do not defend more than once.** Every extra defensive move is a tempo taken from ...h5 and ...g4.

sections.title: The Bayonet: the knight on e6
sections.body:
9.b4 prepares c5 in one move and keeps the king's knight on f3, from where it can go to g5 and e6 the moment Black plays ...f5. That changes the game: the race is replaced by a fight for the centre.

Black's knight goes to h5 instead of d7 because holding up c5 is no longer possible and f4 is a real outpost. White meets that with Re1 (so that ...Nf4 can be answered by Bf1) and after ...f5 with Ng5. The knight cannot be tolerated on e6, so Black takes it, and a white pawn appears on e6. It cuts Black's position in two, and it is also far from home: Black surrounds it with ...c6, ...Qc8 or ...Nc6-d4 and opens the centre with ...d5 when the long diagonal and the f-file favour him. Most main lines end in equal positions with opposite plans rather than in mating attacks, and Black needs patience here more than memory.

sections.title: 9.Nd2: prophylaxis on both sides
sections.body: With the knight on d2 White is a move faster with c5 and Nc4 than after 9.Ne1, so the straightforward race is bad for Black. He slows White down with ...a5, which costs White a3 and Rb1, and then plays the manoeuvre that belongs to this line: ...Kh8 and ...Ng8. The knight on e7 has no future on g6 here, because White has not played f3 and f4 is not yet a target; from g8 it goes to f6 or h6, the bishop gets h6, and the king is off the a2-g8 diagonal. White's knight on d2 is passive on the kingside, so Black can afford to build up slowly and sacrifice on g3 when the pieces are ready.

sections.title: The Petrosian System
sections.body: White closes the centre before Black's knight is on c6, so there is no ...Ne7, and he pins the f6-knight to make ...f5 hard to arrange. Black's set-up is a chain of small moves, each with a precise point: ...a5 secures c5 for a knight; ...Na6 rather than ...Nbd7 keeps d7 free; ...h6 fixes the bishop's diagonal; ...Qe8 breaks the pin; ...Nh7 clears the f-pawn; ...Bd7 connects queen and rook so that b4 loses a pawn; ...h5 threatens to trap the bishop with ...g5 and ...h4 and so forces f3; and then ...Bh6-e3 exchanges or activates the bad bishop through the hole f3 has left. Only after that does ...f5 come.

sections.title: The Gligoric System and the bishop dance
sections.body: 7.Be3 keeps the king in the centre and the tension in place, and it takes the sting out of 7...Nc6: after 8.d5 Ne7 9.Nd2! White has not castled into the attack and is ready for the queenside. The repertoire therefore hits the bishop with 7...Ng4 8.Bg5 f6. Both sides have made concessions: White's bishop has moved three times, and Black has blocked his own bishop with ...f6 and has a knight to bring back via h6 and f7. Now ...Nc6 is good, because d5 no longer comes with Nd2 in hand. The same positions arise from 7.O-O Nc6 8.Be3 Ng4, and the lines are built to transpose.

sections.title: The Exchange Variation
sections.body: White wins nothing by force (9.Nxe5 Nxe4), and the structure favours Black in the long run: he can cover d5 with ...c6, while d4 is a permanent hole in White's camp. White's chances lie in his lead in development over the next five moves, with Bg5, Nd5 and O-O-O. Black answers each threat exactly, exchanges the knight that lands on d5, plays ...c6, and then manoeuvres a knight towards d4 by ...Na6-c5-e6 or ...Nd7-c5-e6. The ending is equal, and it is the player who knows these manoeuvres who wins it.

lines.name: 9.Ne1 Nd7 10.Be3: 13.Rc1 and the c5 pawn sacrifice
lines.summary: The modern main line. White gives the c-pawn to open the queenside at once; Black takes it, parks a knight on a6 and attacks with ...h5 and ...g4.

next.text: Black can play this without preparation: 7.dxe5 dxe5 8.Qxd8 Rxd8 9.Nxe5 does not win a pawn because of 9...Nxe4 (see the Exchange Variation).
White keeps the tension, so Black increases it.

The repertoire move. A second attack on d4 means White cannot go on making useful moves: he has to close the centre (8.d5), release it (8.dxe5) or defend it with a piece that can be harassed (8.Be3 Ng4). Closing it gains a tempo on the knight, but a closed centre is exactly what Black wants, because the f6-knight can then leave without e5 or e4 becoming a problem and the f-pawn can advance.

The Mar del Plata. On e7 the knight looks clumsy, but it is the right square: it supports ...f5 and goes to g6 as soon as the f-pawn has passed, whereas from b8 it would need three moves to do anything.

**Plans:** White attacks the base of Black's chain with c5, opens the c-file and aims at c7, d6 and a7. Black attacks the base of White's with ...f5-f4 and ...g5-g4. White is usually faster; Black is playing for mate.
The knight goes to d3 to support c5 and f4, and the f-pawn is free to defend e4. This is the line where the race is run in its purest form.
The knight has to release the f-pawn, and from d7 it also covers c5, so that White needs b4 or Nd3 before he can break. It will return to f6 once ...f4 has been played.
The most ambitious square. The bishop supports c5, eyes a7 and will defend the king from f2. The drawback is that ...f4 comes with tempo.
White must keep e4 protected by a pawn. 11.exf5 gxf5 only helps Black, who gets e4 covered and a mobile centre with ...f4 or ...Nf6 and ...e4 in the air.
Never ...fxe4: after fxe4 White has the f-file and Black has no pawn break left.
The attack is under way. Black intends ...Ng6, ...Nf6, ...Rf7, ...Bf8, ...Rg7 and ...h5 in whatever order White's threats allow, and then ...g4.
The modern main line. White wants c5 without spending a move on b4 or Nd3, and with the rook already on the c-file the pawn can be offered.

The move order matters. After 13...Nf6 14.c5 Ng6 15.cxd6 cxd6 16.Nb5 White has the c-file and the b5-knight for free and Black is a tempo short. By keeping the knight on d7 for one more move Black makes White pay for c5 with a pawn.
White gives the pawn to open lines before Black has finished regrouping.
With the knight, so that the chain d6-c7 stays intact.

The only square that works: 15...Nd7 16.Nb5 wins back c7 or a7 at once with a bind. From a6 the knight guards c7 and attacks b4. It is out of play for the attack, but Black is a pawn up and still has everything he needs on the kingside.
The usual move: the knight covers b4's weakness by threatening a7.

Developing with a threat to take the knight is one of the few times the bishop leaves c8 willingly, and it can go back. 17.Nxa7 regains the pawn but sends the knight to the edge of the board, three moves from the kingside.

White supports the knight and keeps the bind.

**Verdict:** White has lasting pressure for the pawn: the a6-knight is tied down and b5 is a fine outpost. Black has an extra pawn and an untouched attack: ...h5 and ...Rf7 come next, then ...g4, and the bishop can take on b5 whenever the knight becomes dangerous. All the recent repertoire books treat 13.Rc1 as the critical test of 10.Be3; in practice both sides win games from this position.
Protects b4 first and keeps Nb5 for later.
Covering c7 before it is attacked. Black continues ...h5, ...Bf8 or ...Bh6 and ...g4, and meets Nb5 with ...Bd7.
The slow way.
The 13.Nd3 line by transposition, see there.
Aiming at a7 as well as c7.
Not 14...a6, when the knight goes to a7 and takes the c8-bishop; the trick is shown under 13.Nb5. After ...b6 the knight will be driven back by ...a6 when it suits Black.
A different way to attack, with pieces: ...Rh6 or ...Rg6 and ...Qe8-h5, while the knight stays on d7 to hold c5. It is rarer and less well mapped; a reasonable second weapon.

The alternative, and Kasparov played both. From e8 the knight guards c7 and d6 in advance, but it does nothing to hold up c5, so White gets his break a move sooner. Worth knowing as a surprise; the plans are the same.

A sound second system, not the repertoire. The knight waits for d5 to go to c5 and Black keeps ...Qe8, ...Ng4 and ...c6 in reserve. It avoids the long forcing lines, at the price of leaving White the choice of structure.
The old main line: solid, with ...c6, ...Re8 and ...exd4 to come. The knight blocks the c8-bishop and puts no pressure on d4, so White builds up at leisure with Re1, Bf1 and Rb1.
Gives up the centre for play against e4.
White has more space and a small, lasting pull. Black's set-up with ...c6 and ...d5 or ...Nbd7-c5 is playable but it is a different opening from the one in this chapter.

lines.name: 10.Be3: 13.a4 a5
lines.summary: Korchnoi's 13.a4 prepares a5 and c5. Black stops the pawn with ...a5 and ...b6, accepts a knight on c6 and gets on with the attack.

next.text: Korchnoi's move. The a-pawn is to go to a5, after which c5 arrives with more force, a6 can break up the queenside and the bishop on f2 bears on b6 and a7.
The modern answer. The queenside is now much harder to open: White needs b4, and after ...axb4 Black has the a-file and the c5-square is still covered. The price is the hole on b5.
Heading for b4 after the pawn exchange, or supporting c5.
Now c5 is ruled out for a long time and b4 can be met by ...axb4. The move also takes b6 away from White's bishop.
The knight has done its work on d7 and returns to support ...g4.
The point of White's play: the knight cannot be left there.

**Verdict:** the structure has changed in Black's favour in one respect and White's in another. The pawn on c6 cramps the queenside and gives White d5 for the other knight, but it is cut off from its supporters, Black's d6-pawn is no longer a target and the centre is closed for good. Black attacks the pawn with ...Qe8 or covers d5 with ...Be6, and then plays ...h5 and ...g4. Chances are level.
White wants to recapture on b4 with the bishop and free f2 for the knight.
Black simply continues; ...Nf6, ...Ng6 and ...g4 follow.
The older move, which allows 14.a5. It is playable, and it was the scene of a model attack.
Keeping the queenside closed.
The bishop goes straight back to the diagonal where it belongs.
Korchnoi-Kasparov, Amsterdam 1991. The bishop came to g5 via h6 and the queen to h6 via f8; White's king did not survive the h-file.

lines.name: 10.Be3: 13.Nd3 and 13.b4, the classical race
lines.summary: White prepares c5 the slow way and Black has time for the full Gligoric set-up. Two famous games show how the attack is carried out.

next.text: The old main line. The knight supports c5, but it has taken a move and it no longer defends g2 from e1.
Now that c5 can no longer be prevented, the knight goes where it is needed for ...g4.

Gligoric's move, and the key to the whole system. The rook covers c7 along the rank, so the open c-file gives White no entry, and it clears f8 for the bishop, which in turn will clear g7 for the rook.
White doubles on the c-file. 16.Kh1 is the modern refinement, making room for the bishop on g1; Black's set-up does not change.
Covers d6 and so frees the knight on f6 and the queen from defensive duty.
Always with the pawn: the chain stays whole.
The standard pawn sacrifice. Black does not want the g-file opened by exchanges, he wants the dark squares and the h-file.

Taimanov-Najdorf, Zurich 1953. The bishop comes to g5 and e3, the queen to g5 or h4, the knights to f4 and h4, and the c8-bishop waits for h3.

**Verdict:** White's doubled rooks hit nothing, because c7 is covered and there is no second target, while every black piece has a route to the king. This is why White looked for faster methods (13.Rc1, 13.a4) and why the line is still worth playing against anyone who chooses it.
The other way to prepare c5.
Here the bishop can come out, because it gains time against Nb5.
Black does not defend c7 a second time.
The rook is left to its fate. The pawn on g3 opens the diagonal for the queen and the knight comes to h5.

Piket-Kasparov, Tilburg 1989. Black has two pieces for the rook and the dark squares; he won in a few more moves. White's play can be improved, but the game shows how little the queenside matters once ...g3 has been played.

lines.name: 10.Be3: 13.g4 and 13.Nb5
lines.summary: White blocks the kingside before attacking on the other wing, or probes a7 first. Black switches to the h-file, and answers Nb5 with ...b6.

next.text: White stops ...g4 once and for all and means to play on the queenside with his king safe. The cost is that his own king's position has become rigid.
Keeping the pawns on the board and putting the question to g4 at once.

The plan is the h-file: ...Rh6, ...Ng6, ...Nf6 and, when everything is ready, ...hxg4 followed by an invasion on h2 or h4, or a sacrifice on g4.

**Verdict:** the attack is slower than usual and White's queenside play is as fast as ever, so Black must not hurry: he first brings every piece to the kingside and keeps c7 and d6 covered with the knight on d7 and the bishop on f8. The position is closed and manoeuvring, with chances for both sides.

The other treatment, taken en passant: after 14.hxg3 Black plays ...Ng6 and ...h5-h4 or ...Nf6-h5. It opens the position for White's bishops as well, and it gives up the f4-pawn that cramps him, so it is the second choice.
The knight attacks a7, which the bishop on f2 is also eyeing.

The right pawn. The knight will be driven away with ...a6 next, and Black has gained two moves that are useful against c5. White argues that b6 and a6 are targets for a4-a5; theory considers the position balanced.
Black continues with ...Ng6, ...Nf6 and ...h5 as usual.
The natural move loses the piece Black cannot do without.
The knight is immune: 14...Rxa7 15.Bxa7 b6 traps the bishop only for a moment, as b4 and c5 will dig it out and White has won the exchange. Otherwise Nxc8 follows and the attack has lost its bishop.

lines.name: 10.Nd3 f5 11.Bd2: the main line
lines.summary: The bishop stays out of range of ...f4 and White breaks with c5 at once. Black regroups with ...Rf7, ...Ne8, ...Bf8 and ...Rg7 and sacrifices a pawn with ...g4.

next.text: The knight supports c5 immediately and the bishop will go to d2, where ...f4 does not gain a tempo.
11.exf5 is met by 11...Nxf5 with ...Nd4 to come, and after 11.f4 exf4 Black gets the e5-square for a knight: opening the centre does not suit White here.
Back at once: the knight attacks e4, and c5 cannot be held up anyway now that the knight is on d3.
The one purely defensive move. Queen and knight both aim at c7, and the rook alone is not enough. The knight will return.
White covers g4 and h3 before Black gets there.
Covers d6 and makes room for the rook. The a7-pawn is left hanging on purpose.
The knight takes up its post.
Now that everything is ready on the kingside the knight is sent away; the hole on b6 no longer matters.
The knight returns for the breakthrough.
The break comes as a pawn sacrifice, because White has h3 and f3 covered three times.

**Verdict:** the theory ends here. For the pawn Black has g3 for the knight, an open h-file, the queen coming to g5 or h4 and the rook on g7 behind it all, while White's queenside has no target left. The line has been tested for decades and Black's compensation is regarded as full: it is White who has to find the only moves.
The pawn can be taken, and this is the tactical point of Black's set-up.
The rook hits the queen and the knight on a7 has no way back.
Material is level and Black's rooks are active. Analysts who distrust this ending play 19...Bd7 first, with the bishop then tied to the queenside; the main line is the principled choice.
White keeps the tension on d6.
Provoking a weakness.
Black has been made to play ...b6, which weakens c6, and White's bishop has taken three moves to reach e1. Black goes straight for the king.
White defends first: the knight covers g4 and h3.
Against Nb5 and Qc7. Black continues ...a6, ...Bf8 and ...g4 as a pawn sacrifice, exactly as in the main line.
An attempt to reach c7 at once.
Kotronias's recommendation, which he gives two exclamation marks: Black answers a threat to c7 by attacking.

The pawn on g3 changes everything. If White closes the kingside with 16.h3 his king is locked in and Black prepares ...Bxh3 at leisure. Against the critical 16.Bb4 and 16.Ba5 Kotronias gives 16...Nfxd5, clearing the diagonal from d8 to h4 at the cost of a piece, with at least a draw for Black in every line. His summary is worth remembering: once a pawn stands on g3, the d8-h4 diagonal is what matters.
The blockade.
The main line. The pawn stays on f4, where it cramps White, and Black will use the h-file.
Black doubles on the h-file and decides later whether to open it. The king's side is no longer a place where White can be mated quickly, but neither can he ignore it.

lines.name: 10.Nd3 f5 11.f3 f4 12.b4
lines.summary: White leaves the bishop on c1 and pushes the queenside pawns as far as they will go. Black ignores them and plays ...h5 and ...g4.

next.text: White can also start with this move; 11...f4 12.Bd2 g5 13.c5 Nf6 then transposes to the 11.Bd2 lines.
The bishop stays at home, where it is not in the way, and every tempo goes into the pawn storm: c5, a4-a5 and a6 or c6.
With no bishop on d2 or f2 White's kingside has fewer defenders, so Black can go for ...g4 without the full regrouping.
The knight is needed against ...g4.

Still the right square: it covers c7 and b7 along the rank against cxd6, a6 and c6 ideas.

**Verdict:** a pure race. In Thybo-Jones, 2021, Black preferred 16...Kh8 and after 17.a6 bxa6 18.c6 gave up the queenside completely for ...g4, ...Bh6 and ...Nh4, winning a wild game. The lesson is the same either way: White's pawns can reach the sixth rank without creating a target, and Black must not be distracted.

lines.name: 10.f3 f5 11.g4: the Benko Attack
lines.summary: White takes space on the kingside himself, to meet ...f4 with a blockade. Black keeps the tension and regroups with ...Kh8 and ...Ng8.

next.text: A flexible move. After 10...f5 White can still transpose with 11.Be3 f4 12.Bf2 g5 or 11.Nd3 f4.
Benko's idea. White wants Black to close the kingside, after which he has a free hand on the other wing.
Black does not oblige. The king leaves the g-file and the diagonal, and g8 is cleared for the knight, which will come to f6 while the bishop goes to h6 to exchange itself for White's good bishop.

**Verdict:** Black keeps the tension on f5 and g4 and improves his pieces: ...Bh6, ...Ngf6, ...a5 and ...Nc5. White's king is the more exposed if the position opens, and his extra space on the kingside is something he must defend for the rest of the game. Chances are equal.
The bishop avoids the exchange on h6 for the moment.
The same plan: ...Bh6 next, or ...f4 only now, when the bishop has to lose a move.
What White is hoping for.
The kingside is closed: ...g5 is met by h5 and ...h5 by g5, and Black has no pawn break left while White plays c5 undisturbed.

lines.name: Bayonet 9.b4 Nh5 10.Re1: 12.Bf3 c6
lines.summary: White's knight comes to e6, Black takes it and a white pawn lands there. Black breaks the centre open with ...c6 and ...d5 and reaches a level middlegame.

next.text: The Bayonet. White prepares c5 with one move and keeps the knight on f3, so that ...f5 can be answered by Ng5 and Ne6. The pawn on b4 is loose, and f4 is weak now that the c1-bishop has other duties.

In the 9.Ne1 lines the knight goes to d7 to hold up c5. Here c5 cannot be held up: 9...Nd7 10.c5 simply gives White his break with tempo. So the knight goes where it has a target, f4, and the f-pawn is released at the same time.
The main line. The rook makes room so that ...Nf4 can be met by Bf1, keeping the bishop, and it will stand well on the e-file once ...f5 has been played.
Black sticks to his plan. 10...Nf4 11.Bf1 a5 is a system of its own, with play on the queenside.
The knight heads for e6 and uncovers the bishop's attack on h5.

The knight has to move, and on f6 it attacks e4 again and takes g4 away from White's pieces. 11...Nf4 12.Bxf4 exf4 is the other line: Black gets the long diagonal, but e6 is still available to the knight and theory prefers White.
The bishop defends e4 and aims down the long diagonal at b7, which will matter once the centre opens.

The key move of the whole variation. Black attacks d5, the pawn that would support a knight or a pawn on e6. After ...h6, Ne6 Bxe6, dxe6 the pawn on e6 is cut off from its base and Black's centre is free to advance with ...d5. Playing ...h6 first comes to the same thing.
Development, with c5 or b5 to follow.
Now, with d5 gone, opening the centre is right: Black exchanges the pieces that could blockade his pawns.
The centre advances with tempo and the e6-pawn is isolated deep in Black's camp.
Takes c5 from the bishop, which would otherwise pin the knight against the rook, and prepares ...Qd6.

The queen defends e6 and eyes g6.

**Verdict:** equal, and well explored. Black has a broad centre and will attack e6 with ...Rf6 and ...Qd6, or advance with ...e4 when the long diagonal is under control. White has the bishops and pressure on d5 with Bb3 and Rad1. If the e6-pawn falls without compensation Black is better; if the centre is blockaded on the light squares White is. Most games from here are drawn.
The bishop looks at e5, and there is a concrete idea behind it.
The point: an exchange sacrifice for the long diagonal and the pawn on e6.

The queen attacks b4 and e6 and leaves the pin. White has a pawn and the dark squares for the exchange; Black's king is safer than it looks and the e6-pawn can still be rounded up. Theory regards the chances as level.
White tries to keep d5 supported by opening the c-file himself.
White lets the bishop on e4 go and takes the pinned knight instead.
The e6-pawn falls and the ending is equal.

The main alternative, and a sound one for those who want to avoid the forcing lines with Ng5. Black breaks up the queenside before c5 arrives. After 10.bxa5 he recaptures with the rook or plays 10...c5; after the more testing 10.Ba3 he gets the c5-square and an active bishop.
Black follows with ...f5 and ...Nc5 or ...Nf6. White has the b-file and the a-pawn; the game is slower and more positional than after 9...Nh5.

lines.name: Bayonet 10.Re1: 12.f3 Kh8
lines.summary: White defends e4 with the pawn and keeps the bishop for the queenside. Black answers with the prophylactic ...Kh8 and wins the e6-pawn by regrouping his knights.

next.text: The solid choice. The e4-pawn is secure for good and the bishop stays on e2 to support c5. In return White weakens the dark squares round his king and puts no pressure on b7, so Black has time.

Prophylaxis with two points. After Ne6 and dxe6 White often gains time on the a2-g8 diagonal with c5 and Qb3 or Bc4; with the king on h8 nothing comes with check. And g8 is free for a knight, which is how the e6-pawn will be surrounded.

A useful waiting move: the rook protects b4 and leaves the long diagonal. Against White's other tries (13.Be3, 13.b5, 13.c5) the ideas are the same: ...h6 or ...Ne8 to question the knight, then the e6-pawn.
The knight is finally developed to the square it was driven from on move eight, and it is on its way to d4.

The second knight steps back to let the queen and rook out and to cover e7.

**Verdict:** the e6-pawn is surrounded. Black will play ...Nd4, evict the d5-knight with ...c6 and collect the pawn with a knight or with the queen from e8. White keeps the bishop pair and some initiative while this takes place, which is enough to hold the balance and no more.
The knight does not wait to be asked.
Black has a clear route to the pawn: the bishop goes to f6 and the knight to g7. The knight also eyes f4.
Next ...Ng7 and ...Nxe6. White has to find counterplay with c5 before the pawn goes; if he does not, Black is simply a pawn up with the better structure.

lines.name: Bayonet 10.g3
lines.summary: White takes f4 from the knight at the cost of a target on g3. Black plays ...f5 and ...f4 and the fight is again about the knight on g5 and the pawn on e6.

next.text: White keeps the knight out of f4 for good. The price is paid on the light squares around the king, and the g3-pawn gives Black's f-pawn something to bite on.
Now that g3 is there to be attacked the pawn goes forward. Black threatens to open the king with ...fxg3 and ...Nh5, and the knight on g5 is short of squares: ...h6 will force it to e6.
The king defends g3 and h3. 13.gxf4 exf4 would open the long diagonal and give Black h5 and e5 for his knights.

The same idea as in the 10.Re1 lines: d5 is undermined before the knight is driven to e6.

**Verdict:** after ...h6, Ne6 Bxe6, dxe6 Black picks up the e6-pawn with ...Qc8, and White's compensation is the bishop pair and pressure on d6 with Qb3, Rd1 and c5. The pawn on f4 keeps White's king permanently uneasy. Theory rates the position as balanced; in practice Black's play is easier.
White ignores the kingside, and the result is one of the best-known forcing lines of the Bayonet.
The queen attacks e6 and h3 at once.
Black gives the rook: the threat is ...Qxg3+.
Taking the knight exposes the king to ...Rxf2 and the queen checks. With accurate play from both sides the complications burn out to equality, and White is the one who has to know them.
As in the 10.Re1 line, and Black uses the same recipe.

After ...h6 and Ne6 Bxe6, dxe6 the pawn on e6 is cut off, and the extra move g3 has only weakened White's king. The bishop can drop back to g2, which is solid and gives Black time for ...Qc8 or ...fxe4 and ...d5.

lines.name: Bayonet: 10.c5 and 10.Nd2
lines.summary: White allows ...Nf4. Black gets the bishop pair and the long diagonal after 10.c5, and a kingside attack with tempo after 10.Nd2.

next.text: White breaks at once and does not mind the knight coming to f4.
Otherwise the bishop on e2 goes, or the knight stays on f4 for ever.

The character of the game has changed. Black has the bishop pair, an open long diagonal and e5 for his pieces; White has a lead in development, the d4-square and pressure on the c-file. The f4-pawn can become weak if Black is careless.
The rook takes the knight out of the bishop's reach and prepares cxd6 and Nb5.

Black supports the f4-pawn with ...g5 and gives the knight g6, from where it reaches e5. The move also rules out Ng5-e6.

**Verdict:** a balanced fight between structure and bishops. Black keeps the queenside closed as long as he can (...a6 against Nb5, ...dxc5 only when it wins time), builds up with ...g5, ...Ng6 and ...Ne5, and eventually pushes ...g4. White plays for cxd6 and an invasion on c7 or for e5 to free his pieces.
The knight is going to c4 after c5, to attack d6. As Kotronias points out, the drawback is obvious: Black's knight reaches f4 with gain of time.
White gives the bishop a square on a3 and the rook one on a3 or a2 before deciding about the bishop on e2.
Black gives up the e4-square to get the e7-knight into the game.
White has to drive the knight away.

Kotronias's main line. The queen lines up behind the f5-knight, so that ...Nd4 will uncover it against h3, and ...g4 is coming to support the knight. The careless 16.Nb3 Nd4 17.Be4 loses at once to 17...Nxf2, as in Petrosian-Rashkovsky, 1974. Black has full play for his slightly worse structure.
Keeping the bishop.
The standard attacking move; ...g5 and ...g4 will come with tempo against the bishop.

lines.name: 9.Nd2 a5: the old main line
lines.section: Mar del Plata: other ninth moves
lines.summary: White's knight heads for c4 and the queenside attack is a move faster. Black slows it with ...a5, regroups with ...Kh8 and ...Ng8 and sacrifices on g3.

next.text: The knight is going to c4 once c5 has been played, to attack d6, and f3 is possible without moving it again. On the queenside White is a tempo ahead of the 9.Ne1 lines. On the kingside the knight defends less than it would from e1 or f3, and it blocks the bishop for the moment.
Because White is faster, Black first makes b4 cost two preparatory moves, a3 and Rb1, and after ...axb4 he will have the a-file as well.
Preparing Rb1 and b4.
Now that b4 has been delayed the knight releases the f-pawn in the usual way.

The move that defines this line. The e7-knight has no future on g6, because White has not played f3 and there is nothing on f4 to attack; from g8 it comes to f6 or h6 and frees the bishop's path to h6. The king is also off the diagonal on which c5 and Qb3 would come with check. Note that Black keeps the tension on f5: ...f4 is not played until it gains something.
White secures e4. 13.Qc2 Ng8 usually comes to the same thing.
Both knights now watch e4 and h5.
Preparing c5.
The knight threatens to settle on f4.
Keeping it out, and giving Black a target.
A developing move with tempo on the knight.
The rook defends the knight's retreat and, along the third rank, the pawn on g3.

The thematic sacrifice. Black cannot make progress by quiet means once g3 is covered, and White's queenside is about to break through, so the pawn cover goes now. The quieter 19...Bh6, offering the exchange of bishops first, is also played.
The second knight follows, and g3 cannot be held: ...Nxg3 and ...f4 are both threatened.
The only way to keep some lines closed.
White counterattacks rather than recapture.

Karpov-Kasparov, Tilburg 1991. Black has a rook and four pawns for three minor pieces, and one of the pawns is on g2. The game became a famous marathon that was eventually drawn.

**Verdict:** the sacrifice on g3 is sound and gives Black at least equal chances; White's best practical policy is to avoid it with an earlier deviation, which is why 9.Nd2 lost its place as the main line to 9.b4 and 9.Ne1.

Kotronias's repertoire move. The idea is to answer 11.Rb1 with 11...a4, fixing the queenside so that b4 can be taken en passant, and 11.b3 with ...c6 or ...c5. It is the choice for those who would rather restrain White than race him.
The same position by the other move order.
White plans Ba3 and b4 without a3.
The knight provokes b4 and then steps aside.
The c5-square is secured, the bishop on a3 has moved three times and Black continues with ...f5 and ...Nc5. Equal.
The straightforward race is too slow here.
After ...f5 White plays c5 and Nc4 at once and d6 is under fire before Black's attack has started.

The other reputable system. Black closes the queenside completely and plays ...Ne8 and ...f5. It is solid, but after Rb1 and b4 White has the only open file and Black has little to bite on; the choice of players who want a slow game.

lines.name: Rare ninth moves: 9.Bg5, 9.Bd2, 9.Be3, 9.a4, 9.Kh1
lines.section: Mar del Plata: other ninth moves
lines.summary: Developing and waiting moves. Black answers with ...Nh5 or ...Ng4 where that gains time, and otherwise with the normal ...Nd7 and ...f5.

next.text: White is ready to give up the bishop: after 9...h6 10.Bxf6 Bxf6 11.b4 he has gained time for the queenside and Black's bishop pair is slow to count. That is the most common line and a perfectly good one for Black.
The active choice, in keeping with the rest of the repertoire. The knight avoids being exchanged on f6, heads for f4 and leaves the bishop on g5 with nothing to pin.
Uncovering the bishop against h5.

**Verdict:** Black has the bishop pair and the usual kingside advance, and White's light-squared bishop, his best defender of g2 and h3, has gone. White is quick with c5 because his knight is already on d3. A normal Mar del Plata race with chances for both sides.
A modest developing move that connects the rooks and prepares Rc1 and b4.
The knight is aimed at f4 and the f-pawn is free without the knight having had to retreat.
The knight is heading for d4 and the other one returns to f6. Black's pieces are active and the weakening g3 gives him something to play against. Equal.
This walks into a tempo.
Black has ...f5 in with the knight actively placed on g4, from where it drops back to f6 when asked. He is at least equal.
White wants a5 before deciding on anything else.
With the a-pawns fixed White's b4 is gone for good and c5 needs long preparation with b3 and Ba3. Black plays ...Nd7 and ...f5 with an extra tempo's worth of safety on the queenside.
A waiting move with a point: after the knight leaves f6 White plays g4 and Rg1, discouraging ...f5.
Black develops as usual and decides after seeing g4 whether to play ...f5 anyway or to switch to ...a5 and ...Nc5; the king on h1 and the pawn on g4 are not obviously useful then.

lines.name: 8.Be3: White keeps the tension
lines.summary: White defends d4 instead of closing the centre. Black chases the bishop with ...Ng4 and ...f6 and then strikes with ...f5.

next.text: White avoids the Mar del Plata by defending d4 once more. The bishop is exposed on e3, and that is what Black plays on.
The fighting move: the bishop is hit before h3 can be played.
Blocking the bishop for a moment, but the pawn will go on to f5.
White claims that the knight on g4 and the pawn on f6 are misplaced. Black has gained two moves, and uses them.
Black has ...f5 in without having had to retreat the knight first, and e4 is attacked.

The knight returns to the centre with gain of time.

**Verdict:** after 12.exf5 Bxf5 or 12.Nxe5 Nxe5 Black's pieces are all active, he has e5 and d4 for his knights and the f-file for his rook. White's only trump is the d5-square, and it is not enough for an advantage.
A third visit.
The queen steps out of the attack and keeps an eye on e5 and h5. Black threatens ...h6 and ...f4.
A Mar del Plata in which ...f5 is already played and White's bishop has gone home. After 12.Ng5 Nf6 Black is comfortable.
The bishop stays active and can be chased.
Gaining space with tempo; the knight will come back via h6 to f7, where it guards e5 and d6. The price is the f5-square.
Towards the centre, opening the f-file. Black has ...g4 and ...Nd4 to come and the bishop on g3 bites on e5. White will try c5 to open lines before Black is coordinated. Chances are equal.
The Mar del Plata structure with White's bishop outside the chain.
Black is ready for ...f5; the knight on h6 supports ...g4 and covers f7 and f5.

The solid alternative, and Pavlovic's recommendation. The rook makes ...exd4 a threat to e4, so White must act, and the point is seen if he closes the centre. After 9.dxe5 dxe5 10.Qxd8 the ending is equal but gives Black little to play for, which is why the repertoire prefers 8...Ng4.
The knight cannot be driven away and taking it costs the e-pawn.
Black has regained the pawn with a freer game.

lines.name: 8.dxe5: the delayed exchange
lines.summary: White exchanges on e5 with the knight already committed to c6. Black trades queens, gives a bishop for the f3-knight and plants a knight on d4.

next.text: The only move with any bite: the pin threatens Nd5.
The simplest. 9...Bg4, keeping the queens on, is the alternative for those who need to win.
Black intends to remove the knight that guards d4 and to occupy the square.

**Verdict:** the knight on d4 is as good as either of White's bishops, which have nothing to attack. Black covers c7 with ...c6 or ...Ne8 against Nd5 and Nb5 and brings the rooks to the d-file. The position is equal and dry, and Black should not expect more than half a point against accurate play.
The rook steps out of the pin and covers f6 and f7. After 11.Nd5 Nxd5 12.cxd5 Nd4 Black has no problems.

lines.name: Petrosian System: 7.d5 a5 8.Bg5
lines.summary: White closes the centre early and pins the knight to stop ...f5. Black unpins with ...Qe8, forces f3 with ...h5 and activates his bad bishop via h6 and e3.

next.text: White closes the centre before the knight has come to c6, so there is no ...Ne7 and no automatic kingside attack. He keeps the choice of where to castle and intends Bg5, to make ...f5 hard to organise.
The c5-square is the natural home for Black's queen's knight in this structure, and ...a5 secures it against b4 before the knight sets out.
Petrosian's idea. With the knight pinned Black cannot play ...Nh5, ...Ne8 or ...Nd7 to free the f-pawn.
Asking the question while the answer costs White something: on e3 the bishop is hit by ...Ng4, and on h4 it can later be shut in or trapped.
Development first. The pin is broken with the queen, not with the g-pawn.
The knight makes way for f3 and is ready to meet ...Nc5 with b3, a3 and b4.
The pin is broken without weakening anything. The queen also supports ...Nh7 and ...f5 and looks at a4.
Clearing the f-pawn, and from h7 the knight supports ...h5 and can come to g5.
A precise move. The queen now protects the rook on a8, so 13.b4 loses a pawn to 13...axb4 14.axb4 Nxb4. White has to spend another move on preparation.
So that ...a4 can be answered by b4.
The threat is ...g5 followed by ...h4, trapping the bishop, so White must make room for it.
The move ...h5 was played for this as well. White's f3 has opened the diagonal to e3, and the bishop that was shut in behind its own pawns becomes Black's most active piece.
The straightforward choice: the bad bishop is exchanged for White's good one.

**Verdict:** balanced. With the dark-squared bishops gone Black's king is safe and his remaining bishop is the better one. He continues with ...h4, ...Qg5, ...Kg7 and ...Nf6-h5-f4, or with ...f5 when White is busy elsewhere. White will play b4, and after ...axb4, axb4 Black keeps the queenside closed with ...b6 or strikes back with ...c5. Neither side can easily break through, and the better manoeuvrer wins.
Keeping the bishops on is also possible: the bishop is safe on c5 and annoying, and White needs b4 to shift it. A matter of taste.
The sharp alternative, which leads to a famous exchange sacrifice.

Yusupov-Kasparov, Barcelona 1989. For the exchange Black has the long diagonal, e5 and d3 for his knights and a mobile pawn pair; White's rooks have no open file. Black won, and the sacrifice is still considered sound, but the main line asks less of Black's memory.
White prepares f3 and Bf2 without allowing a check on e3.
Fixing the queenside: b4 can now be taken en passant and the knight has c5 for good.
Starting the queenside play before castling.
The same answer as in the main line: now b4 is not possible, and Rb1 can be met by ...a4.
The old way of breaking the pin, which the main line was invented to avoid.
White breaks up the pawns before Black has consolidated: after 11...g4 the knight goes to d2 or h2, f5 is a hole that only White can use and Black's bishop on g7 has no future.
Black has gained ...h6 and ...f5 for nothing and stands well.
The old main line. The knight reaches c5 as well, but it blocks the bishop and takes d7 from the other knight, and Black usually has to accept 8.Bg5 h6 9.Bh4 g5, with a weakened kingside.
A flexible relative of the main move, recommended by Gallagher: Black keeps ...a5 in reserve and may save it altogether. The plans are the same, and it often transposes.

lines.name: Petrosian System: 8.Be3, 8.O-O and 8.h3
lines.summary: White's quieter eighth moves. Black uses ...Ng4 against a bishop on e3 and otherwise develops with ...Na6, heading for the main-line set-up.

next.text: The bishop takes c5 away from the knight and White keeps Nd2 and g4 in mind. It is also a target.
Black has been made to play ...f6, which blocks the bishop for the moment, and in return the pin has gone and the knight on g4 has a good route home.

The knight goes to f7, where it covers g5, e5 and d6 and makes ...Bh6 possible.

**Verdict:** Black completes the set-up with ...Nf7, ...Bd7 and ...Qe8, and then chooses between ...Bh6, exchanging the bad bishop, and ...f5. White's bishop on h4 is out of play once the f-pawn has moved on, and his queenside advance needs the same a3, b3, Rb1 and b4 as in the main line. Equal chances.
White commits his king, which rules out the plans with g4.
The main line by transposition.
Defending e4 so that the knight can stay on f3.
The knight ties White to the e4-pawn, and Black follows with ...Bd7 or ...Nh5-f4.
The plan with Be3 and g4, restraining ...f5.
This position belongs to the h3 systems and is covered in that chapter; Black's set-up with ...Nc5, ...Bd7 and ...Qe8 or ...Nh5 is the same.

lines.name: Gligoric System: 7.Be3 Ng4 8.Bg5 f6 9.Bh4
lines.summary: White delays castling and keeps the centre fluid. Black chases the bishop and, once it is committed to h4, plays ...Nc6 after all, reaching a Mar del Plata with extra features.

next.text: The Gligoric System. White supports d4, keeps the tension and has not castled, which makes Black's usual attack less attractive.
The bishop is attacked before h3 can be played. The alternatives 7...exd4, 7...Na6, 7...c6 and Nunn's 7...h6 are all respectable; this is the most direct and the one most repertoire books choose.
The bishop is blocked, but only until the pawn moves on to f5.
The bishop stays on the diagonal of the queen. As long as it is there the f-pawn is pinned in effect, since ...f5 would uncover an attack on d8, so Black has to prepare the advance.

Now the knight comes out after all. The difference from move seven is that after 10.d5 Ne7 White's bishop stands on h4, outside the pawn chain, where ...g5 will hit it with tempo, and the knight on g4 has a good route home via h6 and f7.
The knight on g4 is attacked and f3 is prepared.
Not a bad square in this structure: the knight goes to f7, where it defends d6, the base of the chain, and supports ...g4 later.
Giving the bishop f2.

**Verdict:** a Mar del Plata race with two differences. Black's king's knight stands on h6 instead of f6, heading for f7, where it guards d6 and makes the c5 break less dangerous. And White's king is still on e1: he can castle long, or play g4 to block the kingside, so Black must be ready to switch to the h-file with ...Nf7 and ...h5. Chances are equal.
A positional alternative. Black blocks the queenside before turning to the other wing; after 13.dxc6 bxc6 he has the b-file and control of d5. It scores well and suits players who dislike races.
Keeping the tension, and transposing to the line 7.O-O Nc6 8.Be3 Ng4 9.Bg5 f6 10.Bh4, where the continuation is discussed.

The other main line, which Vigorito covers alongside 9...Nc6. Black gains space at once and brings the knight to f7, at the cost of weakening f5 and h5 before White has committed his centre. It is sound, and a matter of taste.
What White is hoping for.

A Mar del Plata in which White has saved a move on castling and has the knight on d2 at once. He is ready for b4 and c5, his king can stay in the centre or go to the queenside, and Black's attack has no target. Theory gives White the better game.

lines.name: Gligoric System: 9.Bc1
lines.summary: The bishop goes home, claiming that ...f6 and the knight on g4 are misplaced. Black develops with ...Nc6 and gets ...f5 in.

next.text: White has lost no time, since Black's last two moves are not obviously useful, and h3 is a threat.
The most natural move now that d5 would not come with Nd2 ready. The older 9...exd4 10.Nxd4 f5 opens the game at once and is also playable.
Transposing to the line 7.O-O Nc6 8.Be3 Ng4 9.Bg5 f6 10.Bc1, where Black's play is explained.
Closing the centre with the king still at home.

White hopes to use the knight's position with g4 or h4-h5. Black answers with ...Nf7, after which h5 can be met by ...g5, and then plays ...f5 or ...c5. The knight on f7 is well placed and White's king has no safe home, so the chances are balanced.

lines.name: Exchange Variation: 7.dxe5
lines.summary: White trades queens and tries to use his lead in development. Black meets the threats to c7 and f6 exactly, plays ...c6 and equalises; the d4-square is his long-term asset.

next.text: The only dangerous move. The knight on f6 is pinned against the rook, and Nd5 threatens both it and c7.
The rook leaves the pin, so that Nd5 can be met by ...Nxd5. On e8 it also guards e5, which frees the bishop and the knights from that duty.
Black challenges the pawn at once, before White can support it with Rc1 or Nd2-c4.
The knight keeps both b6 and c5 in view and does not block the c8-bishop for long. The bishop on d5 looks strong, but it will be exchanged or driven back.
Heading for c4 and d6.

**Verdict:** equal. The strong bishop is exchanged, after 16.Bxe6 Nxe6 the knight attacks g5 and looks at d4 and f4, and neither side has a weakness the other can reach. In the long run Black's structure is the healthier one, because he controls d5 with pieces while d4 can never be covered by a white pawn. The side that understands the knight manoeuvres wins these endings, and that is usually the King's Indian player.
Development with a threat: Nd5 or Nb5 would now hit c7 with the rook on the d-file.
The knight covers c7 and is on its way to c5.
The knight heads for d5 by c2 and e3.
Taking d5 away for good. Black follows with ...Nc5, ...a5 and ...Ne6-d4, and it is White who has to be careful: his e4-pawn and the d4-square are permanent weaknesses.
This wins nothing.
The pawn comes straight back, because the knight on e5 is attacked by the bishop.
Black has the more active bishops and no problems at all.
Trying to win the exchange.
The check gains the decisive tempo.
Black has won a piece.
The same idea without the pin.
The knight will challenge the bishop from b6 or f6. Black is equal for the same reasons as in the main line.

chapters.title: Saemisch and Four Pawns Attack
chapters.subtitle: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.e4 d6 5.f3 and 5.f4
chapters.intro:
These are White's two big-centre systems against the King's Indian. In the Saemisch (5.f3) White supports e4 with a pawn, builds Be3, Qd2 and long castling, and often follows with an h-pawn storm. In the Four Pawns Attack (5.f4) he occupies the centre at once with all four pawns and tries to crush Black with e4-e5 before he can organise a counter.

The repertoire answers both the same way, with the break ...c5. Against the Saemisch it is 5...O-O 6.Be3 c5, which leads to three different structures (the Benoni after d5, an open centre after dxc5, a knight on e5 after Nge2 Nc6 d5) and has the support of nearly every popular study. Against the Four Pawns it is 5...O-O 6.Nf3 c5, which after 7.d5 e6 8.Be2 exd5 9.cxd5 produces a Benoni in which White's extra f-pawn is both strength and weakness: it gives him e4-e5, but it leaves e3 and g3 without pawn cover and takes the f-pawn's defence of the king away.

Second systems get their own games: in the Saemisch the classical 6...e5 with ...Nh5 and ...f5 (and the Panno 6...Nc6 as a rarer alternative), in the Four Pawns 6...e5. The notes try to say, for each move, what it takes away from the other side, because the structures repeat and the move orders are what matter.

sections.title: Why 6...c5, and how the Saemisch is built
sections.body:
The move f3 gives White four things at once: e4 stays protected by a pawn for ever, the d1-h5 diagonal and d2 are free for the queen, the bishop on e3 can go to h6, and long castling with a pawn storm becomes possible. It costs him the f3 square for the knight (the g1-knight must go to e2, in front of the f1-bishop) and it leaves the pawn complex e4-f3-g2 to be attacked by ...f5, ...Nh5 or ...h5-h4.

Black cannot prevent the build-up, so he strikes at the centre before White has castled: ...c5 hits d4, keeps the g7-bishop open (after ...e5 it is blocked) and forces White to choose a structure. The three structures are:

- **7.Nge2 Nc6 8.d5 Ne5**: a knight on e5 and the h-pawn against the knight on g3 (first two games).
- **7.d5 e6**: the Benoni, with the Saemisch pawn on f3 (second file).
- **7.dxc5 dxc5 8.Qxd8 Rxd8 9.Bxc5**: Black gives up a pawn for development and a lead in the endgame (also second file).

sections.title: The Benoni structure after 7.d5 e6
sections.body:
After the exchange on d5 the structure is a Benoni, with the difference that White has played f3 and Black's dark bishop on g7 is not blocked. White wants to hold e4 with the pawn chain, develop the knight to g3 or c1 and castle; he often goes for the queenside, since the king on the kingside would meet ...h5-h4. Black's plan has three parts:

- **A knight on e5.** The b8-knight goes to d7 and e5, where it cannot be driven out by f4 (f4 would give up e4). Then ...Nfd7 or ...Nh5 brings the second knight to the party.
- **...h5-h4-h3** against a knight on g3. In the Saemisch Benoni the knight has few squares, and the pawn on h3 fixes g2 and keeps g4 weak.
- **...a6 and ...b5.** The b-pawn is a gambit pawn: with the rooks on b8 and e8 and the queen on a5, the opening of the b-file justifies the sacrifice. White's counter is a4, which stops ...b5 but makes b5 a pawn offer rather than a weakness.

The typical tactic is ...Bxg4 sacrificed against g2-g4: after fxg4 Nfxg4 the queen comes to h4 and White's king is stuck. The pawn on e4 can be taken with ...Nxe4 when the queen on d2 is overloaded.

sections.title: The knight on e5 and the h-pawn plan
sections.body:
This is the line the studies give most space to. After 8.d5 Ne5 White has to deal with ...Nxc4, so he plays 9.Ng3 (which also frees the f1-bishop to protect c4) or 9.Nc1. On g3 the knight is vulnerable to the h-pawn: ...h5 and ...h4 force it to f1, from where it needs two moves to return to the game. The pawn on h4 then goes to h3 as soon as the structure is fixed, so White has to play g3 and loses control of the dark squares f3, h3 and f2.

The knight on e5 is permanent: if f4 ever kicks it, ...Nfg4 or ...Neg4 hits Be3 and h2 and e4 is loose. That is why White's attempts to dislodge it with pawn moves usually end in a sacrifice, and why Black can afford the slow ...a6 and ...b5. The main defensive resource for White is to leave the king in the centre and use the queenside as a base: the endgame after queen trades is level.

sections.title: The pin on c3: 8.Qd2 Qa5
sections.body:
White's Qd2 puts the queen on a diagonal with the c3-knight, and 8...Qa5 uses it: the knight cannot move without allowing ...Qxd2+. The queen also looks at a2. White has two main replies:

- **9.O-O-O** commits the king. The attack is then g4 and h4, but Black's ...a6 and ...b5 arrive first and the king on b1 stands in front of the pawn Black has just broken. The calm answer is 10...Rd8, which prepares ...dxc5 with the rook hitting the queen. White can trade queens with Nd5, leaving a level endgame that Black can play for the win with ...f5.
- **9.d5 Ne5** and the knights go to b6 and e5: the knight on c3 is pinned, so c4 and a2 are under attack at the same time. White's c4-pawn needs two extra defenders, and the b5 break comes with tempo.

sections.title: The pawn sacrifice 7.dxc5
sections.body:
White takes the pawn, trades queens and then sits on it with the bishop. Black gets compensation because White's kingside is undeveloped (the Bf1 and the Ng1 are both locked behind f3 and e4), because the rook on d8 controls the open file, and because c4 will be weak once the bishop has to leave c5. Black's plan is always the same: a quick ...Nd7-e5 or ...Nb4, ...Be6 or ...Ba6 against c4, and ...Rac8; he regains the pawn in most lines.

The bishop on c5 has to leave once ...b6 or ...Nd7 attacks it, and from a3 it eyes e7 but does nothing for the king. White has several tenth moves (Nge2, Ba3, Rd1, Nd5, Be3), and the games take them one by one; against all of them the same recipe works.

sections.title: 6...e5: the closed set-up with ...Nh5 and ...f5
sections.body:
The classical way. The pawn on e5 shuts in the dark bishop, but it fixes the centre, and with f3 played White can neither play f4 nor keep the bishop on e3 without losing a tempo to ...f4. Black's pieces go to the kingside: ...Nh5 aims at f4 and g3, ...f5 breaks the e4-pawn, and ...f4 and ...g5 follow when White has castled long. It is a race, as in the Mar del Plata, and Black is better placed for it than there because White's own structure (f3, e4, Be3) is a target.

After 8.Qd2 the move 8...f5 is the main line. The Bronstein sacrifice 8...Qh4+ 9.g3 Nxg3 10.Qf2 Nxf1 11.Qxh4 Nxe3 gives up the queen for two bishops and pawns; White has scored well against it in the elite games, so it is shown only as a side-line.

sections.title: Bg5, Nge2 and the Panno
sections.body:
The side lines are met by moves that transpose into the main structures. After 6.Bg5 the bishop pins the f6-knight, but Black simply plays ...c5, 7.d5 e6 8.Qd2 h6, and the bishop has to choose between h4 and e3; it goes back to e3 and the game is the Saemisch Benoni with the extra moves Bg5-e3 and ...h6. After 6.Nge2 Black plays ...c5 as well, because 7.Be3 Nc6 is the main line, while 7.d5 e6 8.Ng3 exd5 9.cxd5 h5 is a Benoni in which the h-pawn gets its hit against the knight at once. The study's 6...a6 is an alternative: 7.Be3 Nc6 8.Qd2 Rb8 is the Panno.

The Panno 6...Nc6 is a different opening, with the plan ...a6, ...Rb8 and ...b5. In the main line White blocks the queenside with c5 or plays d5 at once, and Black's knight lands on d4. It is sharper than 6...c5 and less well mapped, and it is given as a single game.

sections.title: The Four Pawns: 6...c5 and the Benoni with f4
sections.body:
White's four pawns on c4, d4, e4 and f4 are the biggest centre in the opening, and they are held by pieces that cannot all be developed at once. Black attacks the centre where it is weakest. The pawn d4 is undermined with ...c5, and if White closes the centre with d5 the pawn on e4 becomes the base of the chain: it is then attacked by ...Nxe4, ...Re8 or ...Bg4, while the f4 pawn is the only pawn that supports e5. After 7.d5 e6 8.Be2 exd5 9.cxd5 Black has three plans:

- **9...Re8** pressures e4. White's answer is the break 10.e5; the lines are sharp.
- **9...Bg4** is the safe line: Black trades his bishop for the f3-knight and aims at ...Re8, ...a6 and ...b5 or ...c4.
- **9...Nbd7** is the quiet line from another study: the knight covers e5 so that the break is harmless, and Black plays ...Re8, ...a6, ...Qc7 and ...Rb8 or ...c4.
- **9...b5!?** is the gambit.

The pawn on f4 is also a weakness: with the f-pawn gone from f2, e3 and g3 are no longer covered by pawns, a bishop on e3 is hit by ...Ng4, and the king has lost the pawn that shelters it.

sections.title: White's e5 break and the b5 sacrifice
sections.body:
After 9...Re8 White's thematic break is 10.e5: if Black takes with 10...dxe5 11.fxe5 Ng4 the pawn on e5 is attacked three times (Ng4, Bg7, Re8) and White cannot hold it. 12.e6 fxe6 13.d6 is the usual way to keep the initiative: the pawn on d6 cramps Black's position, and the pieces come out with castling and the knight to e4. Black develops with ...Nc6 and ...Bd7, and the question is whether the attack on d6 and the weakness of e6 will be enough. White can also play 12.Bg5 Qb6 13.O-O, when 13...Nxe5 14.Nxe5 Bxe5 15.Bc4 Qxb2 has scored well for Black. In the main line 14...Bd7 is the study's move; the natural 14...Nd4 15.Ne4 has been very good for White. The trick 10.Qc2? Nxe4!! is in the second game, and 6...e5 as a second system is the last game.

The other tactical idea in this structure is against the bishop on d3. After 8.Bd3 exd5 9.cxd5, the move 9...b5! uses the fact that the bishop is loose and the pawn on e4 is attacked: if 10.Bxb5 then 10...Nxe4 11.Nxe4 Qa5+ forks the king and the bishop. White gets two pawns for the piece in the end, but his structure and king are broken. The same fork on the e1-a5 diagonal works wherever the e4 pawn has no support and the knight on c3 is gone.

sections.body:

- "Kaboom With The King's Indian Defense!", Lichess study by Chessmate_0204, https://lichess.org/study/hEPV1nVh (876 likes): the Saemisch 6...c5 7.Nge2 line and the Four Pawns 6...c5 7.d5 e6 lines, including the e5 break and the b5 sacrifice
- "Kings Indian Defense", Lichess study by mlgfoxzx, https://lichess.org/study/tPDKaTiu (469 likes): the Four Pawns main line 6...c5 7.d5 e6 8.Be2 exd5 9.cxd5 and its three replies
- "The King's Indian Defense", Lichess study by heyucatchthis, https://lichess.org/study/4HN6lhFd (302 likes): the Saemisch 6...c5 7.Nge2 Nc6 8.d5 Ne5 and the Four Pawns 6...c5 7.d5 e6
- "King's Indian Defense", Lichess study by MisterCV, https://lichess.org/study/jNUkcl81 (133 likes): 7.dxc5 with 10.Nge2 b6, and 9...Bg4 in the Four Pawns
- "The Indian Defense ( King's Indian Defense )", Lichess study by IAM_Dhanvi_OISBTM, https://lichess.org/study/GyoMHu7D (137 likes): 6...e5 7.d5 Nh5 8.Qd2 f5
- "King's Indian Defense Repertoire", Lichess study by JoshSG, https://lichess.org/study/RAAxYxtT (1108 likes): 6...Nbd7 against the Saemisch and 6...e5 against the Four Pawns
- "King's Indian Defense", Lichess study by K1N6M4K3R, https://lichess.org/study/zWkdQ9XW (864 likes): consulted for the move orders only
- Move frequencies were checked against the project's book of elite Lichess games (2400+)

lines.name: 7.Nge2 Nc6 8.d5 Ne5 9.Ng3 h5: the h-pawn against the knight
lines.summary: The main line of the Saemisch. Black plants a knight on e5, drives the Ng3 back with ...h5-h4, fixes the kingside with ...h3 and then plays Benoni-style on the queenside. White's knights and king end up in each other's way.

next.text: The Saemisch. The pawn holds e4 for good, takes f3 away from the g1-knight and prepares Be3, Qd2 and long castling, often with g4 and h4-h5 to follow. The price is real: the knight must go to e2, where it blocks the bishop, and the complex e4-f3-g2 becomes a target for ...Nh5, ...f5 and the h-pawn. Black cannot stop the build-up, so the answer is to hit the centre at once instead of waiting for the storm.

Black castles before there is a target: White's attack needs a king on the queenside and several pawn moves, and none of it is dangerous for a king that sits behind the fianchetto as long as the g7-bishop can be kept.

The main move (about 70% of elite games). The bishop guards d4 and clears d2 for the queen, and Bh6 to trade Black's best piece is always in the air. That is why Black wants play in the centre at once. The sidelines 6.Bg5, 6.Nge2 and 6.Bd3 are in the third file.

The most popular answer and the one the studies recommend. The pawn hits d4 before White has played Qd2, keeps the g7-bishop open (it is shut in after ...e5) and gives Black three structures to choose from: the Benoni after d5, an open centre after dxc5, or a knight on e5 after Nge2 Nc6 d5.

The most flexible move (about half of elite games). White keeps d4, d5 and dxc5 in hand and clears the d1-h5 diagonal. The knight is the weak point: it blocks the f1-bishop, cannot go to f3, and its only useful squares are g3 and c1. Black's whole plan is built around that. 7.d5 and 7.dxc5 are in the next file.
A second attack on d4 and the preparation for ...Ne5 once d5 is played. White must now decide: close the centre with 8.d5, keep the tension with 8.Qd2 (third game) or release it with 8.dxc5.
The tempo on the knight is the point, but it also fixes the centre exactly the way Black wants it for a knight on e5.

The knight is at home here: it hits c4, d3 and f3, and White cannot chase it. 9.f4 would kick it, but then e4 loses its support and ...Neg4 or ...Nfg4 hits Be3 and h2. The immediate threat is ...Nxc4.
This knight leaves e2, so the f1-bishop now protects c4, and it heads for the kingside, where it supports White's pawn storm. Its weakness is a pawn on h4.

Black goes straight for the knight. On g3 it has no good retreat and the h-pawn attacks it for free. If White allows ...h4 the knight has to go to f1, where it does nothing for the rest of the middlegame.
Develops and prepares to castle; it neither stops the plan nor does anything about it.
The knight has to move. 11.Nf5 loses to ...gxf5 and 11.Nh1 is hopeless; Nf1 is the only way to keep the piece in play.
Now the centre. White's knight is far from the action, so Black can afford to open the e-file, trade on d5 and keep the knight on e5 as a monster.
The knight heads for c4, where it hits e5 and d6 (about half of elite games).

The key move. It threatens ...hxg2, so White has to answer, and the pawn on h3 takes away the square from which White would otherwise support f4 and g4. After g3 the dark squares f3, h3 and f2 are weak, and the knight on e5 eyes f3 and g4.
14.g4 is the thematic try, and it fails to a sacrifice:
The knight on e5 is permanent: f4 would lose control of g4 because of the pawn on h3, so the kingside is quiet and Black can turn to the queenside.
Most common. It stops ...b5 in principle, but it allows the break as a pawn offer that opens the a- and b-files for Black's rooks.
The bishop prepares ...b5 and protects the pawn on the file.
The break. White's last pawn move a4 becomes a target and the a- and b-files open for the rooks.
White has won a pawn, but the bishop is attacked and b2 falls: after 21.Be2 Rxb2 the rook stands on the second rank, where it works with the queen on a2 and the knight on e5.

Black has regained the pawn and has the more active pieces. The study rates it as better for Black. The plan in practice: keep the knight on e5, bring the queen to a2 and let the knights on d2 and f1 and the weak king tell.
White cannot keep the knight on b5 and ...Qxb2 follows.
The queen controls c4; it looks odd, but without that square the knight on e5 would be trapped by Nc4.
With White's pawns over-extended Black is better.
Understandable from a Saemisch player: White wants f4.
This amazing sacrifice gives Black an easy position.
The queen comes to h4 and ...Qxg4 is always in the air.
Black wants all the dark squares: the bishop attacks the one on f4 and the knight on d2 behind it.
The knight hits the queen and takes f1 and d1 away, so White can never castle.
Black's attack is too strong.
Takes the knight but loses to the check on the h4-e1 diagonal.
A sharp try to drive the knight away at once.

The idea Grischuk used against Svidler (Candidates 2013, according to the study): a piece for two pawns and an initiative. After Bxc4 the pawn break ...b5 wins the bishop's square, and White's pawns on e4, d5 and f4 are loose while the knight on f1 is out of play.
The bishop is attacked and the b5-square is the one White cannot cover.

Black has two pawns for the piece, the b-file and a lead in activity: the bishop on b5 is attacked, the d5-pawn is hit by the f6-knight, and the white king cannot castle comfortably. The study calls the compensation full.
The other main move (about a fifth of elite games): the bishop eyes the h4-pawn and the queen on d8. Black replies ...exd5 and ...h3 as in the main line.
Stops ...h4 for good but weakens g4: if White ever plays f4 against the knight, ...Ng4 comes with threats on e3 and h2, so the knight on e5 is untouchable.
Black has everything he wants: a permanent knight on e5, a White king with nowhere comfortable to go, and queenside play with ...b5 at leisure.
Also playable and common: 10.Be2 exd5 11.cxd5 and then ...h5 or ...a6. It lets White decide whether to play h4 himself, which is why the study prefers the immediate ...h5.

White avoids the h-pawn plan: from c1 the knight goes to b3 or d3, and b3 is available to hold c4. The price is a knight that has left the kingside altogether, so Black plays the Benoni way (next game).
Playable (about one game in ten) and it hits c4 too, but the knight stands on the edge and has no way back into the game. The central knight is better.
Loses a pawn: 9.Nxd4 cxd4 10.Bxd4 and the bishop on g7 is attacked as well.

The classical set-up and the second system of this chapter (third file). The pawn takes d4 under fire and closes the g7-bishop, but it fixes the centre, and with f3 played White cannot get a strong d4-d5 without allowing ...Nh5 and ...f5. It is less popular than 6...c5 and less well supported by the studies, but sound.

The Panno (last game of the third file). The knight attacks d4 a second time without committing the c-pawn, so Black can follow with ...a6 and ...Rb8 and meet d5 with ...Ne5 or ...Nd4. A different opening from the 6...c5 lines: sharper, less well mapped, and chosen less often in the elite games (about 19% against 31% for 6...c5).

A solid choice that one popular repertoire study recommends (7.Qd2 b6 8.O-O-O c5). It avoids the pawn sacrifice on c5 but gives White a free hand, and it is rare in the elite games compared with 6...c5.

lines.name: 9.Nc1 e6: the Benoni plan with ...a6 and ...b5
lines.summary: White retreats the knight to c1 to avoid ...h5-h4 and to play b3 or Nb3. Black plays it the Benoni way: ...exd5, ...a6, ...Bd7 and the break ...b5.

next.text: Black has no kingside target any more, so he plays the Benoni way.
The standard plan. The knight on e5 holds c4 and d3 and the break ...b5 opens the queenside before White has finished developing.
White stops ...b5 for now.
The pawn offer that opens everything.
White has won a pawn for the moment, but the pressure down the b-file and on the second rank will win it back.
The bishop and the b2-pawn are both attacked. The extra pawn will not last, and Black's knight on e5 and the bishop on the long diagonal keep the initiative.
Black does not mind the exchange: the b-file is open for ...Rfb8 and the queen hits b2.

lines.name: 8.Qd2 Qa5 9.O-O-O: the pin on the c3-knight
lines.summary: White keeps the tension and goes for Qd2 and long castling. 8...Qa5 uses the pin along the diagonal a5-d2 and forces White to resolve the centre, or to try a pawn storm that over-extends him.

next.text: The positional way to play the Saemisch: White waits, connects the queen with Bh6 and wants to castle long. It is the second most popular eighth move (about 44% of games).
The queen pins the c3-knight against the queen on d2 (if the knight moves, ...Qxd2+), eyes a2 behind it and prepares ...cxd4. White's king is nowhere yet, and the centre is already under pressure.
The consistent move. White commits to the attack with g4 and h4, but his king stands in front of the very pawn break Black is about to play. 9.d5 (next game) is the other main move.
Preparing ...b5, and the a-pawn also takes b5 from the knight on c3.
Protects a2 and frees the c3-knight to jump to d5 or b5.
