The rook prepares ...cxd4 and, above all, ...dxc5 with the rook hitting the queen on d2 with tempo. It is the quiet and safe choice.
The best way to neutralise the pressure: trade queens.
d4 is attacked three times and defended three times, so the exchanges are equal.
The queens are off and the position is level. Black can fight on with ...f5, ...Rac8 and ...b5; White's pawn on d5 needs protection and his king is not yet safe from a rook on c8.
An equal ending in which the better-prepared player has the initiative: ...Kf7-g6, ...Rac8 and ...b5 are the usual ideas.
The storm.
The queenside pawn break comes first: the king on b1 is the one under fire.
The critical test: a knight sacrifice that tries to open lines before ...b3.
The only move: ...b3 uncovers the queen on d2. Black must keep calculating, but White has no follow-up and his king is the one in danger.
Pointless: the rook on d8 does nothing for the king and the knight on e5 is perfect.
Almost a Benko Gambit, with the difference that White's king is on b1 and his kingside attack is nowhere.
Black trades the c5-pawn for the b2-pawn and has the initiative.
More ambitious and more common in elite games: the pawn is offered at once to open the queenside against the king on b1. A good choice for a player who wants to play for a win; 10...Rd8 is the safer.
The other main move (about a quarter of the games): it keeps the queen back and prepares ...Bb7 and ...Rb8. Slower, and it gives White a free hand with d5 or O-O-O.

lines.name: 8.Qd2 Qa5 9.d5 Ne5: ...Nfd7-b6 and the break ...b5
lines.summary: After 8.Qd2 Qa5 White can close the centre. Black plants a knight on e5, brings the f6-knight to b6 to attack c4 a second time and breaks with ...b5; White cannot hold everything.

next.text: The knight is attacked, but the queen on a5 has already pinned c3, which changes the usual plans.
The knight leaves e2 so that the f1-bishop defends c4, and heads for the kingside.
The f6-knight goes to b6, adding a second attacker to c4, and it clears f6 for ...f5. White cannot protect c4 in time.
The direct reply, but it leaves a2 loose.
The pawn offer works because the queen on a5 stands behind a2; there is no need to prepare it with ...a6.
14...f5 meets the threat of f4 trapping the knight on e5: after f4 Black has g4 for the knight.
Material is level, and Black's pieces coordinate far better than White's.
A good Benko-style gambit for Black: the f1-bishop is hit at once and the knight on e5 is ready for ...c4 and ...Nd3.
Looks natural: the pawn protects c4 twice over.
The long diagonal is now open for the g7-bishop.
The knight on c3 is attacked twice and defended once, and ...Bxa1 follows.
A repetition is available to both sides; Black can play on with 14.Nb5 Qxd2+ 15.Nxd2 a6 16.Nc3 f5 and a kingside expansion.

lines.name: 7.d5 e6 8.Qd2 exd5 9.cxd5 a6: the Saemisch Benoni
lines.summary: White closes the centre at once and Black strikes with ...e6. After the exchange on d5 the pieces go to the same squares as against 7.Nge2: a knight on e5, the h-pawn against Ng3, and ...b5 on the queenside.

next.text: White gains space and fixes the centre at once (about one game in five). The chain e4-f3 stays intact and the g7-bishop is blunted if Black cannot open the centre.
Black must challenge d5 before White plays Nge2-g3 and h4. The e-pawn breaks the grip on d5, opens the e-file against the pawn on e4 and clears the way for a knight to e5.
The most popular move (62% of elite games). The queen connects with Bh6 and prepares long castling. 8.Nge2, 8.Bd3 and 8.dxe6 are in the next games.
The exchange has to be made now: after a quiet move such as ...a6, dxe6 and Bxe6 would give White the chance to improve the pawn on f3.
The natural recapture.
The standard plan: ...b5, and the knight to e5 or c4. The pawn move also takes b5 from the knight.
Almost always played (96% of elite games), since ...b5 would otherwise come with a gain of space. It does leave b5 as a pawn offer.
The rook eyes e4, ready for ...Nxe4 when the queen on d2 is overloaded, and it frees f8 for the bishop. The other main plan is 10...Nbd7 (40% of games), with the same knight route to e5.
11.Be2 and 11.Bd3 are the other tries; Black plays ...Nbd7 and ...Ne5 against all of them.
The knight goes to g3 and runs into the h-pawn.
The usual race of the pawn against the knight: from g3 the knight has no moves except f1.
The rook goes behind the b-pawn so that after axb5 axb5 the a-file is the only open one and Black's rook is not on it.
The pawn goes to h3, where it fixes g2 and stops White from playing h3 himself.
16.g3 and 16.gxh3 are the alternatives; neither stops the break on b5.
The knight on b5 is attacked by the rook and the knight on e5 hits g4 and f3, so White's bishop on e2 is overloaded.
The queen joins the queenside and the white king is stuck in the centre. White's weak points are b2 and the diagonal a7-g1, and Black's pieces are far more active.
The reason ...h4 is not a pawn sacrifice: the knight takes e4 with an attack on the queen on d2 and uncovers the queen on d8 against the bishop on h4.
A discovered check from the rook on e8.
The queens come off, White has won the h-pawn, Black the e4-pawn and the dark bishop is free.
Black has ...f5 with the knight on h5 hitting f4, and White's kingside pieces are uncoordinated.
Black accepts the exchange and the b-file is his: ...Nbd7, ...Rb8 and the queen hits b2.
Gives up the chain e4-f3: the move f3 has been played for nothing, and Black has a free hand with ...Re8, ...Nbd7 and ...Ne5.

lines.name: 7.d5 e6 8.Nge2 exd5 9.cxd5 Nbd7: the knight to e5 and ...Nh5-g3
lines.summary: White develops the knight first. The structure is the same, but with the queen still on d1 Black can play ...h5-h4 against Ng3 and bring the f6-knight to h5.

next.text: White commits the knight and keeps the queen flexible. The plan is Ng3 and Be2, with long castling later.
The exchange is again the best answer (62% of games); 8...b6 is the second most played, but gives White an easier game.
Preparing ...b5 and keeping the rook on b8 away from the a-file.
The knight returns by f1-d2 and c4, hitting e5.
The knight heads for f4 or g3. White's pieces get in each other's way: the f1-knight cannot return, and the e2-bishop has to cover the king.
The knight is in the centre again and f4 would lose the pawn on e4.
The thematic jump: the knight on g3 attacks f1 and e2, and after hxg3 hxg3 the pawn on g3 and the open h-file give Black attacking chances against the king. The study stops here.
The pawn on h3 fixes the kingside and the knight on e5 is permanent.
The knight on e5 attacks g4, so the pawn push only weakens f4 and h4.

lines.name: 7.d5 e6 8.Bd3 exd5 9.cxd5 Nbd7 10.Nge2 Ne5 11.Bc2 b5!
lines.summary: With the bishop on d3 White tries to make the knight on e5 trade itself off. Black trades and breaks with ...b5. The move 8.dxe6 is a mistake: the g7-bishop gets d4 and e5.

next.text: White develops and eyes b5 and h7. Because the bishop stands on d3 the knight on e5 can be traded off.
The knight eyes d3: the bishop must decide.
Retreats and avoids the exchange, but the bishop no longer watches b5.
The break works because the bishop has left b5 and the knight on c3 is overloaded.
The knight forks the bishop on e3 and the pawn on b2.
A check that wins a tempo.
The pawn is recovered, and the knight hits the queen.
Black has regained the pawn and has the better coordination: White's knights are awkward and the king is stuck in the centre.
The queen cannot guard both e4 and e2; Black wins material.
The point of f3 is to hold the chain e4-d5, and White destroys it himself.
The backward d6-pawn is a small price for the dark bishop and the squares d4 and e5.
Natural, but it runs into a double sacrifice.
The point: once the knight on c3 takes b5 and the knight on e5 moves with check, the g7-bishop sees the rook on a1 along an empty diagonal.
The knight attacks Be3 and offers itself: if fxg4, the knight on e5 is free to take d3 with check.
Black has won the exchange.

lines.name: 7.dxc5 dxc5 8.Qxd8 Rxd8 9.Bxc5 Nc6 10.Nge2 b6: the gambit
lines.summary: White wins a pawn and trades queens, but Black's lead in development, the d-file and the weak c4-pawn give full compensation. The bishop has to leave c5 and ...Ba6 and ...Nb4 regain the pawn.

next.text: White takes the pawn (about a third of elite games) and heads for a queenless middlegame.
Black recaptures with the d-pawn so that the d-file is open for the rook.
White is a pawn up, but his kingside is undeveloped (the f1-bishop and the g1-knight are both locked behind f3 and e4) and his king is still in the centre.

Black's lead in development is the compensation. The knight eyes b4 and e5 and the rook on d8 controls the open file. White has five tenth moves (Nge2, Ba3, Rd1, Nd5, Be3), and against each the idea is the same: gain a tempo against the bishop and attack c4.
The most popular move (about 35% of games).
The b-pawn chases the bishop to a3 and prepares ...Ba6 against c4.
The bishop retreats, losing a tempo: from a3 it eyes e7 and keeps c1 free for long castling.
The standard set-up: the a-pawn prevents b4 and prepares ...Ba6 and ...Nb4.
The knight jumps to d5 to trade pieces and relieve the pressure.
The knight hits a2 and d5 at once.
Black has regained the pawn and the knight returns to b4. The white king stands on b1 behind a damaged queenside.
An equal position. Black's plan is ...Bd7, ...Rac8 and ...a4, against the bishop on a3, which is White's only active piece.
The other main move, played in about half the games: the knight attacks the bishop and heads for e5.
The knight on f4 is attacked and White's pieces are uncoordinated.
The king step avoids the pin on the a3-f8 diagonal; ...Nc2+ and the trade of the dark bishops follow.

lines.name: 7.dxc5: 10.Rd1 Rxd1+ and the other tenth moves
lines.summary: After 10.Rd1 Black exchanges rooks, trades the dark bishop for the knight and goes after c4 with a knight on e5.

next.text: White trades rooks to take the d-file from Black, but gives up castling for good.
The king stays in the centre and the rook on h1 is out of play.
The knight attacks the bishop and the bishop must decide.
Trading the dark bishop for the knight wrecks White's pawns: after bxc3 the pawns on c3 and c4 are weak targets and Black's knight goes to e5.
The knight hits c4 and f3.
Threatens ...Nf2+ and ...Ne3+.
The pawn on c4 falls: White's bishop is on a3, his king is on d2, and Black has a lasting initiative.
Everything is protected; Black has an easy game.
Too slow: it does not prevent anything.
White cannot defend the pawn on c4.
Black gets rid of the bishop and regains the pawn with ...Na5.
The knight reaches e5 and the bishop on d3 is attacked.
Black goes on with ...Nd7-e5 to collect c4.

lines.name: 6.Bg5 c5 7.d5 e6 8.Qd2 h6: the bishop must decide
lines.summary: White pins the f6-knight with Bg5. Black plays the same ...c5 and ...e6 break, and ...h6 forces the bishop to choose between h4 and e3, so the game transposes into the Benoni structures of the main lines.

next.text: The second most popular sixth move (about one game in five). The bishop pins the f6-knight against the queen and keeps open the plan Bxf6 to damage Black's dark squares; it also avoids the exchange sacrifice and the tempo loss ...Nh5 after Be3.
The same central break as in the main line. 6...h6, 6...a6, 6...Nc6 and 6...Nbd7 are all played, but ...c5 is the move that keeps the chapter's structures.
Almost always played (89% of games). The queen protects the bishop and prepares O-O-O.

The study's move: it forces the bishop to declare itself at once (it is played in about one game in twelve; the usual move is 8...exd5). The bishop cannot take on h6 safely, and on e3 it has lost two tempi relative to the main line, while the pawn on h6 is useful for the later ...h5.
The usual move (98%).
The knight on g3 has the same problem as before.

The knight is in the centre, and Black's plan is ...Nh5, ...f5 or ...Rb8 and ...b5. The position is the Saemisch Benoni with the pawn on h6 already advanced, which is one tempo less for the pawn storm and a free tempo for the bishop move Bg5-e3. Equal.
Wins a pawn for the moment.
Black has given up a pawn but has a lead in development and an active bishop on h6; the study judges the counterplay sufficient. White hardly ever tries it.
The more common move order, playable too: 9.cxd5 h6 follows.
Commits the knight before the structure is clear.
Black has the usual play: the knight on e5, the pawn against g3, and ...Rb8 and ...b5 on the queenside.

lines.name: 6.Nge2 c5 7.d5 e6 8.Ng3: the knight development, and 6.Bd3
lines.summary: White develops the knight before the bishop. Black plays ...c5 as always; against 7.d5 the h-pawn again goes against the knight on g3, and 7.Be3 transposes into the main line.

next.text: The knight develops first (about 11% of games) and the bishop's square, e3 or g5, is chosen later. White hopes to avoid the problem of a knight that has no square: Ng3 is available at once.
The same break.
The knight goes to g3 at once (71% of games): no more Ne2, and the bishop on c1 still has the choice.
The h-pawn goes forward against the knight; with the bishop still on c1, the pawn on h4 forces Nf1 and the knight is then stranded.

The knight on f1 is out of play, so Black turns to the queenside with ...Rb8 and ...b5, and keeps ...Nbd7-e5 in reserve. The elite games from here also include ...Nh7 and ...Nh5, but there is nothing to choose between the plans; the structure is the same as in the first file.
Black gets the e4-pawn back.
The study's choice: the pawn prepares ...b5 and sacrifices a pawn for play. After 7.Be3 Nc6 8.Qd2 Rb8 it is the Panno (last game of this file).
Black trades the bishop on d3 and has the standard play with ...a6 and ...b5; the second knight can come to e5 via d7.

lines.name: 6...e5 7.d5 Nh5 8.Qd2 f5: the closed centre and the race
lines.summary: The classical set-up. Black closes the bishop in and plays on the kingside: ...Nh5, ...f5 and later ...f4 and ...g5, while White castles long. A race in which the pawns on f3 and e4 are the targets.

next.text: 7.Nge2 is the other main move (next game).
The knight goes to f4, the square that the pawn on e5 gives it. White's bishop is on e3, so Nf4 will be answered by Bxf4 exf4, which gives Black a pawn on f4 and an open e-file.
The pawn break is the main line (about two thirds of the games).
White castles into the pawn storm. 9.Nge2 f4 10.Bf2 g5 is the other main line and leads to the same pawn race.
Black prepares ...b5 to open lines against the king on c1.
The knight lands on c5, hits the bishop and prepares ...b5.
The break.
The queen goes to b4, hits the pawn on b2 and eyes the knight.
Black has the bishop pair and White has an extra pawn: the d5-pawn, the e4-pawn and the king on b1 are targets. The study stops here.

The immediate storm, played in about one game in eight: it gains time with ...f4 and attacks before White has castled further, but it leaves the queenside alone. A reasonable alternative when White has no good plan against it.
Black has gained time with ...f4 and the bishop on f2 is passive.
The Bronstein queen sacrifice.
Black gets two bishops and two pawns for the queen, but White scored well in the elite games here, and the king on e1 is not in as much danger as it looks. An adventure, not a repertoire move.
The same pawn race: ...f4 gains a tempo against the bishop on e3.

lines.name: 6...e5 7.Nge2 c6 8.Qd2 Nbd7 9.d5: Black in a flexible Benoni
lines.summary: The other main line against 6...e5. With ...c6 Black prepares ...exd4 and ...a6, and meets d5 with ...cxd5 and ...a6. White's long castling and Bh6 are dangerous, so the structure needs care.

next.text: The most flexible: the d-pawn can go to d5 (the first game) or stay and keep the e5 tension.
The pawn on c6 supports ...d5 or ...exd4 and prevents Nb5. It keeps the centre flexible; the cost is that the knight on b8 has fewer squares.
About two thirds of the games.
The most common (79 games in the book), preferring the clear structure to long castling.
The knight heads for f4, which the pawn on e5 supports; White's knight on c1 can do nothing about it.
White's attack is quicker than Black's counterplay: the king on g7 is exposed, and the elite games from here favour White heavily. So the pawn break against long castling needs care.

lines.name: 6...Nc6 7.Nge2 a6 8.Qd2 Rb8 9.Nc1 e5: the Panno
lines.summary: The Panno: Black prepares ...b5 and meets d5 with a knight to d4. A sharper alternative to 6...c5; here it is a single game.

next.text: Prepares ...Rb8 and ...b5. The knight on c6 is attacked after d5, so Black's pieces must be ready.
The rook goes behind the pawn so that the break ...b5 comes with a tempo.
Black closes the centre and plans the knight jump to d4.
The knight is strong on d4: Bxd4 gives up the dark bishop for it and exd4 leaves White without a centre.
Black opens the b-file and the e-file together.
Black has sacrificed a pawn for open lines and the pressure on e4.
Black has played this in elite games with a fair score, but it is sharp. The Panno is a good second weapon only for a player ready to learn it as a separate opening.
The other main move. The knight hits c4, and the book shows 9.b3 b5 and 9.Nc1 Nd7 as the usual replies.

lines.name: 6.Nf3 c5 7.d5 e6 8.Be2 exd5 9.cxd5 Re8 10.e5: the thematic break
lines.summary: Black attacks the four-pawn centre with ...c5 and ...e6, and meets 10.e5 by taking, hitting e5 three times with ...Ng4 and going a pawn up after 12.e6 fxe6 13.d6. Sharp, and the main line of the Four Pawns Attack.

next.text: The Four Pawns Attack. White occupies the centre with four pawns and threatens e4-e5 or f4-f5 before Black has organised anything. The price: the pawns on f4 and e4 cannot be supported by pieces quickly, e3 and g3 are no longer covered by pawns, and the king loses the shelter of the f-pawn. Black's job is to hit the chain at its base.
Black castles first; the king is far from the centre where the pawns are, and the attack on the chain with ...c5 is not delayed.
White develops and adds a protector to e5 and d4 (the move 6.Nf3 is by far the most common). The bishop e2 and castling follow.
The main line (about two thirds of the elite games and the move every study recommends). The pawn hits d4, the base of the chain, and the g7-bishop is left open to the long diagonal.
White closes the centre (94% of elite games). The other main try is 7.dxc5.

Black challenges d5 at once, opens the e-file against the pawn on e4, and keeps the g7-bishop's diagonal. The pawn sacrifice ...b5 is also possible (and sometimes played), but ...e6 is the structure the notes follow.
The most common move (58%). 8.Bd3 is the next-to-last game; 8.dxe6 is also played.
9.exd5 is rare and gives up the centre.
The rook attacks the pawn on e4 at once, and Black prepares ...Nxe4. It is the sharpest of the three moves (see the other games for 9...Bg4 and 9...Nbd7). The break 10.e5 is White's answer.
The break. If White does not play it, ...Nxe4 usually becomes available, so it is the natural move (84% of games).
The pawn on e5 is attacked three times (Ng4, Bg7, Re8) and White cannot hold it.
White pushes it through to open the f-file and create a strong passed pawn on d6.

13.dxe6 Qxd1+ 14.Bxd1 Bxe6 would simply leave Black a clean pawn up with the more active pieces. The pawn on d6 cramps Black and is protected by the queen on d1, so Black cannot win it at once. White has given a pawn for it: Black is a pawn up.
The knight attacks d4 and heads for e5 or b4.

The bishop holds e6 and c6 and unblocks the rooks. Black is a pawn up and White has the pawn on d6, the more active pieces and the open f-file as compensation: a sharp, double-edged position in which the first to coordinate wins.
Natural, since the knight eyes e2, f3 and c2, but White's knight lands on e4 with great effect.
White scored 41 wins in 57 games in the elite games after this, so it is the move to avoid.
Black has won the pawn on b2 and traded White's knight; the elite games from this line favour Black.
The solid line, in the next game.
The line from another popular study (fourth game).
A balanced line in the elite games: the knight on d4 is Black's best piece and White's queen is driven back.
The queen takes aim at c3 and c5 at once; the pin along the a5-e1 diagonal is why White cannot simply defend c5.
The queen returns to a5 to pin the knight on c3 again, and the bishop pins the knight on f3. Black has regained the pawn and the pieces are active; the elite games from here are level.
The second system, with the pawn trade 7.fxe5 dxe5 8.d5 (last game). It leads to a closed centre where Black plays ...c6 and ...b5.

The modern alternative (about 9%): the knight goes to c7 or b4 later and ...e5 follows. It is not covered in a game here; 7.Be2 e5 8.fxe5 dxe5 9.d5 reaches the same structure as 6...e5 with the knight on a6 instead of b8.

lines.name: 9...Re8 10.Qc2? Nxe4!!: the tactic behind the rook
lines.summary: The point of 9...Re8 is that the pawn on e4 is attacked twice. After a careless move such as 10.Qc2 the knight sacrifice on e4 followed by ...Bf5 and ...Na6 wins material.

next.text: Defends e4 once, but the queen steps onto the very diagonal Black is about to open.
A knight sacrifice that few players find: the pawn on e4 is attacked by the rook and the knight, and after Nxe4 the knight and the queen stand on the same diagonal.
The bishop attacks the knight on e4, which is pinned in front of the queen, and the rook on e8 attacks it as well. Two attackers against the knight, the queen behind it.
Protects the knight a second time.

The point: ...Nb4 attacks the queen, which is the only defender holding the knight on e4. The move is very hard to find; the study says only a few players do. After Nb4 the knight on e4 is lost and Black is clearly better.
The same idea: ...Nb4 attacks the queen.
Stops ...Nb4 but misses the pawn sacrifice.
The pawn attacks the bishop and opens the diagonal; if Qxc4, the rook attacks the queen with tempo.
The knight on c5 attacks both the queen and the bishop on d3, and the knight on e4 falls as well.

lines.name: 9...Bg4 10.O-O Nbd7 11.h3 Bxf3 12.Bxf3 Re8: the solid line
lines.summary: Black trades his bad bishop for the f3-knight, which was the only piece defending e5 and d4. After 12...Re8 there is no tactical danger and Black plays ...a6 and ...c4 or ...b5 in a Benoni where White's centre is a target.

next.text: The pin is annoying but not dangerous.
The knight develops and covers e5, so the break e4-e5 is no longer a threat. The alternative 10...Re8 is also played; 10...Nbd7 is the line recommended by the studies.
The bishop goes before it is driven away: after h3 and g4 it would have no good retreat.
The rook hits e4, whose only defender is the f3-bishop. The knight on d7 cannot go to e5 yet (fxe5), so Black waits and prepares ...a6 and ...b5.
13.g4 h6 14.a4 a6 15.h4 is White's plan to use the space; ...h6 and ...Ne5 follow, and g4 weakens f4.
14.a4 prevents ...b5, so Black switches to the other lever.

The pawn takes d3 from White's pieces and gives the knight the square c5; the bishop on f3 has no targets, and the knight on d7 gets the square c5. Black has scored very well from here in the elite games.
White has the two bishops, but Black has the outpost on c5 and the pressure on the c-file; results in the elite games favour Black.

lines.name: 9...Nbd7 10.O-O Re8 11.Qc2 a6 12.a4 Qc7: the knight first
lines.summary: The line recommended by a popular study: the knight goes to d7 first so that e5 is covered and the break ...Rb8 and ...b5 or ...c4 can be prepared at leisure. White's choice is between Nd2 and Qc2.

next.text: The knight covers e5 and f6, so the break e4-e5 achieves nothing: after e5 dxe5 fxe5 Nxe5 the pawn is lost. The rook adds pressure on e4.
Protects e4 and prepares Bf3 or Nd2.

The queen guards e5 and the c-file, and Black prepares ...b6 or ...Rb8 and ...c4. The elite games from this position favour Black slightly, so the plan is reliable: slow, sound, and White has no pawn lever left except f4-f5.
White tries Nd2-c4 and f4-f5 ideas; Black continues with ...b6 or ...c4.

lines.name: 8.Bd3 exd5 9.cxd5 b5!: the pawn sacrifice against the bishop
lines.summary: With the bishop on d3, e4 has only one defender and the bishop itself can be hit. 9...b5 uses both facts: Bxb5 Nxe4 and the fork on a5 wins the bishop back.

next.text: The bishop defends e4 and prepares O-O, but it can be hit by ...b5 and ...c4.
A pawn sacrifice that attacks the bishop's support: Bxb5 allows ...Nxe4, and Nxb5 allows ...c4.
The knight takes the pawn and uncovers nothing yet: the point is the queen check on a5.
The check forks the king and the bishop on b5.
Black has won the piece back: White's queenside pawns are broken and the king can no longer castle.
Black has the better position: the bishop covers the light squares, White's pawns on c3 and a2 are weak and the king is in the centre.
White has won a pawn, but Black has the open c-file, the long diagonal and the king on f2 to aim at. This is the more testing line for Black: the study thought 12.Kf2 better for White than 12.Nc3.
Black takes space on the queenside with his pawns while the queen hits the king on g1.
Black has given a second pawn, but White's pieces are tied to the defence of e4 and the king is still in the centre.

lines.name: 6...e5 7.fxe5 dxe5 8.d5 c6: the closed centre
lines.summary: The second system. Black trades the pawns, White closes the centre with d5, and ...c6 and ...b5 open the queenside. Sharp and covered by the studies, but 6...c5 is the better practical weapon.

next.text: 8.Nxe5 is the greedy move.
Black attacks the centre at once.
Black develops with tempo and the bishop on d5 is exposed, while White has the extra central pawn. The line is double-edged and balanced in outline; the studies give it without evaluation.
Black has regained the pawn and White's king cannot castle comfortably.
Black threatens ...Nxe4 and the bishop on b7 hits the long diagonal. The elite games choose ...Re8 or ...Na6 here; the study's move is shown as the plan.
The bishop on d3 and the king on e1 lose to the tactic on the e-file.
The knight on e4 is pinned against the king and attacked by the bishop and the rook, so White loses a piece.
Black wins material: the rook on f4 attacks the knight and the bishop is lost.

chapters.title: Modern Defence: 3.Nc3 systems
chapters.subtitle: 1.e4 g6 2.d4 Bg7 3.Nc3 d6
chapters.intro:
After 1.e4 g6 2.d4 Bg7 3.Nc3 d6 White chooses between the 150 Attack (4.Be3), the Austrian Attack (4.f4), the classical 4.Nf3 and a handful of rarer moves. The repertoire answers each with a system that has the same character as the King's Indian: the king's knight and the king stay home until the position has shown what White is doing, the bishop on g7 is the long-term trump, and the counterplay comes from two breaks, ...c5 and ...e5.

There are two families. Against 4.Be3, 4.Nf3 and 4.Bg5 Black plays the Tiger's Modern set-up with ...a6, ...b5, ...Bb7 and ...Nd7, and brings out the king's knight only after the d4-pawn has been exchanged. Against 4.f4, 4.Be2, 4.g3 and 4.Bc4 he plays ...Nf6 at once, which leads to Pirc and King's Indian positions that this player knows. The second option against 4.Be3 is the Pirc move 4...Nf6, and against 4.f4 it is the Tiger move 4...a6. Where a line can reach the same position by two routes, the notes say so.

The chapter is built from the moves of well-liked Lichess studies, which were cross-checked against the project's book of elite games. Where the study moves were not played in the book the notes say so.

sections.title: Why 3...d6, and what the Modern does with the knights
sections.body:
White has a big centre and Black has no pawn in the middle. 3...d6 is the move that makes this tolerable: e4-e5 no longer has a target (there is no knight on f6 to attack), the c8-bishop is freed, and the pawn can be played to e5 itself later. After 3...Nf6? 4.e5 Ng8 White has gained two tempi.

The consequence for the whole chapter is a rule: **do not play ...Nf6 and do not castle until it is clear what White's pieces are doing.** Against Be3 and Qd2 it keeps Bh6 and the h-pawn attack from having a target. Against Nf3 and Be2 there is nothing to be afraid of and the knight comes out at once. The decision is made at move four and not before.

3...c6 and 3...a6 are also playable, but 3...d6 is the most solid and by far the most common, and it keeps every plan of this chapter available. In the elite database White scores about 49% against 3...d6 whichever of the main fourth moves he chooses, so the choice is one of comfort and not of theory.

sections.title: The Tiger structure: ...a6, ...b5, ...Bb7, ...Nd7, ...c5
sections.body:
Black's plan is Sicilian in nature. ...a6 prepares ...b5; the pawn then threatens ...b4 to drive the c3-knight away from the defence of e4, and the bishop on b7 attacks that pawn. White must protect e4 (Bd3, f3 or Qd3), and that settles his set-up. The queen's knight goes to d7, not to c6, because a knight on c6 would block the c-pawn, while from d7 it supports both ...c5 and ...e5.

The standard sequence is:
- **...c5 and, after dxc5, ...Nxc5**: the knight hits e4 and d3. Since d4 has gone, e5 no longer counts as White's, and ...Ngf6 can be played without fear.
- **...c5 and, after d5, ...Ngf6**: Black gets a Benoni-type structure with the b5-b4 expansion, as in 4.Nf3.
- **After a4, ...b4** and ...c5 to attack the centre while the knight is on e2.

The structure is flexible but has a price: the pawn on b5 or b4 and the squares c4 and a5 become targets if White's centre holds, so ...c5 has to follow soon after ...b5.

sections.title: The 150 Attack: how Black avoids Bh6
sections.body:
The pattern is well known from the Pirc and the Dragon: Qd2, Bh6, long castling, h4-h5, g4 and the white attack runs over the g- and h-files. Black's answer is a waiting game. There is no knight on f6 and no castled king, so Bh6 Bxh6 Qxh6 has no point beyond the trade. Black meets the pawn storm with ...h6 (which also occupies the very square Bh6 aims at), or stops it with ...h5, and starts his own play on the queenside with ...Rc8 and ...c5.

What decides the move choices:
- **...h6 or ...h5.** ...h6 prevents both Bh6 and Ng5 and answers h5 with ...g5, closing the wing. ...h5 prevents h5 for good but weakens g5, which gives White a knight outpost after Nh3, and this is the sharp line. Both are good; ...h6 is the safer one.
- **The king stays in the centre** until ...c5 and the exchange of the d-pawn have changed the structure. It is dangerous only if White can open lines there before Black does.
- **...Rc8 before ...c5.** The rook supports ...c5 and ...b4, and after dxc5 Nxc5 the knight is protected.
- **If White plays Bd3 and Nf3 instead of the pawn storm,** Black answers with ...c5 at once, before White's pieces are placed and while d4 has no extra defender.

sections.title: ...c5 or ...e5: choosing the break
sections.body:
Black has two ways to hit the centre and they work together more often than they compete:
- **...c5** is the main break. It trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn, opens the c-file for the rook and the long diagonal for the g7-bishop. After dxc5 Nxc5 the knight attacks e4 and cannot be driven away by a pawn. It is the right answer when White has castled long, because the c-file then points at his king, and when he has not castled at all, because every move spent on defence delays his development.
- **...e5** is the second break, played when the white pieces on d4 and e3 can be hit with tempo. In the model above, after 9.Re1 cxd4 10.Bxd4 e5! the bishop is attacked and has to return to e3, and Black has a firm Dragon-like centre: the d6-pawn is solid, the knight reaches f6 with a hit on e4, and the bishop on b7 keeps pointing at that square. It blocks the g7-bishop in exchange for central space, so it is chosen when the diagonal matters less than the centre.

In the Tiger set-ups do not play ...Ngf6 before the d-pawn has been exchanged: e4-e5 would then be a threat. In the Pirc-style lines (4...Nf6) the knight is already on f6 and the break ...c5 is played with that in mind.

sections.title: The Austrian Attack: a Pirc with ...Nf6 and ...O-O
sections.body:
Against 4.f4 the repertoire does not use the Tiger's set-up but moves the king's knight at once. The Austrian is the Pirc's sharpest line, and Black has the usual trumps: after e5 the f4/e5 pawn chain is a target; the knight on h5 attacks f4, and the long diagonal opens as soon as the d-pawn goes.

The main line with 6.Bd3 Nc6 7.e5 dxe5 8.fxe5 Nh5 9.Be3 Bg4 is the model: the pin on f3 and the knight on h5 combine to break up White's centre, and the plan is ...f6 and ...Nxe5 with pressure on the e5-pawn. The move 6.e5 is met by ...dxe5 fxe5 Nd5 (not by the passive ...Nfd7, which loses time) and 6.Be3 by the solid ...c6.

The second option is 5...c5, the Dragon formation. It scores very well in the elite database and the lines are forcing: dxc5 Qa5, then ...Qxc5 and ...O-O, and the perpetual check in the Bb5+ lines is a safety net. Against 4.f4 the Tiger move 4...a6 is also playable, and is the second option in the games.

sections.title: When White plays e5
sections.body:
In the Tiger's set-up Black does not mind if the e-pawn advances: with the knight still on g8 e4-e5 hits nothing, and Black simply attacks the pawn with ...dxe5 or the base d4 with ...c5. What he must watch is the e6 push: with pawns on f4 and e5 White threatens e5-e6, breaking the f7-pawn. There are two ways to deal with it. Either play ...e6 to stop it for good (a weakness on f6 and d6, so only if the knight can be brought to d5), or allow e5-e6 and recapture ...fxe6, relying on ...Nf8 or ...Nh6 to cover f7 after Ng5.

With the Pirc move order the same pawn break appears as 6.e5. There Black takes at once: ...dxe5 fxe5 Nd5 and the white centre has to prove itself. If the knight is exchanged, ...c5 and ...Bg4 give Black the better pieces.

sections.title: The Hippo and Semi-Hippo
sections.body:
The full Hippo is the most flexible form: Black plays ...b6, ...Bb7, ...d6, ...e6, ...Nd7 and ...Ne7 (often with ...h6 and ...a6 as well), builds a compact wall of pawns and pieces and waits for White to commit. Its price is time: against Qd2 and long castling the study finds it too passive. In this chapter only a modest version appears: the **Semi-Hippo with ...h6, ...a6 and ...b5**, which Black can adopt against 5.h4 and the 150 Attack.

The aim is to deprive White of a target. With the pawn on h6, h4-h5 meets ...g5 and the kingside is locked; Bh6 and Ng5 are impossible; and Black develops by ...b5, ...Bb7, ...Nd7, ...Ngf6 and ...c5. The danger is passivity if White can play f4 and e5 (hence the Semi-Hippo, with active ...b5, and not the Full Hippo, with ...b6, for most lines). If White gets the full pawn centre, Black needs ...c5 or ...e5 in time.

sections.title: Tactics on the long diagonal and f7
sections.body:
Two kinds of tactics matter in this chapter. The first is the diagonal a1-h8: the bishop on g7 hits d4 and c3. Whenever d4 is attacked twice (by ...Nc6 and ...Bg7) and White's centre is stretched, ...Nxe4 followed by ...d5 and ...Nxd4 can win a pawn. In the Bc4 line White cannot take on f7: Bxf7+ Rxf7 gives a bishop for a pawn, and the knight on e4 is hit by ...d5.

The second is f7 itself: with the bishop on c4 and a queen or knight joining it, f7 is the pressure point, and Black does not leave it under-defended. So against 4.Bc4 he plays ...Nf6 immediately, which prevents e5, and castles before ...Nc6. Against 4.Bc4 Nf6 5.Qe2 he plays 5...c6! (the book shows 5...O-O and 5...Nc6 doing worse) and answers e5 with ...dxe5 and ...Nd5.

sections.title: The quiet systems: King's Indian and Pirc structures
sections.body:
When White plays Nf3, Be2 or g3, nothing is threatened and Black can use King's Indian methods: ...Nf6, ...O-O, ...Nc6, ...e5. After d5 the knight goes to e7 and the position is a Mar del Plata without the c-pawn on c4, with plans ...Nh5-f4 and ...f5, or ...Bd7 and ...c6 to open the queenside. After dxe5 dxe5 the position is level and the d-file easy to hold.

The role of ...a6 in these lines is to prepare ...b5 or to keep the knight on b4 safe after d5. White's a4, as in the main line, takes b5 away, so Black switches to the ...Nc6, ...e5 plan. The same structure arises from 4.Be2 (6...a6 and 7...Nc6), and 4.g3 gives a related set-up with ...e5 and the exchange on d4, so the repertoire needs only one family of plans for all the quiet systems.

sections.title: Sources
sections.body:
- "The Tigers Modern", Felixdanmark, https://lichess.org/study/OjJZuCKK (374 likes): the ...a6, ...b5, ...Bb7, ...Nd7 and ...c5 plan, the 6.a3 line with 10...e5
- "Defensa Pirc conceptos básicos - Pirc Defense", the_luiz, https://lichess.org/study/HIwKTrVU (310 likes): the Austrian and 150 attacks in the Pirc order
- "Modern Defense, Standard Line (White)", Coldfield1994, https://lichess.org/study/oH1IQYBq (293 likes): the move-order map of the 3...d6 position and the 5.h4 lines
- "Pirc Defense", ahmedshaf, https://lichess.org/study/r7IsnoO1 (128 likes): the Austrian Attack, the Dragon formation
- "Tiger's Modern: Sharp reply to e4", BlindFool, https://lichess.org/study/CoHp4wPV (114 likes): the Austrian, Classical, Flexible Dragon, Bg5 and Bc4 lines
- "Pirc Defense: Austrian Attack", FatPigz69, https://lichess.org/study/sFabvhrU (109 likes): the Kurajica, Weiss, Unzicker and Dragon lines of the Austrian
- "Modern Defense For Black Complete Repertoire", Positionalchess101, https://lichess.org/study/4cqQt2Q1 (73 likes): the Nf3 and 150 Attack lines
- Move frequencies and scores were checked against the project's book of elite Lichess games (the Lichess masters database could not be reached)

lines.name: 150 Attack: 5.Qd2 b5 6.f3 Bb7 7.O-O-O Nd7 8.h4 h6
lines.summary: White sets up Qd2, f3, long castling and a pawn storm. Black delays ...Ngf6 and short castling so that Bh6 has nothing to hit, kills the storm with ...h6 and strikes with ...Rc8 and ...c5.

next.text: White's most flexible move. The Modern is built on not showing the knights early, so Black does not hurry either.
The standard order. With the pawn on d6 and the king's knight still at home, e4-e5 has no target and only costs White time.

The 150 Attack. Qd2 and Bh6 aim to trade off Black's fianchettoed bishop, f3 and O-O-O prepare the king, and h4-h5 comes against whatever Black has built. Against a Pirc set-up (...Nf6 and ...O-O) it is the most dangerous system for Black, because the castled king and the knight on f6 are the targets.

The Tiger's Modern, named by Hillarp Persson, with a logic borrowed from the Najdorf. ...a6 prepares ...b5 and ...b4, which drives the c3-knight away from the defence of e4, and the bishop on b7 then hits the pawn. It also takes b5 away from White. Above all it is a waiting move: Black commits his knights and his king only when the position has shown what White is doing.
Protects e4 against ...b4 and ...Bxe4, and prepares g4 and Nge2 or Nh3.

The queen's knight goes to d7, not the king's knight to f6. From d7 it supports ...c5 and ...e5. The king's knight stays at home until the d4-pawn has been exchanged: then e4-e5 is no longer a lever and Bh6 no longer hits a castled king. With the king on e8, Bh6 Bxh6 Qxh6 only trades a pair of bishops and puts the white queen on the edge of the board.
White starts the storm before Black has done anything: h5 and hxg6 would open the h-file.

The right reply. The pawn takes h6 away from the bishop (Bh6 is gone for good) and g5 from the knight (Ng5 is gone too), and if White plays h5 the answer ...g5 locks the wing. White has to find his play in the centre or on the c-file, where Black is ready.
Takes the king off the c-file, which is about to open, and guards a2 and c2. Other tries: 9.Nh3 Rc8 10.g4 c5 (Black's move order is the same) or 9.g4 Rc8.
The rook belongs on the c-file for the break that is coming: after ...c5 and dxc5 the knight recaptures with a gain of time (it hits e4) and the rook already stands behind it.
White gains space on the kingside, but he has now spent several moves on the wing where his own king is not.
The break. Whatever White does about the pawn on d4, Black gets the e5-square under control and can then bring out the king's knight without fear of e5.
Two pieces now hit e4. White's king's bishop is still at home and the b2-b3 and Nge2 moves needed to cover everything cost time.
Hits the knight and the bishop on g7 at once.
Black takes the bishop that White would like to keep, so that the knight on c5 cannot be harassed and the d4-square belongs to nobody.

The knight on c5 is defended by the rook on c8. Black continues with ...Ngf6, ...Qc7 or ...e5, depending on the move. The position is balanced: White has the more advanced pawns, Black has the more active pieces and the open c-file, and his king, still in the centre, is in no danger.
Pressure on c3 and a2, and ...b4 comes next.
The other way to stop h5. It leaves g5 as a hole for a white knight, which is the main line of the next game, where the same structure arises from the move order 7.h4.

Nothing has been won by the trade. The queen on h6 stops short castling, but it is far from the centre, Black develops with a threat on e4, and the king is not going to castle short in the next moves anyway. Equal.
Transposes to the main line.
Too early. Now e4-e5 comes with tempo, and with ...O-O to follow the Bh6 and h4-h5 attack is on.
Natural, but it hands White a tempo-gaining pawn move.
White has gained two tempi with the pawn and Black has a worse version of a Pirc.

lines.name: Critical test: 7.h4 h5 8.Nh3 Nd7 9.Ng5, the knight on g5
lines.summary: White plays h4 before castling, Black stops h5 with ...h5, and the white knight lands on g5. Black ignores it, plays ...Rc8 and ...c5 and gets sharp counterplay.

next.text: Before castling. Black cannot allow h5 for free.

The pawn stops h5 for good. The cost is the g5-square, which a white knight can use and which Black cannot control with a pawn. This is the critical test of 7...h5, because a knight on g5 cannot be challenged by a pawn.
The knight heads for g5, where it is safe from pawns and hits e6 and f7. It does not block the f-pawn.
Black does not chase the knight (there is no good way to). He lets it stand where it is and starts the counter-break; the knight on g5 is far from d4 and the centre.
11.Kb1 is the other main choice and also met by ...cxd4.
The bishop takes the best diagonal and pins down the g7-bishop's activity.
The king's knight can finally come out: after ...Nxc5 the e5-lever is gone, and from f6 it adds to the pressure on e4 and will let the king castle.
Castling is possible now: the pawn on h5 keeps the h-file shut and the knight on g5 has nothing to bite on.
A useful waiting move: it covers f4 and h4 and prepares Bg2.
The central break comes with a threat to the bishop on d4.
Now c3 is under attack and the e4-pawn is overloaded.
The point of the whole sequence. After the exchange the knight on e4 attacks both the queen and the knight on g5.

The knight forks Qd2 and Ng5. The study continues with 18.Qxb4 Qc7 and finds strong compensation for Black. The sequence is forcing and double-edged, so it should be checked at the board before it is relied on. A calmer path is 14...Qc7 (the move most often played) with a normal game.

The Semi-Hippo way. Without the g5-hole for a knight, the pawn on h6 meets h5 with ...g5 and the wing is locked. It is also good, and the safer choice if the sharp knight line below does not appeal; the price is that White has gained space with h4-h5 and the pawn on g5 can become a target for f3-f4.

lines.name: Quiet 6.Bd3: 6...Bb7 7.Nf3 Nd7 8.O-O c5
lines.summary: White protects e4 with the bishop and develops normally. Black treats it as a Najdorf-type position and strikes at once with ...c5, before White's king is safe.

next.text: Defends e4 with the bishop, which makes ...b4 harmless. Against it, Black develops the same pieces and prepares the same break.
The knight prepares ...c5 and keeps the other knight at home. Moving it to f6 now would run into e5.

Hit the centre before the white pieces are placed. If White waits (9.Rfe1 cxd4 10.Nxd4 Ngf6 11.f3 O-O), Black has a good version of the Dragon: the knights are developed, the king is safe and the long diagonal is open.
The most common reply. White opens the d-file and wants to harass the knight.
Wins a tempo on the knight but loosens the queen's wing.

The bishop pair is gone, but White's pawn structure has holes on b4 and d3, and the pressure on e4 is back with tempo. Black has a comfortable game: he castles, plays ...O-O, ...Rc8 and ...Qb6 or ...Nd5 depending on the move. Equal.
Stops the e5 trick and prepares ...cxd4.
Natural, but it walks into the pin on the d-file.
Black loses material: the knight on d7 is attacked and the queen on d2 stands on the same file as the rook on d1, so ...Qxd2 does not save it.

lines.name: 5.h4: 5...h5 and the Semi-Hippo 5...h6
lines.summary: White starts the h-pawn storm at move five. Black stops it with ...h5, and if White goes for Nh3-g5 he trades the knight with ...Bxh3.

next.text: White starts the storm before developing. The point is that ...Nf6 now runs into h5.
Stops the pawn. It is the same idea as in the previous game, and the structure often comes out the same way.
The knight prepares Ng5.
Black swaps off the knight before it reaches g5. It gives up the bishop pair, but White's rook on h3 is badly placed, the h-pawn is stuck and Black's structure has no weaknesses.
Defends e4 and covers g4.

Black has completed his development and can still choose between castling and keeping the king in the centre. The game is balanced; the typical plan is ...c5 or ...b5 and ...Qc7 followed by long-term pressure on e4.
Playable too.
Transposes to the previous game.
Semi-Hippo. If White plays h5 Black answers ...g5 and has a very solid wall. After 6.Qd2 b5 the play is like the main line with the h-pawns locked.

lines.name: 5.Nf3 b5 6.Bd3 Bb7 7.O-O Nd7 8.a4 b4 9.Ne2 c5 10.c3
lines.summary: White develops normally and keeps the bishop on d3. Black expands with ...b4 and ...c5; the exchange on c3 leaves White with an isolated a-pawn and a weak c3, and Black has ...Ngf6 and pressure on e4.

next.text: The flexible developing move. It reaches the same position as 4.Nf3 a6 5.Be3.
Now e4 is covered, so ...b4 does not win a pawn.
The same set-up as against the 150 Attack: the queen's knight to d7, the king's knight at home.
Challenges the pawn on b5. Black may play ...b4, and this is the route that costs White the c3-knight's best square.
Retreats to the centre; the knight will be able to go to g3 and cover e4.
Strikes at the centre while the knight is still on e2. The pawn on d4 is attacked by c5 and g7, and White must resolve it.
White attacks the b4-pawn and tries to open lines before ...c4 or ...Ngf6 comes.

The queen eyes c3 and the pawn on e5 break, and ...Ngf6 comes next, adding a second attacker to e4. White has a weak c3-pawn and an isolated a4-pawn. He must defend e4 with Ng3 (12.Qc2? runs into ...c4, and the bishop on d3, blocked by the knight on e2, has no good retreat). The study gives White a slight edge, but Black has real play in the centre and on the queenside in return.
The knight takes on d5 and Black wins a pawn: the white pawn on d5 is attacked by the knight and has no good defender.
When White prevents ...b5 with a4, the pawn goes to b6 instead. The bishop still goes to b7 and the structure is a calm Hippo-style one.

lines.name: 5.Nf3 b5 6.a3 Bb7 7.Bd3 Nd7 8.O-O c5 9.Re1 cxd4 10.Bxd4 e5
lines.summary: White spends a tempo on a3 to stop ...b4. Black plays ...c5 anyway, opens the position and answers Bxd4 with ...e5, getting a Dragon-like centre with pressure on e4.

next.text: Stops ...b4, but it costs a tempo and does nothing for the centre. Compare with the previous game, where the pawn went to a4 only when it was needed.
Black does not wait.
Defends e4 once more; 9.Qd2 cxd4 10.Bxd4 is the other main try.

The ambitious reply, and the one Hillarp Persson favours. The bishop is attacked and has to retreat to e3, and Black gets a pawn centre with the a1-h8 diagonal closed for the moment. The bishop on b7 and the knight on f6 will hit e4 together.
The bishop cannot stay: after ...exd4 it would be lost, and Bxe5 loses it to ...dxe5.
Two pieces attack e4, and White cannot move the bishop on d3 without losing the pawn.
The king is safe: the centre is blocked, so there is no quick opening for White.
The rook takes the open c-file and hits the knight on c3, which only the b2-pawn and the queen defend.
The queen hits b2 and d4 and Black can answer 15.Bf1 with the exchange sacrifice ...Rxc3, as the study game did. A dynamic position with equal chances and the more active pieces for Black.
Natural, but 11.e5 opens the position at the right moment for White. The structural advantage that Black has gained (the d6/e7 pawns against an unopposed e-pawn) is gone.
Simpler.
Also good and simpler: Black trades the bishop that was attacking his position, develops with tempo on e4 and keeps a healthy structure.

lines.name: Second option: 4...Nf6 5.f3 c6 6.Qd2 b5 7.O-O-O Nbd7 8.Kb1 Qa5
lines.summary: A Czech-Pirc set-up against the 150 Attack. Black plays ...c6, ...b5, ...Nbd7 and ...Qa5, delays short castling and counterattacks on the queenside.

next.text: The Pirc order. It can be chosen when White has shown his hand: 4...Nf6 is as common as 4...a6 in the elite games, and the structures are close relatives. The price is that Bh6 and the pawn storm now have a target, so Black must handle his king with care.
The 150 Attack proper.

The Czech-Pirc move, and the one the study recommends against the 150 Attack: ...c6 prepares ...b5 and ...Qa5, and it keeps the king in the centre for now. The study stresses: against this attack, delay short castling. After 5...O-O 6.Qd2 White has a famous attacking pattern with Bh6, h4-h5 and Qg5, and Black has to know it exactly.
White commits his king to the queenside, where Black is about to attack.
Develops without blocking the queen's route and prepares ...Qa5. From d7 the knight also covers b6 and e5, and it supports ...b4.
Takes the king off the c-file, where a queen on a5 would otherwise be annoying. Other tries: 8.h4 h5 9.Nh3 and 8.Bh6 Bxh6 9.Qxh6 Qa5.

The queen hits c3 and a2 and prepares ...b4, which would drive the knight from c3 and weaken e4. Both kings are on the queenside and the pawn storms run in opposite directions: Black's on the queenside, White's with g4 and h4 on the other wing. Unbalanced and with chances for both; the book scores are nearly even, and Black's king can still choose between castling short and staying put.
Transposes.

lines.name: Austrian Attack: 4...Nf6 5.Nf3 O-O 6.Bd3 Nc6 7.e5 dxe5 8.fxe5 Nh5
lines.summary: The main line of the Pirc Austrian. White pushes e5 to cramp Black, Black takes twice and pins the f3-knight, aiming at the base of the e5-pawn with ...f6.

next.text: The Austrian Attack, 16% of the elite games after 3...d6. White builds a pawn centre and prepares e5. The two plans are an attack on the kingside (Nf3, Bd3, O-O, Qe1-h4) and a pawn push to e5 followed by a space advantage.

The Pirc move order. Against 4.f4 the repertoire does not use the Tiger set-up as its first choice, because the knight on f6 pressures e4 at once and White has to make up his mind. 4...a6 is the second option (see the last game of this file).
Black castles: against the Austrian the king is safer than the centre, because White's pieces are not yet aimed at g7. The fianchetto bishop will become strong once the e5 push has been dealt with.
Supports e4 and prepares O-O. The other tries are 6.e5, 6.Be3 and 6.Qe1 (see the next games).
The most popular reply: the knight puts a second attacker on d4 and prepares ...e5 or ...Bg4. 6...Na6 is the alternative, aimed at ...c5 and ...Nb4, and it answers e5 with ...Nd7.
The most testing. White cramps Black and expects the knight on f6 to run away.
Taking is the main line: it opens the d-file and the diagonal of the bishop on g7.
8.dxe5 is also played; the resulting positions after ...Qxd1 are drawish.
The knight steps off the attacked square. From h5 it covers f4 and g3, and it clears f6 for the pawn.
The pin on f3 makes e5 a real target: it is attacked by the knight, by the bishop and soon by the f-pawn.
Breaks the pin.
The pawn undermines the base of the chain. After the exchange of the bishops on e2 and f3 Black has a good game; the position is dynamic, and the book scores 46% for Black against 41% for White.
White has castled, so Black strikes in the centre.
The exchanges leave Black with a healthy game: the knight escapes to f5 and the bishop on e5 is strong.
Black's knight is bounced around, but it lands on a6 and c5 is a good square; the pawn on c6 hits d5.
Transposes.

lines.name: 6.e5 dxe5 7.fxe5 Nd5 8.Bc4 Nxc3 9.bxc3 c5
lines.summary: The Unzicker Attack. Black takes the pawn, hits the c3-knight and breaks the centre with ...c5.

next.text: The Unzicker Attack, 36% of the games here. The pawn attacks the knight at once.
Taking. The other knight retreat gives White a lasting space advantage.
Attacks the knight on d5 a second time, so Black has to decide what to do with it.
The exchange doubles the white pawns and opens the b-file, and it is the main choice of the elite players.
The break. White's pawn centre is lopsided: the pawn and the queen both hit d4, and once the e5-pawn is gone the bishop on g7 joins in.
The pin on f3 weakens the support of the e5-pawn, and ...Nc6 will pile up on it. Black has equal chances and a flexible position; White has two bishops and a pawn centre but weaknesses on c3 and e5.
The line of one of the studies.
Playable, but the book shows White scoring better, and Black's queen has been drawn to d5 without a concrete aim.
The knight hits f4 and the bishop hits e5, so White's centre is the one under pressure; the queenless middlegame is equal. (After 8...Ng4 9.Ke1 White scores well in the book.)
Passive: the knight blocks the bishop and White keeps the space.
A useful extra move, and White scores more than 55% in the elite database.

lines.name: 6.Be3 c6: the solid answer
lines.summary: White develops with Be3 and Qd2. Black plays ...c6, ...Nbd7 and ...Nd5 and gets a very solid, drawish position.

next.text: Prepares Qd2 and long castling. 6...Ng4 is available but the white bishop is happy to go to g1; the Kurajica line 6...b6 is critical but difficult for Black.
The pawn prepares ...Nbd7 and ...Qa5, and takes d5 away from White's knight.
Prevents ...Ng4 and ...Bg4.
The knight attacks both the bishop on e3 and the knight on c3.
Black has a healthy pawn on d5, which blocks the e5-pawn, and the open c-file.

The queen hits b2 and d4. White has to defend the pawn, and the position is exceptionally balanced: in the elite database this line is drawn in about 85% of the games. A reasonable choice when a draw would do; the alternative is 6...Nc6 for a sharper game with more risks.
The Kurajica line.
White's pieces are more active and Black's weaknesses on e7, c7 and b7 are hard to hold; the study's author thinks that Black can only hope to draw.

lines.name: Second option: 5...c5 (the Dragon formation)
lines.summary: Black strikes at once with ...c5. After dxc5 Qa5 the bishop on g7 has an open diagonal, and the forcing lines with Bb5+ lead to a draw or better.

next.text: The Dragon formation. It trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn and removes the cramping chain at its base. In the elite database Black scores 44% against 45% for White, better than after 5...O-O (40%), and it is the more active choice; its price is theory.
The queen hits the knight on c3 and the pawn on c5 will be taken back next move.
Hits the queen.

Black pins the knight and brings the queenside knight out to c6. White has better development; Black has the bishop pair's diagonal, a firm centre and the usual Dragon play. The book scores 49% for Black here against 34% for White.
Black forces a draw by repetition. White can avoid it with 11.Nxb5 Qa5+, which is sharper.
Black has the bishop pair against a weakened centre.

lines.name: Second option: 4...a6 (the Tiger against the Austrian)
lines.summary: Black meets the Austrian with the same set-up as against the 150 Attack: ...a6, ...b5, ...Nd7 and ...c5, saving the king's knight for later.

next.text: The Tiger's Modern against the f4 set-up. The knight stays on g8, so e5 attacks nothing, and ...b5 and ...c5 start the counterplay.
The knight prepares ...c5 and keeps the bishop's diagonal open; 6...Bb7 is the other main choice and is more popular; 6...Nd7 keeps ...c5 in one move.
White castles.
Strikes at the centre before White has found a plan.

The e4-pawn is attacked and the knight on c5 can't be hit by a pawn. White's pawns on e4 and f4 are now targets. Black has equalised: the next moves are ...Ngf6, ...Bb7 and ...O-O, with pressure on e4.
The rook leaves the long diagonal. Black's pieces come out with ...Bb7 and ...Ngf6.
A line from one of the studies. White has lost the e6-pawn, Black's pieces become active, and the white attack has run out of steam.
The same plan as against 4.Be3: ...b4 and ...c5.

lines.name: 4.Nf3 a6 5.a4 Nf6 6.Be2 O-O 7.O-O Nc6 8.h3 e5 9.d5 Ne7
lines.summary: The classical set-up. White stops ...b5 with a4, Black switches to ...Nf6, ...O-O, ...Nc6 and ...e5 and reaches a Mar del Plata-like structure without the c-pawn on c4.

next.text: The second most popular move. White develops the knight, defends d4 and keeps Be3, Be2 and h3 in reserve. Black is now free to bring out the knight, because e5 can be met by dxe5.

Why not 4...Nf6 at once, which reaches the Pirc Classical? That is also fine (62% of the games). 4...a6 is chosen because it keeps the Tiger structure available: against 5.Be3 and 5.Be2 Black plays ...b5, and against the quiet 5.a4 he switches to the King's Indian plan.
Stops ...b5 for good, since ...b5 axb5 axb5 loses the pawn or the rook to Rxa8. It is White's most popular reply (33%).
The knight finally develops. e5 can now be met by ...dxe5 dxe5 Ng4 with equal play, and White's most dangerous plan is not available.
The key move, and the critical moment of the system: Black needs a plan, and this is it. ...Nc6 puts a second attacker on d4 and prepares ...e5. White has to choose between d5, Be3 and h3.
Takes g4 away, and makes ...Bg4 and ...Ng4 impossible. Black plays ...e5 anyway.
The main line. 9.Be3 exd4 10.Nxd4 Re8 and 9.dxe5 dxe5 are equal too.

As in the Mar del Plata, the knight goes to e7: it supports ...f5 and from there to g6 or c8 if the position needs it. Black has two plans: **...Nh5 and ...f5** (play on the kingside, the knight lands on f4) or **...Bd7 and ...c6** (open the queenside). White's plans are Nd2-c4, Bg5 and the lever c2-c4 followed by c5.

Prepares ...f5. The knight on h5 eyes f4 and g3, and the f-pawn is free to advance. The position is a typical Mar del Plata type: White will try c4-c5 on the other wing, and Black has the f5 break. Equal, with chances for both, and it suits a King's Indian player.
Black strikes in the centre and e4 is the weakness.
Black has a clear plan: ...Bf5, ...c5, and a pawn on d4 that hampers the bishop on c1.
Black has strong play against e4: the knight on b4 hits d5 and c2.
The 150-type position. Black plays ...Bb7 and ...Nd7, see the 4.Be3 chapter.
Also good: it goes straight into the Pirc Classical, and one would choose it to avoid the Tiger structures altogether.
The Pirc Classical. The repertoire reaches this structure by 6...a6 against 4.Be2.

lines.name: 4.Nf3 a6 5.Be2 b5 6.O-O Bb7 7.Re1 Nd7 8.Bf1 c5 9.d5
lines.summary: Against the quiet Be2 and O-O Black plays the full Tiger plan. After White blocks the centre with d5, ...Ngf6 and ...b4 give Black a Benoni structure with play on the queenside.

next.text: Develops and keeps a4 in reserve; the pawn push a4 comes later.
The bishop goes to b7 before the knight goes to d7: it hits e4 at once, so White has to keep the pawn protected and has no time for d5.
Defends e4 and prepares e5 and Bf1.
The same plan as against the 150 Attack.
Unblocks the rook on e1, so that e4-e5 gets support, and keeps the bishop out of reach of a later ...c4.
Hits the centre before e5 can be prepared.
Blocks the bishop on b7, but takes the pawn out of d4's firing line.
The knight finally comes out: e5 is controlled by the d6-pawn and the bishop, so the move can't be punished.
The most dangerous try: it forces ...b4 and gives the knight the c4-square.
The knight starts its trip to c4, where Black has no pawn that can hit it.
Prepares ...e6, to break the d5-pawn.
Stops a4-a5 and the knight reaching b6.
Protects the b2-pawn so that the knight can leave c4.
The bishop heads for c4: trading the strong knight is the only way to deal with it.
The knight challenges the bishop.
Black has a solid game. The position is roughly equal; both sides have their play, and the main strategic idea is Black's bishop pair against the white knight on c4.
A fully good alternative: after 6.a4 it transposes into the previous game, and Black chooses it when he prefers the King's Indian structures to the queenside expansion.

lines.name: 4.Be2 Nf6 5.Nf3 O-O 6.O-O a6: transposing to the Nf3 lines
lines.summary: Against 4.Be2 Black plays the Pirc Classical with ...Nf6 and ...O-O and uses ...a6 and ...Nc6 to reach the same positions as after 4.Nf3. 4.Nge2 and 4.h4 are covered in the variations.

next.text: A modest move, popular in the elite games (68% of them are answered by ...Nf6).
Black does not need the Tiger structure here: there is no threat.
The same move as in the previous games. It prepares ...b5, and after 7.a4 it keeps the options of ...Nc6 and ...e5 open. 6...c6, 6...Nc6 and 6...Bg4 are all playable alternatives.
The position of the first game of this file.
Transposes to the 4.g3 line below.
The pawn must be stopped at once. The weakness on g5 can be a problem, but the knight on f3 is pinned by ...Bg4 and Black's structure has no weaknesses.

lines.name: 4.g3 Nf6 5.Bg2 O-O 6.Nge2 e5 7.h3 Nc6 8.Be3 exd4 9.Nxd4 Bd7
lines.summary: The fianchetto line is a King's Indian with the knight on e2. Black plays ...Nf6 and ...e5, exchanges on d4 and trades White's strong knight; the play is level.

next.text: 4...a6 is also played, but against the fianchetto the Pirc move is natural, because the bishop on g2 is not hitting anything and the knight on f6 pressures e4.
The knight keeps the f-pawn and the long diagonal of the bishop free.
Black strikes in the centre at once: with the knight on e2 there is no d5 and Nd2 plan available, and the game is open.
Prepares Be3 and stops ...Ng4; 7.O-O is the other main line.
Unpins the knight and prepares ...Nxd4 and ...Bc6.
The rook adds pressure on e4.
Black trades the white knight, which was his most active piece.
Black continues ...Bc6: the pieces are traded off, and the pressure on e4 and the open e-file give Black an easy game. Level.
The normal King's Indian: the plan is ...e5 and the d4-exchange.

lines.name: 4.Bg5 a6 5.Qd2 b5 6.a4 b4 7.Nd5 a5 8.c3 c6 9.Ne3 Nf6
lines.summary: Against 4.Bg5 Black avoids the Pirc ...Nf6 and plays the Tiger set-up. Without a bishop on e3 the ...c5 break is easier, and the knight on d5 can be chased away by ...c6.

next.text: Aims at the pin on f6 and at e7, and prepares Qd2 and long castling. Against a Pirc order (4...Nf6) it is more dangerous, because White may play e5 or Qd2 with threats against the knight (in the elite games White scores 53% against 4...Nf6 and 46% against 4...a6).
The Tiger answer: no knight to pin, and Black waits for White to commit. Against the bishop on g5, Black's counterplay with ...c5 is easier than against Be3, because the bishop no longer protects d4.
Threatens Bh6, but without a knight on f6 and a castled king the threat has little point.
Challenges the pawn at once.
Gains time on the knight.
The knight is well placed in the centre.
Protects the b4 pawn and stops a5, which would leave Black weak on the queenside.
Attacks b4 and prepares to open the queenside.
Kicks the knight.
The knight has to retreat; e3 is the natural square, from where it covers c2 and f5 and keeps an eye on d5.
Hits e4 and forces f3, which blocks the knight on g1.
White has a pawn, but Black has a lead in development and a clear plan: ...h6 forces the bishop to decide, and ...e5 and ...Nc5 give Black the centre.

A forcing sequence from the study: 18.fxe4 Nxe4 19.Qb4 Nxf2 20.Kxf2 c5 and the white king is exposed, Black has the bishops and a big centre. It is a model of what Black is playing for here, rather than a line to expect move for move: Black has real compensation for the pawn.
Black develops as in the Tiger lines: ...Ngf6 and ...c5 follow.

lines.name: 4.Bc4 Nf6 5.Nf3 O-O 6.O-O Nc6 7.h3: the Mad Dog
lines.summary: White aims at f7 with the bishop on c4. Black develops with ...Nf6, ...O-O and ...Nc6; after the slow 7.h3 the knight takes on e4 and ...d5 forks bishop and knight.

next.text: The bishop aims at f7. White hopes for an attack with Qe2 or Qf3 and a knight to g5, but with ...Nf6 Black has e5 under control and can answer almost everything with ...d5.
The knight comes out at once: it prevents e5 and attacks the e4-pawn.
Castling removes the king from the f7 problem: f7 is now defended by the rook and the king.
The Mad Dog. The knight puts d4 under pressure with the bishop on g7 behind it. White must now deal with the possible ...Bg4 pin and ...Nxe4.
Looks natural, since it prevents ...Bg4, but it neglects e4. White scores badly after this move in the elite database.
The pawn forks the bishop on c4 and the knight on e4.
Three pieces attack d4 and only two defend it. The knight is protected.
Black wins a pawn: after 11...Bxd4 the queen can't take on d4 because ...Qxd4 would win it, and the bishop on e4 is loose. The study judges the position as slightly better for Black.
White has lost a piece for a pawn.
White has given up a bishop for a pawn and Black's pieces are more active.
The e5-pawn is attacked by the knight and the bishop, and Black has easy equality.
An alternative that scores very well in the elite games (63% for Black after 7.h3).

lines.name: 4.Bc4 Nf6 5.Qe2 c6! 6.e5 dxe5 7.dxe5 Nd5 8.Bd2
lines.summary: White prepares e5 with Qe2. Black answers with ...c6, which takes d5 and b5 away from White and meets e5 with a trade on d5.

next.text: Defends e4 and prepares e5. In the elite database it is uncomfortable for Black after 5...O-O (6.Nf3 and 6.e5 both score above 54% for White) and after 5...Nc6 (6.e5 scores 67%).

The best-scoring reply in the elite database (47% for Black against 36% after 5...O-O and 32% after 5...Nc6). The pawn takes d5 and b5 away from White's pieces, meets e5 with ...dxe5 and ...Nd5, and prepares ...b5 and ...Qa5. Black castles later, when the bishop on c4 and the queen on e2 are no longer aimed at his kingside.
The critical test.
The knight attacks c3 and takes the sting out of the e5-pawn.
Black has easy development: ...O-O, ...Nb6 or ...Nxc3 and ...Qa5 are all possible, and the e5-pawn is weak. In 29 elite games White scored 34% and Black 52% here.

chapters.title: Dragon: Yugoslav Attack
chapters.subtitle: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 g6 6.Be3 Bg7 7.f3
chapters.intro:
The Yugoslav Attack is the reason the Dragon has a reputation. White builds the King's Indian Sämisch set-up against a fianchetto that has no ...e5 in it: Be3, f3, Qd2, queenside castling, then h4-h5 to open the h-file and Bh6 to remove the bishop that defends the king. A King's Indian player knows the bishop on g7 and the pawns in front of it; what is new is everything else. The centre is half open, Black has no pawn on c7, and the game is a race in which the c-file plays the part that the f-file and the pawn storm play in the King's Indian.

Black's assets are permanent and White's are not. Black has two centre pawns against one, a bishop that points at b2 and c3, and a half-open file aimed at the white king. White has more space and the faster-looking attack, but if the attack is held or the queens come off, Black is normally the one who is comfortable. That is why so many lines here end with White forcing a draw or steering into a slightly better ending, and why the opening rewards knowing exactly which defensive move is needed and not merely the general plan.

The repertoire: against **9.Bc4** the Topalov Variation (10...Rc8 11.Bb3 Nxd4 12.Bxd4 b5), which is Gawain Jones's main recommendation and the most played line among strong players today, with the Soltis Variation behind it because White can force it by move order. Against **9.0-0-0** the break 9...d5, with 12...Bxd4 and 13...Qb6 in the main line. Against **9.g4**, 9...Be6. The other major systems (the 12.Kb1 lines, the Chinese Dragon, 10...Qa5, Giri's 9...Nxd4, the old 12...e5, the Dragadorf) each get a line of their own so that the whole map is visible.

sections.title: The tabiya and White's three roads
sections.body:
Everything White has played serves one plan. 7.f3 holds e4 and takes g4 from the knight, so that the bishop on e3 cannot be chased; 8.Qd2 lines up Bh6 and clears the way for castling long.

- **9.Bc4** stops ...d5 by force and points the bishop at f7. The price is time: the bishop will be hit by ...Ne5 or ...Na5, and on b3 it is a target for ...a5-a4. This is the sharp road, covered in the first three groups of lines.
- **9.0-0-0** saves the bishop move and allows 9...d5. White gives up the direct attack for pressure in a half-open centre. Strong players choose it most often, because White needs to remember less and risks less.
- **9.g4** also discourages ...d5 (10.g5 would hit the knight that supports it) without spending a move on the bishop.

Move order matters less than it seems before move 9. Black can castle on move 7 or play 7...Nc6 first; the only real error is 6...Ng4, which loses material to 7.Bb5+.

sections.title: The c-file, the c4 square and the b-pawn
sections.body:
Black's play runs down the c-file towards c3 and b2. The classical way to use it is ...Ne5-c4: the knight attacks the queen and the bishop on e3, White has to take it with the b3-bishop, and after ...Rxc4 Black has removed the piece that both attacks f7 and covers the white king, and has a rook on the fourth rank that can double, swing, or give itself up on c3. The queen joins from a5 and the b-pawn runs to b4 to dislodge the knight that holds White's queenside together.

The Topalov Variation gets at the same targets in another way. Black trades knights on d4 first and plays ...b5 at once: the bishop on b3 is then short of squares (...a5-a4 threatens to trap it), the knight on c3 can be hit by ...b4, and White has no time for the slow h-pawn attack.

White's standard prophylaxis is **Kb1**. It takes the king off the c-file, covers a2, removes checks on the c1-h6 diagonal and makes Nd5 possible in positions where ...Qxd2 would otherwise come with check. The quiet 12.Kb1 is considered the critical test of 11...Ne5 for exactly this reason: Black's standard moves all become a little less effective.

sections.title: The exchange sacrifice on c3
sections.body:
The move to learn first. A rook for the knight on c3 wrecks the pawns in front of the white king, removes the only defender of e4, a2 and d5, and leaves the Dragon bishop without an opponent on the long diagonal. Black rarely needs to win material back quickly: a pawn and the shattered structure are normally enough even after a queen trade, and with queens on the white king is in danger for the rest of the game.

- It is strongest when the white queen has been drawn away, typically after Bh6 Bxh6 Qxh6: the queen on h6 attacks but no longer defends c3 or b2.
- It works as defence as well as attack. Without the knight on c3 there is no Nd5, and White's attack usually needs that move to remove the knight on f6.
- It should be checked, not played by reflex, when White has already played Kb1 and can answer with bxc3 and c4, or when Black has no second wave (queen to a5 or c7, the other rook to c8).

The diagram is a classical example: Black has taken on e4 with the knight because the queen on d2 was tied to the bishop on h6, and now gives the rook to keep the extra pawns and the bishop.

sections.title: The race on the h-file and why Black plays ...h5
sections.body:
White's attack has three parts: open the h-file with h4-h5 (as a pawn sacrifice if need be), exchange the g7-bishop with Bh6, and remove the knight on f6 with Nd5, g4-g5 or Bxf6. When all three succeed, the queen and rook mate on h7 or h8. Black cannot stop all of them by passive means, which is why the old main lines with ...Nc4 and the h-file open were a pure race.

The Soltis move 12...h5 changes the terms. The h-file stays closed unless White gives up material with g4, and after g4 hxg4 Black has an extra pawn and a g-file that is blocked by his own pawn. The cost is the g5 square: the bishop goes there, pins the knight against e7 and prepares e5 or Bxf6. Black's answer is ...Rc5, a rook that defends along the fifth rank and is ready to take the bishop on g5: that sacrifice drags the h4- or f4-pawn off its file, kills f4-f5 and gives the knight a permanent post on e5.

The same logic explains the modern habit of **delaying castling** (the Dragadorf and the early ...h5 lines). A king that has not gone to g8 gives h4-h5 nothing to open, and ...h5 played before White has committed anything stops g4 and Bh6 for good. What Black gives up is time and the ...d5 break.

sections.title: What the Dragon bishop is worth
sections.body:
More than a rook, in many positions. The bishop defends the king and attacks b2 with the same move, and the dark squares around both kings belong to whoever keeps a dark-squared bishop. The theory is full of lines where Black lets a rook go to keep it: in the diagram Black has left the rook on f8 to be taken, because after Bxf8 Qxf8 the bishop pair and the dark squares give more than enough. The rook lift to c5 followed by ...Rxg5 is the same trade.

The practical rules:

- When White plays Bh6, the usual answer is ...Bxh6, pulling the queen to h6, followed by ...Rxc3 or a queen move with tempo. With a rook already on e8 Black can keep the bishop with ...Bh8, which is the main point of the waiting move ...Re8.
- When White plays Bd4 to offer the trade, Black decides by the pawn structure: in the Topalov line it happens on g7 and Black is fine because the queenside play is already rolling; after 9.0-0-0 d5 the choice between 12...Bxd4 and 12...e5 is the choice between a sound structure and keeping the bishop.
- White's Nd5, when it forces ...Nxd5 and Bxg7, removes both of Black's kingside defenders at once. Check what the recapture on d5 does before allowing it.

sections.title: The Topalov plan
sections.body:
Trading on d4 looks like a concession, since it brings the bishop to the long diagonal opposite ours. The point is tempo. With the knight gone from d4, ...b5 cannot be met by Ndxb5, and the threat of ...a5-a4 makes White react on the queenside before the kingside attack has started. If White plays a3 to give the bishop a square on a2, then ...b4 opens a file whatever White does, usually as a pawn sacrifice.

White's best answer is 13.Nd5, exchanging both the f6-knight and the bishops. That leads to the structure of the next section, and to a main line that has been analysed out to a forced draw. Every other 13th move gives Black the initiative: the lines are short and worth knowing exactly, because several of them (14.a4, 13.Bxa7) lose quickly for White.

Why this and not 11...Ne5: after 11...Ne5 White has 12.Kb1, the line the theoreticians trust most for White, and Black has to choose between several difficult defences. The Topalov move order cuts it out. What it cannot cut out is the Soltis, because White can start with 10.h4 and after 10...h5 the knight belongs on e5 again. So both systems have to be known.

sections.title: The d5-pawn structure and the endings
sections.body:
When White answers ...Nxd5 with exd5 the game changes character. The e-file is half open and e7 is a fixed target; White doubles on it and Black cannot play ...e6 without leaving d6 weak. In return the bishop on b3 bites on its own pawn, the c-file is Black's, and c5 is a fine square for a rook that defends e7 sideways from e5 or c7 when needed. Black's counterplay is ...b4, and it is usually worth a pawn: the a- and b-files open against a king that has no minor piece near it.

Endings in the Dragon are better for Black than the opening's reputation suggests.

- With the usual structure (e7 and d6 against c2, and the white f- and g-pawns advanced), Black's extra centre pawn and the weaknesses White made while attacking count for more as pieces come off. Giri's repertoire heads for such endings on purpose.
- After an exchange sacrifice on c3, rook and knight or rook and bishop against two rooks is often easy to play for Black as long as one pawn has been collected: White's queenside pawns are targets and the rooks have no open file.
- After 9.0-0-0 d5 and ...bxc6 it is the other way round. Black has the split queenside pawns and White the c5 outpost, so there Black needs the pieces on and the b-file active; drifting into a quiet ending is how those lines are lost.
- In the pawn-grab line 12.Nxd5 cxd5 13.Qxd5 Qc7 White can take both rooks for the queen. Material favours White, coordination favours Black, and practice says the queen is at least as good.

sections.title: The ...d5 break
sections.body:
If Black can play ...d5 safely, Black plays it: the break frees the position and removes the only structural problem, the hole on d5. After 9.0-0-0 it is a pawn sacrifice. White can win the pawn with 12.Nxd5 cxd5 13.Qxd5, but then 13...Qc7 opens three files and two diagonals against the white king, and the theory has held for Black for decades.

So White normally declines with 12.Bd4, asking to trade the bishop. The position that results is the main line of the whole Dragon today: Black has two pawn islands on the queenside and a hole on c5, White has a king that sits on the open b-file's target square. Black's plan is concrete: queen to b6 with tempo, then to c7, rooks to d8 and b8, the bishop to f5 or e6, the knight to f4 or b6, and ...h5 to hold up g4. White tries to plant a knight on c5 and trade pieces.

The tenth-move alternatives (10.Qe1, 10.Kb1, 10.Nxc6) all try to get the benefits of the main line without allowing this easy development; each has one precise answer, given in the lines.

sections.title: Tactics to know
sections.body:
For Black:

- **...Rxc3**, above. Its cousins are ...Rxc4 structures where the rook is sacrificed on c4 after b3, and ...Rxb2 when the b-file is open.
- **...Nxe4**. It works when fxe4 is impossible or bad because of what is uncovered: the bishop on g7 against d4 and b2, or a rook on c4 against d4, as in the diagram, where 18.fxe4 Rxd4 costs White at least a pawn and 18.Bxc4 Nxd2 the queen.
- **...Bxg4, ...Nxg4 and ...Nxf3**. Once White has played g4 and h5, a piece for two or three kingside pawns often ends the attack and leaves Black's pawns rolling.
- **...Bh6 or ...Qa5 with a pin on the c1-h6 diagonal**, when the king is still on c1.
- **...Nc3+ in-between moves** when the b-pawn has reached b4 and the knight is on d5.

For White, the ideas to watch on every move:

- **Bh6**, and after ...Bxh6 Qxh6 the threats Nd5, h5 and g4-g5.
- **h5** as a pawn sacrifice, and **g4** against the Soltis pawn, to open the h-file.
- **Nd5**, removing the f6-knight. With queens on d2 and a5 it carries the in-between check Nxe7+ after ...Qxd2, which is why Kb1 (so that ...Qxd2 is not check) changes so many lines.
