- **Nf5**, a knight sacrifice on the square g6 guards, to open the g-file after ...gxf5.
- **e5**, opening the d-file against the bishop on d7 and clearing e4 for the knight.
- **Rxh5** in the Soltis, giving the exchange to reopen the file Black closed.

sections.title: Move orders, the Dragadorf and early ...h5
sections.body:
White has three ways to reach the 9.Bc4 lines and they are not equivalent.

- **10.0-0-0** allows the Topalov Variation (10...Rc8 11.Bb3 Nxd4), and after 11...Ne5 it keeps 12.Kb1.
- **10.h4** must be answered by 10...h5. After 11.0-0-0 Rc8 12.Bb3 Ne5 the Soltis is on the board and White has avoided the Topalov, but has also spent h4, so the 12.Kb1 lines are gone.
- **10.Bb3** allows 10...Nxd4 11.Bxd4 b5 at once, the original form of Topalov's idea; 10...Rc8 keeps both of the main systems available.

The Dragadorf (...a6 and ...b5 with the king in the centre, the knight on d7 and the bishop on b7) and the lines with an early ...h5 are playable alternatives to the whole main-line complex. They avoid most of the theory and the h-file attack; they give White a freer hand in the centre and make ...d5 hard to arrange. One line shows how they are set up.

sections.title: Sources
sections.body:
- Gawain Jones, *Grandmaster Repertoire: The Dragon 1* and *The Dragon 2* (Quality Chess, 2015): move-order guide, Dragon themes, the chapter on White's other 13th moves in the Topalov Variation, the introduction to 9.0-0-0 and the chapter on White's offbeat tenth moves (publisher's excerpts)
- Anish Giri, *The Dragon Sicilian* (New In Chess, 2022): introduction, the chapter on 9.Bc4 Nxd4 and the index of variations (publisher's excerpt)
- Carsten Hansen, *The Sicilian Dragon: Move by Move* (Everyman Chess, 2016): contents and the opening of the chapter on 9.0-0-0 d5 10.exd5 (publisher's excerpt)
- Chris Ward, *Sicilian Dragon: The Real Deal!* parts 2 and 3 (ChessBase, 2022), course outlines, and his monthly Dragon updates at chesspublishing.com (summaries of the September 2013, May 2016, September 2019, October 2021, May 2023 and March 2025 updates)
- "Sicilian Defence, Dragon Variation" and "Sicilian Defence, Dragon Variation, Yugoslav Attack", Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicilian_Defence,_Dragon_Variation
- John Donaldson, review of Jones's *The Dragon*, https://www.jeremysilman.com/book-review/dragon-the/
- Richard Webb, review of Giri's *The Dragon Sicilian*, British Chess News, https://britishchessnews.com/?p=21487
- Lichess Elite Database (games of players rated 2400 and above), used to confirm how each line is played in practice

lines.name: Topalov Variation: 13.Nd5, the main line
lines.summary: White trades knights and bishops to slow the queenside down. Black sacrifices the b-pawn for the a- and c-files, and the main line runs to a position that elite practice has shown to be a draw.

next.text: The first move of the Yugoslav Attack. White will play f3 and Qd2, castle long and push the h-pawn. Compared with the Sämisch King's Indian the centre is half open: White already has the d-file and Black the c-file, so both attacks arrive sooner.
Now ...Ng4 is ruled out for good and e4 is solid, which frees the c3-knight to jump to d5 later.

The bishop stops ...d5 and takes the a2-g8 diagonal, where it attacks f7 and will later shield the king from b3. It will cost White three moves in all, and Black's whole counterattack is built on that time.
The c8-square is needed for a rook, and d7 is the square from which the bishop does not get in the way; on e6 it could be exchanged at once.
White can also start with 10.h4 or 10.Bb3. Against 10.h4 Black has to reply 10...h5 and play the Soltis Variation; the move orders are sorted out in the first Soltis line.
With a threat: 11...Nxd4 12.Bxd4 Rxc4.
The third move of this bishop.

The Topalov Variation. Black gives up the knight that was heading for c4 in order to play ...b5 with tempo: with no knight on d4 the pawn cannot be taken, and ...a5-a4 will trap the bishop unless White reacts.

**Why not 11...Ne5:** it is the classical move and fully playable, but it allows 12.Kb1, the line with the best reputation for White in the whole 9.Bc4 complex. This move order takes that away, which is why Jones makes it his main weapon.

The point. The threat is ...a5-a4, and after a3 the lever ...b4 opens a file. The bishop on d4 looks imposing, but it is the piece Black's bishop wants to meet: once the dark-squared bishops come off, White's attack has lost Bh6 and Black's queenside play simply goes on.

The most testing reply, and the reason the line is so heavily analysed. White removes the knight that ...b4 would have chased, exchanges our best defender on f6 and gets the bishops off. Every other move lets Black attack for nothing (see the next two lines).
Nothing else: Black cannot allow Nxf6+ followed by Bxf6, which would leave the kingside pawns in ruins.
Now the structure is fixed: White gets the e-file and a target on e7, Black the c-file and a bishop on b3 that is blocked by its own pawn.
Threatening to win the bishop.
Making room on a2. 16.a4 bxa4 just loses a pawn.

The least obvious move in the line. Black is going to sacrifice the b-pawn in any case, and with the king on g7 the white queen would take on b4 or go to d4 with check, gaining the tempo that decides whether the e-file pressure or the a-file counterplay comes first. So the king steps back first.

The older move order 16...b4 17.axb4 axb4 18.Qxb4 Rb8 19.Qd4+ Kg8 has scored clearly better for White.
The natural move: the rook attacks e7 and White plans Re3 and Rde1.

Active defence. The rook attacks d5, which keeps the bishop on b3 and the queen tied to that pawn, and it clears the back rank so that the queen can reach a8 in one move after ...b4. The passive 17...Re8 is what White is hoping for: he doubles on the e-file, pushes the h-pawn, and Black has no counterplay to show for it.
Preparing to double. 18.g4, taking f5 from the bishop, is met by the same sacrifice 18...b4.
The thematic pawn sacrifice: a pawn for two open files against a king that has no minor piece near it.
The queen takes the a-file with ideas of ...Qa1+ and ...Rb8. White's extra pawn is the one on b2, and it is pinned down for the rest of the game.
The bishop finally leaves b3: it blocks the c-file in front of c2 and frees b3 for the pawn, so that the king has air.
The bishop finds its diagonal and attacks c2.
White uses the tempo on the queen to contest the a-file.
Lining up behind the rook against c4 and c2.
All three heavy pieces are on the c-file and White is tied to c2 and c4.
Exchanging the piece that holds White's queenside together.

**Verdict:** equal, and in practice a draw: of the many elite games that have reached this position almost every one was drawn. Black's queen and rooks dominate the dark squares around the king, and White cannot make the extra pawn count because his rooks stay tied to b3 and c2.

This is what the Topalov Variation promises against best play: a forcing sequence that has to be known by heart, at the end of which White has nothing. Whatever White tries earlier is more dangerous for him than for Black.
Centralising, to answer ...b4 by keeping the queenside closed.
White does not take: 19.Qxb4 would open the b-file onto b2 with his own queen standing in front of it.
Black has the a-file for nothing and the better game.
Too slow now that the bishops are gone: there is no Bh6 to follow h5.
The same set-up as in the main line, with ...Qa8 to come, and White has spent on the h-pawn a move that he needed for the e-file.
Keeps the pawn structure healthy but leaves the bishop exposed.
Black carries on with ...b4 and can gain time with ...e6 when it suits. Without pressure on the e-file White has nothing to play for.
The queen is misplaced in front of the bishop.
The threat of ...a4 costs White another tempo, and Black has scored very well from here.
This is the position of the note with 17.Qd4 below, reached by another route.
The queen steps into a discovered attack.
Black has the bishop pair and every dark square on the board.
The other great system. See the Soltis and 12.Kb1 lines.
Giri's recommendation, heading for 10.Bxd4 Be6. It is a complete alternative to everything that follows and has its own line.

Equally good: after 8.Qd2 O-O it is the same position, and Black keeps the option of leaving the king in the centre for a move or two with ...Bd7 and ...Rc8. Just do not mix it with ...a6, which belongs to a different set-up (see the Dragadorf line).
Hunting the bishop at once loses a piece: the knight on d4 no longer blocks the queen's diagonal, and b5 is available with check.
The bishop on d7 is pinned and cannot take the queen.
White wins the exchange and a pawn.

lines.name: Topalov Variation: 13.h4
lines.summary: White ignores the queenside and Black wins the race to the bishop on b3. The lines are sharp but short, and the natural defensive tries 14.a4 and 14.a3 both fail.

next.text: The move White wants to play in every Dragon. Here it carries no threat for two more moves, and that is too slow.
Black does not defend. The bishop on b3 has no retreat, so White must deal with ...a4 at once.
The consistent move: White lets the bishop be attacked and counts on the h-file.

White gives up his fine bishop to remove the defender of h7 and to gain a move for the other bishop. 15.Bd5 has also been tried; Black replies 15...e6 or 15...b4, and there are too few games for a verdict.

The recapture that looks wrong. The pawn keeps the bishop on g7, where it covers h8 and h6 after the h-file opens, and ...f5 will open the long diagonal onto b2 with tempo against e4. The doubled pawns do not matter while the game is this sharp.
The bishop escapes to the square the knight was meant to use.
The bishop is opened and e4 is attacked.

**Verdict:** good for Black. The h-file is open, but h8 is covered and White has no dark-squared bishop left to challenge the one on g7, which now rules the long diagonal. Black continues with ...Qf6 or ...Qa5 and ...Rc5; White's bishop on d5 is handsome and attacks nothing.
Shutting the bishop in before taking on d6.
White has won a pawn and buried the bishop on h8, but the pawn on a2 threatens to queen and the files in front of his king are open. The few games played have gone Black's way.
The natural move, and the risky one: the bishop leaves the king. Jones beat Judit Polgar with it in 2013, but in elite games since then White has scored heavily.
White has a dangerous attack for the piece he is about to lose on b3.
The natural way to stop ...a4 loses material.
Hitting both bishops.
The rook is immune because of 18.Bxc4 Nxd2, and 18.fxe4 Rxd4 wins a pawn, since 19.Qxd4 Bxd4 20.Rxd4 would leave White with rook and bishop for the queen.
After the exchanges on d4 Black is a sound pawn up, and it is White's king that has lost its cover.
Giving the bishop a square, but also giving Black a lever.
Compare the main line with 13.Nd5: Black has opened the a-file without giving up a pawn.
The bishop covers the king from f5 and attacks c2. Black is better.
The Soltis reflex is misplaced. It spends the tempo that makes ...a5 strong, and White opens the kingside with g4 anyway. Black has done badly with it.

lines.name: Topalov Variation: 13.Kb1, 13.Bxa7 and other 13th moves
lines.summary: Everything except 13.Nd5 and 13.h4. Against slow moves Black plays ...a5 and ...b4, against 13.Bxa7 the a-pawn is a sacrifice, and 13.e5 leads to an ending that is pleasant for Black.

next.text: A useful move in nearly every Dragon, but it does nothing about ...a5.
A pawn sacrifice once more: White will be able to win b4, and Black gets the a-file and the long diagonal.
The critical move, going after the pawn.
Jones's move. The queen keeps an eye on c2 and makes room for the rook; the pawn is left to its fate.

**Verdict:** excellent compensation. Black follows with ...Rfb8, ...Qa5 and ...Be6 to exchange the bishop that holds a2 and c2 together, and every black piece has a file or a diagonal leading to the white king. White's extra pawn plays no part, and finding the defensive moves over the board is very hard.
This makes little sense when b4 is not hanging.
The main line of the first game with the a-file opened for nothing. Black is better.
The same mistake as after 13.h4.
Both bishops are attacked, and 17.Bb3 Nxe4 follows as before.
Giving the bishop its square in advance.
Black plays the same way: 14.Kb1 is the main line of this game, and 14.h4 b4 is the note with 14.a3 in the previous one.
White takes a pawn and dares Black to prove something. Jones compares it with the main line: the pawn is a different one, but Black's compensation is the same.
The knight is driven off and the a-file is open for the queen and rook.
Hitting a2 and the bishop on a7 together.

**Verdict:** White has kept the pawn and Black has the a-file, the c-file and a queenside that White can never use. Jones judges the compensation to be full; in elite games White has scored well from here, so this is the line of the Topalov to look at again before playing it in a serious game.
The natural retreat allows a combination.
The bishop is dragged off b3, the square from which it guarded a2.
The king is caught in the corner with ...Qa1+ and ...Rc8 coming, and Black has won most of the games from here.
Keeping the knight for the defence.
Removing the bishop that covers a2 and c2.
Black has the a- and c-files and targets on a2 and b3 for the pawn; White is tied up but solid, and has held his own in practice.
An attempt to simplify by opening the d-file against the bishop on d7.
The bishop steps out of the pin and offers the queen exchange on Black's terms.
An in-between check that sends the king to b1, further from the centre, before the rooks come off.
Jones's suggestion, followed by ...a4 and ...f5. Black has the more mobile pawn majority and the more active pieces in the ending, and the bishop on b3 risks being shut out by ...e6.
Keeping the queens on is riskier for White.
With ...b4 next, and White's bishops on b3 and e5 are both loose.
This puts no pressure on Black at all in the Topalov Variation.
The knight stays on h5, where it blocks the h-file for good, and ...b4 and ...a4 come next. White's kingside pawns will be weak in any ending.

lines.name: Soltis Variation: 13.Bg5 Rc5 14.Kb1
lines.summary: White can force this system with the 10.h4 move order. Black closes the h-file with ...h5, posts a rook on c5 and meets the g4 and h5 sacrifices by taking everything and returning the exchange.

next.text: White starts with the h-pawn. The point of the move order is to rule out the Topalov Variation: with h5 threatened, Black has no time for ...Rc8, ...Nxd4 and ...b5. The price is that White is committed to h4, so the quiet 12.Kb1 systems are gone as well.

The Soltis move, and here the only good one: Jones calls it dangerous to let the pawn go any further. With the pawn on h5 White can open the h-file only by sacrificing with g4. The cost is the g5-square, which is where White's bishop goes next.

Now the knight belongs on e5. With h4 and ...h5 inserted the Topalov plan is less good: after 12...Nxd4 13.Bxd4 b5 White plays g4, and ...h5 has turned from a defence into a target. On e5 the knight eyes c4 and also covers g4 and f3.
The main line. The bishop takes the square ...h5 gave up, pins the knight to e7 and prepares f4 followed by e5, or Bxf6 and Nd5. The alternatives 13.Bh6, 13.Kb1 and 13.g4 are in a later line.

The key move of the Soltis, and not one that anybody finds at the board. On c5 the rook covers d5, so that Nd5 can be answered by ...Rxd5; it frees the b-pawn; and it looks along the rank at the bishop on g5. As soon as the knight leaves e5 Black can take that bishop. The exchange sacrifice removes White's best attacking piece, drags a pawn to g5 where it blocks its own files, and leaves Black's knight and bishop unopposed on the dark squares.
The usual prophylactic move, taking the king off the c-file before the fight starts. 14.g4 and 14.f4 are in the next line.
Jones's recommendation: Black simply gets on with it.
White cannot wait for ...Nc4 or ...b4 and gives a pawn to open the h-file.
Jones prefers taking. After 15...a5, which has also been played, he names 16.gxh5 and 16.Bxf6 as the critical replies.
A second pawn, to pull the knight away from f6.
Now e7 is attacked twice.
The calm defence and the most popular move. 17...Rxd5 at once has also been played.
The standard blow: the rook is given to reopen the file that the knight was blocking.
Heading for h5, with threats against h7 and f7.
Black returns the exchange to remove the knight, which was tying the queen and the rook to e7.

**Verdict:** critical and double-edged. Black is two pawns up for the moment. White will win one back on h5 and has the h-file; Black has the knight on e5, pressure on d4 and b2, and ...e6 to drive the bishop from d5.

This is where Jones's recommended moves lead in practice. It is sharper than anything in the Topalov lines and has to be prepared move by move: here the plans alone are not enough.

The older main line. The rook protects e7 so that the queen is free to go to a5 or c8; Carlsen played it against Radjabov in 2008. It is a sound alternative for a player who wants the rook on e8 before committing the b-pawn.
The third move order.
Keeping both systems: 11.O-O-O Nxd4 12.Bxd4 b5 is the Topalov Variation. The independent alternative is 10...Nxd4 11.Bxd4 b5 at once, the original form of Topalov's idea.
The same position as after 12.Bb3 in the main line.

lines.name: Soltis Variation: 13.Bg5 Rc5 with 14.g4 and 14.f4
lines.summary: White breaks at once without Kb1. Black takes the pawn, hits the queen with ...Nc4 and has the bishop on g5 under fire from the rook.

next.text: White sacrifices at once, saving the king move.
White wants to drive the knight off and follow with f5 or e5.
With tempo, and now the rook really does attack the bishop on g5.

**Verdict:** fine for Black. The queen move does several jobs: it defends g4, it lines up on the c-file behind the rook and knight so that a sacrifice on b2 is in the air, and it leaves the rook free to take on g5. Black is a pawn up with the h-file closed, and the standard assessment is that the early g-pawn advance promises White little.
Black is two pawns up and the knight blocks the h-file. It is the main line of the previous game without Kb1 and ...b5, and White has to prove his compensation without the useful king move.
Chasing the knight to prepare e5. The drawback is that f3 no longer covers e4 and g4, and the bishop on g5 has lost its way back to e3.

The knight goes after the bishop on b3, the piece that makes e5 and f5 dangerous. This is the move elite players have chosen most often, with good results in a small number of games; 15...b5 16.e5 is the sharper alternative.

lines.name: Soltis Variation: 13.Bh6, 13.Kb1 and 13.g4
lines.summary: White's other 13th moves. Against 13.Bh6 Black exchanges on c4 and g7 and brings a rook to h8; 13.Kb1 leads to the sharpest test of the Soltis; 13.g4 is premature.

next.text: The direct attempt to remove the bishop.
The solid answer. Black removes the b3-bishop first and lets the dark-squared bishops come off on g7, where the king recaptures and clears h8 for a rook.
The only way to open lines.
The point of recapturing on g7 with the king: the rook reaches the h-file in one move and White's attack runs into a defender of equal value.

**Verdict:** good for Black. He strikes in the centre before White can play f5 or e5, and after 20.Nde2 Nxe4 he has won a second pawn. The position stays sharp, but Black has a healthy plus score in this line and none of the usual worries about the h-file.
A flashy try that fails.
Black has bishop, knight and a mass of passed pawns for a rook and is winning; he has won every elite game from here.
Without the dark-squared bishops this exchange holds no terror.
Black has no weaknesses and plays ...b5 and ...Qb6 or ...Qa5; the kingside is closed.
The classical sacrificial line, and still playable.
The queen on h6 is far from the defence and Black has the usual compensation: the wrecked pawns, the c-file and the knight on e5. It asks more of Black's memory than the main line.
Useful and flexible, and in practice the most dangerous move: White keeps Bg5, Bh6 and g4 all in hand.
The modern way, sacrificing two pawns for the files.

Black has two extra pawns and White two open files. Black's ideas are ...Rfc8 and a sacrifice on c3; White doubles on the g- or h-file. This is the line in which White has scored best against the Soltis in elite games, and it should be studied before 11...Ne5 is chosen in a game that matters.
The older plan: the knight defends c3 so that Bh6 can follow without allowing ...Rxc3.
Black is in time on the queenside and has scored well.
Premature: White has neither played Kb1 nor pinned the knight.
The precise defence. The queen gets a route to f6 and h4, and the bishop on b3 is shut out.
White has no way through and is two pawns down.

lines.name: The 12.Kb1 system and the Burnett Variation
lines.summary: The line that drives many Dragon players to the Topalov move order. White makes a useful waiting move, and Black's sharpest answer is a rook sacrifice on c4.

next.text: The modern main line, reckoned the critical test of 11...Ne5. White makes the one useful move that commits nothing. The king leaves the c-file and covers a2; ...Qa5 no longer comes with a pin or a check; Nd5 becomes possible because ...Qxd2 is not check; and since h4 has not been played, the Soltis set-up has nothing to block.

The established move and Jones's choice for those who play 11...Ne5. The fashionable 12...a6, which Carlsen used against Ivanchuk in 2008, he considers too slow to be best; White's critical reply is 13.h4.

With the king already safe White can start with the g-pawn. That rules out ...h5, and h4-h5 will follow. The old verdict was that White is simply better, because Black's standard counterplay is too slow.
Counterplay has to be immediate.
The critical test. The rook has no good square: 15...Rc8 16.Ndxb5 loses a pawn, and 15...Rc5 runs into 16.Ne6, when the bishop takes on c5 and the d-file opens against the queen.
The Burnett Variation: Black leaves the rook where it is. It is the c3 sacrifice in another form, as Jones points out, with the rook given on c4.
The first target is c4, and the b-file is open for the other rook.

**Verdict:** Black has given the exchange and a pawn, and has real compensation. The white king has no pawns in front of it on the b-file, the pawns on a2, c2 and c4 are all weak, and Black's bishops, the rook on the b-file and the knight heading for f4 are all active while White's attack has not started. Jones presents this as a complete answer to 12.Kb1, and Black has won most of the few elite games played. It is the right choice for a player who wants 11...Ne5 as the main system.
Getting on with the attack and leaving the rook alone.
A race. Black attacks a2 and d5, White plays h5; the position is unclear and both sides have won games from it.

The most popular of the waiting moves. The rook covers e7, which frees the queen, and it lets Black answer Bh6 with ...Bh8 and keep the bishop. The main line runs into a version of the Soltis in which White sacrifices two pawns.
With great complications; White has full compensation and Black has to know a lot.

lines.name: Chinese Dragon: 10...Rb8
lines.summary: Black supports ...b5 with the rook and aims to open the b-file with ...Na5-c4. It avoids the 12.Kb1 lines, and after 12.Bh6 Black defends with the unusual ...e5.

next.text: The Chinese Dragon. The rook goes to the b-file instead of the c-file: ...b5 is supported, and after ...Na5-c4 and Bxc4 Black recaptures with the b-pawn and has an open file against b2. It is a way to play the 9.Bc4 lines without meeting 11...Ne5 12.Kb1.
The bishop retreats before ...b5 arrives with tempo.
Threatening ...Nc4, and keeping ...Nxb3 in hand for the moment the bishop becomes dangerous.
The most topical move: before the b-file opens White removes the bishop that would use it.
The queen has been drawn to h6, so Black can advance without worrying about b2 for the moment.

A move Dragon players are taught never to make, and here it is the point. The knight has to leave d4, where it supported Nd5 and the sacrifices on f5 and e6, and the seventh rank is opened for the defence. The hole on d6 does not matter: the dark-squared bishops are gone and White's pieces are committed to the kingside.
Only now, when the recapture has to be made with the a-pawn.
Covering d6 along the rank.

**Verdict:** Black is fine. The h-file stays closed and the queen on h6 is cut off from the game. If White takes on d6, Black answers ...f6 and has won every elite game played; otherwise ...f6 and ...Rf7 secure the king and Black turns to the weakened queenside. The Chinese Dragon is a serious system with far less theory than the main lines, and a good second weapon.
The original main line.
Black has what the opening was played for.
Forcing a weakness, since b2 is attacked twice.
The rook covers h7 along the rank and the king is safe. Black has the c- and b-files and the better pawn cover, and has won most of the elite games from here.
Opening the b-file for a rook that is already on it.
Black is already attacking. Jones won a miniature here when White played 13.Kb1, allowing 13...Nxe4 with a mating threat on b2 that costs the queen.
The other move order.
This is the note with 12.h4 below.

lines.name: The old main line: 10...Qa5
lines.summary: The queen comes to a5 and both rooks to the c-file. For decades this was the Dragon; 12.Kb1 took the sting out of the queen sortie and it is now a sideline.

next.text: The classical set-up, the one Chris Ward's books taught: queen to a5, king's rook to c8, knight to e5 and c4. Everything points at c3 and a2.
The king's rook, so that the other can stay on a8 behind the a-pawn or go to b8. The drawback is that f8 is no longer available to the king's defence.

The move that put the line out of fashion. With the king on b1, ...Qxd2 is not check, so every Nd5 has to be reckoned with; a2 is covered; and the queen on a5 is more of a target than an attacker. The old main line 12.h4 Ne5 13.Kb1 reaches the same position as the game.

The move with White's best results in practice is 13.Bg5, pinning the knight so that Nd5 becomes a real threat; Black answers 13...Nc4. The simple 13.Nd5 Qxd2 leads to an ending that Black holds without trouble.
Chasing the queen and covering d4 and a1.
The bishop blocks the fourth rank and offers the exchange of Black's best piece.
Clearing the queen's path and preparing to chase the knight.

**Verdict:** playable. A typical position of the old theory: White has the h-file, Black drives the knight from b3 with ...a4 and breaks through to c2 and b2, and exchange sacrifices on c3 are always in the air. Black has done well enough from here in practice. The reason 10...Qa5 is rare today lies earlier, at moves 12 and 13, where White has a choice of promising lines and Black does not.
The other plan: after ...Nc4 Black wants to recapture with the b-pawn and use the b-file, as in the Chinese Dragon. It has scored at least as well as the main line.

lines.name: Giri's 9...Nxd4 and 10...Be6
lines.summary: Black exchanges on d4 at once and challenges the bishop on c4. An old line that Giri has rehabilitated: it avoids the main-line theory and often leads to an ending in which Black has no problems.

next.text: 10.Qxd4 loses the bishop pair to 10...Ng4.

Giri's main recommendation against 9.Bc4. The pieces go straight to their most active squares and the queenside play starts without ...Bd7 and ...Rc8. White must either exchange on e6 or retreat and allow ...Qa5 and ...b5.
Keeping the tension.
The queen controls b5 and d5 from here and presses on c3 and a2.
The new twist. The older 12...Rfc8 13.Kb1 b5 allows 14.a3, stopping ...b4; played at once, the pawn gets there.
The usual precaution when the queens face each other on d2 and a5: Nd5 now threatens to answer ...Qxd2 with the in-between check on e7.
The bishop takes, keeping the knight that defends e7 and the kingside.
The queen makes way for the a-pawn and offers an exchange on d3 or e2.
Gaining space with tempo.

**Verdict:** equal. Black covers e7 along the rank, the king goes to f8, and the knight has d7, b6 and c5 to choose from. White has the bishop pair and Black the sounder pawns and a target on d5; the many elite games from here have slightly favoured Black.

This is the practical alternative to the Topalov and Soltis lines: far less to remember, and positions in which the Dragon's structure is all Black needs.
Trading the bishop that eyes g7 and a7.
The king defends e7 himself. The ending is equal, and in practice a little easier for Black.
This looks strong, since the bishops come off on g7, but there is a tactical flaw.
The in-between check that Giri points out: the bishop on g7 is not going anywhere, and first the knight opens the b-file.
After the queens come off Black regains the pawn against White's ruined queenside, and it is White who has to work for the draw in the rook ending.
The threats on the b-file win the piece back with interest: 18.cxb4 Rxb4+ 19.Qxb4 Qxb4+ 20.Bb2 Rb8.
Passive: the knight gives up d5 and a4.
With the knight on e2 Black can break in the centre: ...Rfd8 and ...d5 cannot be prevented.
This doubles Black's pawns and gives him the d5-square for good: with a pawn on e6 the knight on c3 has nowhere to go.
The critical move: White forgets the h-pawn and plays e5.
The knight stays near the centre when White is not playing for h5.

Keeping the centre closed: 15...Nxe5 16.f4 would return the pawn and give the knight on c3 the d5 square. Black now steers for an ending with ...Rac8 and an exchange of queens on d2, and regroups with ...Kf7 and ...Nb8-c6 to challenge a knight on d4. Giri's verdict is that neither side can make progress.
Blocking the h-pawn; Giri also likes 14...Nd7, meeting h5 with ...g5.
White's kingside play is stopped, since g4 is met by ...Nf4 or ...Ng3, and Black doubles on the c-file.

lines.name: 9.0-0-0 d5: main line with 12.Bd4 Bxd4
lines.summary: The main line of the modern Dragon. Black trades bishops, gains time on the queen and lives with split queenside pawns; with exact play he wins the h-pawn and reaches a balanced ending.

next.text: White saves the three bishop moves of the 9.Bc4 lines and castles at once. The price is that he no longer controls d5.

The principled reply, and a pawn sacrifice. Jones's rule is that when the Dragon player can play ...d5 he should: the break frees the position and gets rid of the hole on d5. The alternatives 9...Nxd4 10.Bxd4 Be6 and 9...Bd7 are playable, but they give White the attacking set-up he wants without the tempi Bc4 costs.
The tenth-move alternatives 10.Qe1, 10.Kb1 and 10.Nxc6 have their own lines.
The structure of the whole variation. Black has split pawns and a hole on c5; in return the b-file is open onto b2 and the bishop on g7 looks through to c3.
White declines the pawn (12.Nxd5 is a separate line) and offers to trade the bishop that makes the b-file dangerous. Once it is gone he hopes to settle a knight on c5.

Jones's choice. Black gives up the bishop, but gains a tempo on the queen and keeps a sound centre: no pawn on e5 means no hole on d6 and an open diagonal for the queen. The older 12...e5 has its own line; 12...Nxc3 13.Qxc3 Bh6+ is a third way that has scored less well.
Offering an exchange that White cannot accept: 14.Qxb6 axb6 would repair Black's pawns and open the a-file.
With tempo, and on the way to c5.

The retreat most strong players choose. 14...Qa5 first, to provoke 15.b3, is the alternative Jones also covers: it loosens the dark squares round the king, but it gives the king air as well, and White's results after 15.b3 have been better.
Pinning nothing yet, but lining up on d5 and f7. 15.Nc5 Rd8 16.Bc4 comes to the same thing.
The rook faces the queen, so that any knight move will come with tempo.
The outpost. From here the knight covers b7, d7 and e6 and shuts the c-file.
Development with a threat.
Covering c2 and stepping out of the way of ...Nb6.

The accurate move. The knight uncovers the rook against the queen, and when the rooks come off the h2-pawn falls. The natural 17...Nf4 18.Qf2 has scored badly: after the exchange on d1 White keeps all his pressure and Black has won nothing.
Black has won a pawn. In return White gets a tempo on the bishop and the only open file.
An in-between move that saves the bishop: the queen is attacked first.

**Verdict:** balanced. Black is a pawn up, White has a knight on c5, pressure on c6 and the more active king, and the elite games from here have divided evenly. Black's plan is to unravel with ...Kg7, ...Nb6 or ...Nf4 and ...h5, creating a passed pawn; White tries to win c6 or a7 first.
Too slow.
Black is fully developed and attacks c2, with ...Nb6 or ...Nb4 to follow; White has done badly here.
Black's pawns are healthy again and the a-file is open. The ending is equal and Black has scored well in it.

lines.name: 9.0-0-0 d5: the old main line 12.Bd4 e5
lines.summary: Black keeps the bishops and offers the exchange on f8. The most played line in practice and the one Giri builds on with 13...Re8; White's pressure is lasting but manageable.

next.text: The traditional move, still the most common one in practice. Black keeps the bishop and gains space with tempo. The cost is the long diagonal, which is closed until ...e4 can be played, and a hole on d6 for White's knight.
The move that made the line: Black leaves the rook to be taken.
White declines and brings the knight to the centre.
The rook steps out of the attack. 14...Rb8 is the sharper try, still offering the exchange; the old textbooks answer it with 15.Bc4.
The critical move, according to Ward: White wants h5 before Black is organised.
Stopping the pawn where it stands, and keeping g5 and g4 under control so that the knight can use f4.
Forcing matters: the bishop on e6 is attacked, and the queens come off.

**Verdict:** a playable ending. Black has driven the bishop back and gains space with ...f5 and ...e4, or ...f4; the knight is as good as the bishop, and the weak pawns on c6 and a7 are hard to attack. White keeps a symbolic edge because of the structure. Practice is close to level, and it is an easier position to handle than the middlegames with 15...h6.

The classical main line, meeting h5 with ...g5. After 16.g4 Qc7 17.g5 h5 18.Bc4 Red8 Black's position holds, but White's bind on the dark squares lasts, and this is the line Jones had in mind when he wrote that Black was suffering.
Taking the exchange gives up the dark squares for good.

Black threatens ...Bh6, pinning the queen, and follows with ...Rb8 and ...Qb4 against b2 while the bishop on g7 comes to life with ...e4. This is the standard example of the Dragon bishop being worth more than a rook.

Giri's recommendation, avoiding the offer. His book treats 14.Nxd5, 14.Bc4 and 14.Ne4 as the main replies. After 14.Nxd5 cxd5 15.Qxd5 Qxd5 16.Rxd5 Be6 Black is a pawn down in an ending that Ward judges tenable, with the bishop pair and two open files. Against the main move, the independent idea is to keep the bishop on c8 and play the queen and the f-pawn.
White has the bishop pair and Black a strong centre and all his pieces in play; the results from here are close to level.

lines.name: 9.0-0-0 d5: the pawn grab 12.Nxd5
lines.summary: White takes the pawn. Black replies 13...Qc7, offering both rooks for the queen, and gets open files against the king whatever White does.

next.text: White has won a pawn and attacks the rook on a8.

The move that makes 9...d5 possible. Black ignores the rook: with the b- and c-files open and both bishops aimed at the king, development matters more than material. Jones's verdict is that taking the material, whether the pawn alone or the two rooks as well, is dangerous for White.
White returns to the defence and offers the queens.
Keeping the queens on and hitting b2.
The queen defends b2 and a2 from the side and eyes e7.
Challenging the bishop that attacks c2.

**Verdict:** Black has lasting compensation: both rooks have files, the bishop on g7 has the long diagonal to itself and the white king will never be comfortable. But care is needed here. The routine 17...Rfc8 18.Bxf5 gxf5 has not done well in elite games, because White gets his rook to d3 and consolidates. This is the one position of the 9.0-0-0 complex to prepare from Jones's fourth chapter before relying on it; the repetition with 15.Qb5 and the ending after 14.Qxa8 hold no dangers.
An offer to repeat.

After 16.Qc5 Qb7 the position repeats, and a draw this way is a common end to the line. A player who wants more can exchange on b5 and play the ending a pawn down with the bishops and both files, which has scored well.
Blocking the b-file at the cost of the long diagonal.
Gaining a tempo on the queen. All Black's pieces are aimed at c2 and c3, and the pawn on b3 has left the dark squares round the king without a defender.
Taking everything.
Mate is threatened on c2 and the queen is attacked, so it has to give itself for the second rook.
White has two rooks and a pawn for the queen but is behind in development.

Black needs this move at some point, to give the king air and to hold up g4. The queen and bishops then go after the queenside pawns. Black has full compensation, as Hansen puts it, and in elite games he has scored heavily; the only question is whether it can be won.
A common mistake.
A double attack on e3 and b2 that wins material.

lines.name: 9.0-0-0 d5: 10.Qe1
lines.summary: The queen leaves the d-file so that the rook attacks d5. Black answers 10...e5 and reaches a version of the old main line.

next.text: An odd-looking move with a clear point: the rook now attacks d5 directly, and the queen watches e4 and e5 from behind. It avoids the heavily analysed lines with 12.Bd4 Bxd4.
Jones's answer, and by far the usual one. Black holds d5 by attacking the knight. The solid alternative is 10...e6.
The knight must recapture. After 12...cxd5 13.Bg5 the bishop pins the knight and uncovers the queen against e5, which is the tactical point of putting the queen on e1.
The same plan as in the old main line: bishop to c5, knight to c5 or d6.

Preparing to answer h5 with ...g5, as in the old main line. After 17.g4 Nf4 Black exchanges the light-squared bishops and has a firm grip on f4.

**Verdict:** White is a little better. This is the old 12.Bd4 e5 structure with the white queen on e1, where it is safer than on d2, and White's results in practice are good. Black's position is sound and the plans are the familiar ones (...Nf4, ...Rd7 and doubling, ...a5), but this is the line of the 9.0-0-0 complex in which Black has to defend most patiently.
The fashionable move among strong players, waiting to see Black's set-up.
A useful move in return. 14...Re8 is the other standard reply; what Black must not play is 14...Qc7, because 15.Nxd5 cxd5 16.Bxd5 wins a pawn.

lines.name: 9.0-0-0 d5: 10.Kb1
lines.summary: A waiting move with a tactical idea: after 10...Nxd4 White plays 11.e5. Black gets a good game by giving the exchange, or by a queen sacrifice.

next.text: The king move improves every version of the pawn grab on d5, and it sets a trap.
The right reply, and the only good one.
The point of 10.Kb1: both knights are attacked.
The knight escapes with tempo on the bishop.
Giri's choice and the usual move. Black has an extra pawn for the moment and keeps the bishop on g7.
Attacking the rook.
The exchange sacrifice Giri recommends and Carlsen has played. The rook is left to be taken so that the knight can come to e3 with tempo.
The knight on e3, protected by the d-pawn, paralyses White's rooks.
Opening the long diagonal.

**Verdict:** dynamically equal. Black has a pawn, the bishop pair and the knight on e3 for the exchange, and White has to return material to free himself, usually by taking on d4 or e3. The line is forcing and worth learning exactly, since one slip by either side decides the game.
Winning the pawn back and centralising the knight.
Opening the bishop.
Black has the two bishops against a strong knight. The position is about equal, but it is easier for White, who has scored well.

The older line, leading to a famous queen sacrifice worked out by Golubev: after 13.Nxd5 Black takes the knight with the queen. Rook, bishop and pawn for the queen, with two fine bishops, is thought to be just about enough, and in practice it has scored well.
The centre is liquidated and Black has no weaknesses, although White's results in the few elite games have been good and accuracy is still required.
Playing as against 10.Qe1 is what White hopes for.
This is the pawn grab of the 12.Nxd5 line with Kb1 thrown in and the bishop on g7 shut in by its own e-pawn. Black has little to show for the pawn.

lines.name: 9.0-0-0 d5: 10.Nxc6 and the minor tenth moves
lines.summary: White takes on c6 first so that Black cannot capture on e4, then goes for Bh6 or Bc4. Black's counterplay on the b-file is fast enough; the other tenth moves are met by 10...dxe4.

next.text: White strengthens Black's centre and opens the b-file, but with the queen pinned on the d-file ...dxe4 is not available, and he gains a move for the attack.
The sharpest idea. 11.exd5 Nxd5 is the main line by transposition.
Both sides are now playing for mate. Hansen prefers 12...Qb6 with the same ideas; the lines run together.
White's main try, driving the knight from f6.
The idea that holds everything together. The bishop cannot be taken: 17.gxf5 g5 and the queen is trapped.
The best square.
Forcing the queens off; 18...hxg6 19.f4 would be dangerous.

**Verdict:** equal. White is a pawn up for a moment, but the pawn on h7 falls and Black has the more compact structure. The lines are sharp and short: know 12...Rb8, the trick 16...f6 and the queen exchange with 18...Qb6, and 10.Nxc6 holds no terrors.
Walking into a discovered attack.
White has to lose a move with the queen.
Black's attack on b2 is decisive; this is how Marin won a model game.
The rook heads for h4.
A complicated position in which Jones likes Black's central pawns.
Jones's improvement. The rook sacrifice on b2 follows, and Black's attack arrives first.
Using the pin to bring the bishop to b3.
Jones's set-up. The bishop on b7 blocks the b-file, but the one on b3 is shut out by Black's pawns, and the game is level.
Not dangerous, since Black's central play is already under way.
The simplest way to stop the attack, in Jones's words.
The pawn on g7 looks frightening and does nothing.
The queen comes to the defence, and after ...Qxg7 Black is a safe pawn up; White has just enough activity to hold.
Trading bishops at the cost of the centre.
White's best chance is this exchange sacrifice.
White has some compensation and no more. 10...dxe4 is a simpler route to equality.

lines.name: 9.g4 Be6 10.Nxe6
lines.summary: White stops ...d5 with the g-pawn and takes the bishop on e6. Black gets the f-file and control of d5 in return for doubled pawns, and plays ...Ne5, ...Qc8 and ...Nc4.

next.text: The third main move. The pawn discourages ...d5, because g5 would drive away the knight that supports it, and it prepares h4-h5 without spending time on Bc4. What it gives up is the f3-pawn's stability and the option of answering ...Be6 with a bishop already on b3.

The established reply, recommended by Jones and by Giri. The bishop takes the diagonal White left empty, covers d5 and c4, and makes ...d5 a threat again. Black does not mind Nxe6: the doubled pawns guard d5 and f5, and the f-file opens against f3.
The most popular move. White takes the bishop pair and a long-term target on e6.
The knight hits f3 and g4 at once and forces the bishop to a passive square.
The queen supports ...Nc4, keeps an eye on g4 and leaves d8 free. The natural 12...Rc8 is less accurate, because 13.Nb5 hits a7 and d6 while the rook is in the queen's way.
Opening the f-file and the bishop's diagonal together. The f3-pawn is now attacked twice, and the knight is ready to recapture on e5 or go to b6 and c4.

**Verdict:** balanced, with the unusual structure Jones warns about. White has the h-file and the bishop pair is gone; Black has the queen on c4, the c- and f-files, and the knight coming to e5. The doubled e-pawns are a strength while the queens are on, since nothing can settle on d5 or f5. Black's plan is ...Rac8, ...Ne5 and ...b5; if White opens the h-file, ...hxg6 keeps the rook on f8 for the defence. Practice slightly favours Black.
Chasing the knight where it wants to go.
Black has exchanged the bishop that held White's position together, and the pawns on e4 and g4 are loose.
A move order that avoids Nxe6: after 10.Bxd4 Be6 11.O-O-O Qa5 Black is in the next line.

lines.name: 9.g4 Be6 10.0-0-0 and 10.h4
lines.summary: White keeps the knight and castles. Black exchanges on d4, plays ...Qa5 and ...Rfc8 with a sacrifice on c3 in the air, and the main line ends in an equal ending.

next.text: White ignores the bishop and completes development.
Before White can play Nxe6 under better circumstances.
The set-up of the 9.0-0-0 Nxd4 lines, with the difference that White has spent a move on g4.
Necessary sooner or later: 12.h4 would lose a pawn to 12...Bxa2. 12.a3 comes to the same thing after 12...Rfc8 13.Kb1.
Threatening the sacrifice on c3.
Taking the sting out of it: with no pawn on a2 the queen has nothing to capture after the rook is given.
Now the pawn on a3 is a target for the b-pawn.
The standard reply to ...b5: with the king on b1 the queen exchange is not check, so White can choose how to recapture.

**Verdict:** an equal ending in which Black still has to be careful. Material and structure are level and Black has the c-file, but White has more space on the kingside and has won more than his share of the games, usually by pushing the h-pawn. Black should centralise the king, keep a rook on the fifth rank and play ...a5 and ...b4 only when it creates a target.
The bishop takes, keeping the knight for the dark squares.
Black is comfortable: the white bishops have nothing to aim at and the queenside pawns are rolling.
The in-between move.
The king is perfectly placed in the centre of an ending, and Black has the c-file and the better bishop.
White cannot ignore the threat.
The king has been driven into the open, Black already has a pawn for the exchange, and the bishops and the other rook join in. Black has won most of the games from here.
Attacking before castling leaves the centre unguarded.
The break White's ninth move was meant to prevent works after all, because the bishop on e6 holds d5.
The knight blocks the h-pawn and the centre is about to open with White's king still on e1. Black has scored very well here.

lines.name: Dragadorf and the early ...h5
lines.summary: An alternative to the whole main-line complex: ...a6 and ...b5 with the king left in the centre, and ...h5 to stop g4 and Bh6 before they happen.

next.text: The Dragadorf: Dragon bishop, Najdorf queenside. Black does not castle and does not put the knight on c6. With no king on g8 the h-file attack has no target, and the b-pawn comes to b5 before White has decided where his own king is going.

The modern refinement, and the version Giri gives in his bonus chapter. The pawn stops g4 for good, and Bh6 loses most of its point while there is no king on g8 to attack. The same idea can be played a move earlier with the knight on c6 (6...Nc6 7.f3 h5), which Ward covers under the same heading.
The natural move, and the one that worries Black least.

**Verdict:** a playable system with its own character. Black has avoided the h-file attack, the Bh6 exchange and nearly all the theory of this chapter; the knight goes to d7 and then c5 or b6, the rook to c8, and ...b4 or ...Qa5 starts the attack. The price is that ...d5 is hard to arrange and that the king has no entirely safe home. Black's results against 9.O-O-O are good; the test is the quiet 9.Be2. It is worth having as a surprise weapon and as a way of understanding why, in the main lines, Black so often wishes the h-pawn were on h5 before White's reached h4.
Aiming at f7 and e6 before Black is developed.
The standard set-up: ...Rc8, ...Nc5 or ...Ne5 and ...Qc7 follow, and the king decides late whether to castle short or stay on e8. Chances are about level.
The positional treatment, and the most uncomfortable one in practice. White castles short, where the pawn on h5 is a weakness in front of Black's king instead of a defender, and plays in the centre.
Black develops in the same way, but has to accept a slightly worse game.

The original Dragadorf set-up, keeping the h-pawn at home: after 9.O-O-O b5 10.g4 Bb7 11.h4 Black usually has to play ...h5 or ...h6 anyway. It has scored well in practice, and it is the choice for a player who wants to keep ...h5 in reserve.

chapters.title: Najdorf: 6.Bg5 and the English Attack
chapters.subtitle: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 a6
chapters.intro:
The Najdorf is the main line of the Sicilian and the most heavily analysed opening there is, but its logic is compact. Black spends move five on ...a6 and then picks one of two structures: ...e5, which gives up the d5 square and leaves a backward pawn on d6, or ...e6, which keeps d5 and f5 covered but leaves Black cramped. The King's Indian will feel half familiar, with its pawns on d6 and e5 and its dark-squared bishop that wants out, but here the centre is open: the d-file is White's, the c-file is Black's, and d5 is a hole for a white knight instead of a pawn that cramps Black.

This chapter covers White's two sharpest sixth moves. **6.Bg5** is met by 6...e6, and against 7.f4 the repertoire is the delayed Poisoned Pawn, 7...h6 8.Bh4 Qb6: Black takes b2 and later a2 and e5 with the queen, plays a long forcing sequence and ends up with three pawns for the exchange in a safe ending. 7...Be7 with Giri's 10...h6, the Anand line 7...Nbd7, the immediate 7...Qb6, the Polugaevsky 7...b5 and 7...Qc7 get a game each, so that the whole map is visible. Against the **English Attack, 6.Be3**, the repertoire is 6...e5 7.Nb3 Be7 8.f3 Be6 9.Qd2 and 9...h5, which stops the g4-g5 storm before it begins; 9...O-O with the full pawn race is the older and sharper alternative, and 6...e6 and 6...Ng4 are also covered. The other sixth moves (6.Be2, 6.Bc4, 6.h3, 6.f4, 6.g3 and the rare ones) are in another chapter.

Everything here is taken from popular Lichess studies (the sources are listed at the end), cross-checked against each other, and the explanations are written fresh. Several of the studies are written from White's side or give the moves without comment; where that matters, the notes in the lines say so.

sections.title: What 5...a6 is for
sections.body:
The pawn does three jobs. It takes b5 away from White's knights and bishop, and that is what makes ...e5 playable: without it, ...e5 is met by Bb5+ or Ndb5 and Nf5 settles on a square no black pawn can challenge. It prepares ...b5, ...Bb7 and ...b4, the queenside expansion that supplies most of Black's counterplay. And it is a waiting move: ...Nc6 or ...e6 would commit the pieces or the pawn structure before White has shown his hand, whereas now Black chooses between ...e5 and ...e6 after seeing the sixth move. With the knight already on c6, for example, 6.Bg5 and 6.Bc4 are harder to meet, because ...a6 and ...b5 would leave the c6 knight loose.

The price is a tempo spent on an edge pawn. Almost every Najdorf line is a race, and the extra pawn move is what White's attacks are measured against: Black cannot afford slow moves, and has to know exactly which counterattack is needed in each position.

sections.title: The ...e5 structure: the d5 hole and the backward pawn
sections.body:
After ...e5 the d-pawn can only be defended by pieces, and it stands on a half-open file that White's queen and rooks will use, especially after long castling. The d5 square can no longer be covered by a pawn, so White's knight wants to settle there, and Black can only get rid of it by a trade. These two weaknesses are the price of the structure; all of Black's piece play is built to make them harmless.

The assets are real. The light-squared bishop stands outside the pawn chain and is Black's good piece, so ...Be6 is the natural move: it covers d5 and c4, and offers a trade. The dark-squared bishop is the bad one: it goes to e7, and its best prospect is a trade for White's bishop, with ...Ng4 or ...Bg5. The knight comes to d7 and often on to b6, where it covers d5 and c4. The rook belongs on c8, on the file Black owns. And Black has a central majority, d and e pawns against White's e-pawn, against White's extra c-pawn on the queenside: ...d5 is how Black cashes it in, and ...b5-b4 how he uses the smaller wing to attack.

sections.title: The ...e6 structure and why 6.Bg5 forces it
sections.body:
6...e5? is a mistake after 6.Bg5: 7.Bxf6 Qxf6 8.Nd5 Qd8 9.Nf5 leaves White with knights on d5 and f5 that can never be challenged. So Black plays 6...e6, which covers both squares, and Bxf6 can be answered with ...Qxf6. The price is that the e-pawn no longer attacks the knight on d4, which stays powerful, and White gets a free hand: f4, e4-e5, the queen to f3 or d2, long castling, and sacrifices on e6, d5 and f5.

Black's light-squared bishop is blocked by the e6 pawn and gets out through ...b5 and ...Bb7, which is why a6 is such an important move here. The d6 pawn is a target for Qg3, and the king has to be handled carefully: in many lines it stays in the centre for a long time. The usual Black counterplay is ...b5-b4 and ...Nbd7-c5, and the break ...d5 is rarely available. The queen has a second job in the Poisoned Pawn lines, where she goes to b6 and takes on b2.

sections.title: The ...b5-b4 expansion
sections.body:
The pawn thrust ...b5-b4 hits the knight on c3, the piece that guards e4 and controls d5, b5 and a4. If the knight leaves, e4 is loose and Nd5 is no longer available as a threat; the pawn on b4 then supports ...a5-a4 against the knight on b3, and the a- and b-files open towards a king on c1 or b1.

Three things have to be checked before ...b5. First, the long diagonal: with the white queen on f3, a rook on a8 can be hit by e5 or by Bxb5 combinations, so the bishop goes to b7 first or the rook to b8. Second, White's sacrifices Bxb5 axb5 Ndxb5, which attack d6 and the queen on c7. Third, Nd5: when the knight arrives Black takes with the bishop (...Bxd5 exd5 Nb6 hits the pawn), because ...Nxd5 would let exd5 attack the bishop on e6 with tempo. In the English Attack ...b5 is usually delayed until White commits with g4; in the 6.Bg5 lines it is Black's reply to long castling.

sections.title: The ...d5 break
sections.body:
If Black can play ...d5 safely he plays it: the pawn removes the backward pawn, opens the position for the bishops and answers the pawn storm in the centre. The best-known example is 9.g4? d5!, when 10.g5 d4 11.gxf6 Bxf6 regains the piece with a better game, and 10.exd5 Nxd5 11.Nxd5 Bxd5 gives Black the stronger centre.

The condition is that White has not yet castled long with the queen on d2. Once the queen is on d2 and White's rook is ready for d1, the same exchanges on d5 open the file for White, and Black is left with a weak king and nothing to show for it, which is exactly why 9.Qd2 d5? is a mistake. So the break is a response, not a plan: it works against an early g4 or an e4 pawn that has lost its support. It also saves the game in Giri's line (19...d5!!) and appears with ...Nc5 and ...Ne4 against the h4 set-up in the 9.a3 line.

sections.title: Sacrifices for the white king: ...Bb3, ...a3 and ...Rxc3
sections.body:
Wherever White's king sits on c1 or b1, its cover is the pawns a2, b2 and c2 plus a knight on c3 or b3. Black's standard answer to a pawn storm is to remove that cover at any price. In the diagram the pawn on a3 forces Nxa3 Rxa3 bxa3 Ra8, giving the exchange and a pawn for the open a- and b-files; objectively White is better, but with the king on b1 it is hard to prove. In the old pawn-race line (9...O-O) the bishop goes to b3 for the same reason: ...Bb3! axb3 axb3 opens the a-file at once. The exchange sacrifice on c3 is the third version: when the white queen leaves the guard of c3, the threat of ...Rxc3 hangs over every queen move, and in the 6.Bg5 lines White has to watch for it (in the Browne feint, for example, h4 and Rh3 are needed to meet it).

The rule is that the sacrifice must open a file at a king that has no minor piece in front of it, and that the second wave, a queen on c7 or a5 and the other rook, is ready to come in. A pawn sacrifice does the same job elsewhere: ...b4 in the pawn-race line, ...g5 against Qf3, and the Poisoned Pawn itself.

sections.title: The race: castling on opposite sides, and when Black keeps the king in the centre
sections.body:
Both players have a plan, and the first one to break through wins: White advances g and h, Black advances b and a. The trade-offs are concrete: every move spent on defence is a tempo lost on attack, and a king that has castled short walks into the pawns that are coming. That is why Black often leaves the king in the middle. In the diagram it stays on e8: long castling runs into the open c-file, short castling invites g4-g5 and h4, and the black pieces have enough to do (...g5! and ...Ne5 in the game) before the king needs to move.

The English Attack gives the same choice in a quieter form. After 9...O-O the king commits and the old pawn race follows, with Black having to know the theory exactly. After 9...h5 the g4 break is gone, so the king can wait in the centre until White decides where he castles: if White castles short with Be2 and Nd5, Black can castle short too (13...O-O in the first game); if White castles long, Black plays ...b5 and ...Qc7 and keeps the king in the middle.

sections.title: The delayed Poisoned Pawn
sections.body:
This is the position that the whole line is built for. Black has eaten b2, a2 and e5 with the queen, and has moved nothing else: the pieces still at home are the problem, with Bd6, Nb5 and Qg3 looming. For the next three moves the game is a race to catch up (...Bc5 pins the knight on d4, ...Qd5 heads for a5 and c5, ...O-O gets the king out), after which Black trades queens and plays the ending with three pawns for the exchange.

Playing 7...h6 first is Black's way to make the line better. The bishop has to decide: Bxf6 gives up the bishop pair for no threat (a game of its own), and on h4 the bishop is loose, so that ...Be7 can hit it. It also rules out the quiet 9.Nb3?, which now loses the f4 pawn to ...Qe3+ because the bishop no longer guards it. The price is that White can answer 8...Qb6 with 9.a3, protecting b2 and, after ...Be7, kicking the queen with Bf2; Black then goes to c7, and the game returns to the ordinary Najdorf structure with a few extra moves. The line demands a lot of memory: from move 11 almost every black move is the only move, and Caruana's 16.c3 with 18.Bc4!! is a serious test. The reasons to choose it anyway are that both repertoire studies (Rob_Jobs and Chessboy197) pick it, that it keeps the g4-g5 storms of the 7...Be7 main line away, and that its main line ends in a safe ending with extra material.

sections.title: Tactics to know
sections.body:
The diagram combines most of the themes of the chapter: g5-g6, Nxe6 and the sacrifice of a piece against Black's exposed king, answered by the quiet ...d5! that saves the game.

For Black:

- **...Qe3+** against Nb3 when the bishop has left g5 and f4 is loose, and the pawn grab on b2, a2 and e5 itself.
- **...Nxe4** after ...Be7 has attacked an undefended bishop on h4 (it works in the 9.a3 and 10.Nb3 lines).
- **...d5** in answer to g4, and the resource ...d5!! in Giri's line.
- **...Bb3** and **...a3** to open files, and **...Rxc3** when the knight on c3 is the only guard.
- **...g5** against Qf3 or the bishop on h4, giving a pawn for the e5 square.

For White, on every move:

- **Nd5**, to trade the f6 knight or settle on the hole; **Nf5**, when no pawn covers the square.
- **Nxe6** against a king that has not castled, and **Bxb5** when ...axb5 allows Ndxb5.
- **e5** with a queen on f3 or g3, hitting the rook on a8; **g5-g6** to break the pawns in front of the king.
- **Qh5** with a pin on f7 when the bishop on g5 hangs; **Bd6** to stop Black castling or to take c5 away from the queen.

Move orders matter. 7...h6 before ...Qb6 is the repertoire; 6.f3 e5 7.Nb3 Be6 8.Be3 Be7 is the English Attack by transposition; in the English Attack 7...Be7 avoids 8.f4 and only then 8.f3 Be6 9.Qd2 h5 is played. Against the quiet 7.Be2 and 7.Bd3 Black develops with ...Be7, ...O-O and ...b5; against the queen moves the queenside pawns (...b5 and ...b4) are faster than White's attack.

sections.title: Sources
sections.body:
- Rob_Jobs, "Sicilian Najdorf", https://lichess.org/study/j43moXo6 (132 likes): the 6.Bg5 chapter (delayed Poisoned Pawn, the quiet seventh moves and the Giri-Vachier-Lagrave and Karjakin-Vachier-Lagrave lines), the English Attack chapter (7...Be7, 9...h5, 7.Nf3 and the eighth-move sidelines, 6...Ng4) and the pawn structure chapter
- NoseKnowsAll, "Winning attempts for white in the Bg5 Sicilian Najdorf", https://lichess.org/study/WotymApK (142 likes): a study from White's side, used for the Be7 main line, Giri's 10...h6, the Anand variation, the Polugaevsky, the 7...Qc7 line and the cross-check of the delayed Poisoned Pawn (9.a3, 9.Qd3, the Browne and Argentine lines)
- ozkalsonmez, "Sicilian Najdorf Repertoire", https://lichess.org/study/0evGkI2d (437 likes), and WhiteCoted, same name and content, https://lichess.org/study/Zjb7bTuA (458 likes): the short repertoire lines for 6.Be3 e5 7.Nb3 Be6, 7...Be6 8.f3 Be7 9.Qd2 O-O 10.O-O-O Nbd7, 6...e6 and the immediate Poisoned Pawn
- Chessboy197, "Najdorf Repertoire ~ Destroy Everyone!", https://lichess.org/study/FKoV27l1 (157 likes): confirms 6.Be3 e5 7.Nb3 Be6 8.f3 h5 and 6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 h6 8.Bh4 Qb6 as repertoire choices
- LeninPerez, "Sicilian Najdorf", https://lichess.org/study/ANrk7cS9 (10177 likes): introductory; the development ideas in the structure notes and the 7...Be7 and English Attack main lines
- BuChD, "My Sicilian Study Book", https://lichess.org/study/1zUXQtM5 (62 likes): the English Attack lines, 7...Be7 as the right move order and the Anti-English; used as a cross-check
- Coldfield1994, "Sicilian, Najdorf, English Attack (Black)", https://lichess.org/study/WNBagPTK (40 likes): cross-check for the 7.Nf3 and 7.Nde2 lines
- K1N6M4K3R, "Sicilian, Najdorf", https://lichess.org/study/G7uH42vS (179 likes): chapter names only, used to confirm the Perenyi line 6...e6 7.g4 e5 8.Nf5 g6 9.g5
- Lichess Elite Database (games of players rated 2400 and above), used by the checker to confirm how each line is played in practice

lines.name: Delayed Poisoned Pawn: 9.Qd2 Qxb2, the main line
lines.summary: Black takes b2, a2 and e5 with the queen while White develops with tempo. With exact play the pawns are kept, the queens come off and Black has three pawns for the exchange in a safe ending.

next.text: The Najdorf. The pawn takes b5 away from both knights and the bishop, and that is what makes ...e5 a real option: after 5...e5 6.Bb5+ White gets a bind on d5 and a knight on f5. It also prepares ...b5 and ...b4 with tempo, and it is a waiting move, because Black sees White's sixth move before committing to a pawn structure. The price is a tempo spent on an edge pawn, so slow play later in the opening is punished.
The most testing sixth move, because it forces Black to choose a structure at once. The threat is Bxf6 followed by Nd5 or Nf5 if Black has played ...e5.

Not 6...e5? 7.Bxf6 Qxf6 8.Nd5 Qd8 9.Nf5, when two white knights stand on d5 and f5 and no black pawn can ever challenge them. With the pawn on e6 Black guards both squares, and Bxf6 can be met by Qxf6. The cost is that the e-pawn no longer hits d4, so Black has to find play with ...b5, ...Bb7 and the queenside pawns.

White takes e5 under control, so that e4-e5 becomes a threat against the f6 knight, and prepares Qf3 or Qd2 and long castling. Black has six serious answers: 7...Be7 (first game of the next file), 7...Qb6 (the immediate Poisoned Pawn), 7...Nbd7, 7...b5, 7...Qc7 and the move of this file, 7...h6.

The delayed Poisoned Pawn. It asks the bishop a question before the queen goes to b6: 8.Bxf6 gives away the bishop pair for nothing, and after 8.Bh4 the bishop can be attacked by ...Be7. It also rules out the quiet Nb3 (9.Nb3 here), which would lose f4 to ...Qe3+ because the bishop no longer guards that pawn. The price is that after 9.a3 White gets Bf2 with tempo on the queen.
White keeps the pin. After 8.Bxf6 Qxf6 Black gets the bishop pair and the ...g5 plan (fourth game).
The queen attacks b2 and d4 at once, and White must either defend the pawn or give it. All Black's later play depends on the fact that nobody has proved the pawn is really poisoned.
The main gambit move. The queen covers c3 and prepares long castling; if the pawn is taken the black queen will be offside while White develops with tempo.
Accepting. Black wants three pawns and a safe king, and the sources agree that White cannot prove the pawn is poisoned.
The queen is attacked, and the only square that keeps her safe is a3.
The only safe retreat. From a3 the queen still eyes a2 and b4.
The main try, and by a distance the most played. It opens the f-file and the e4 square and hits the knight.
Always with the pawn: it opens the f8-a3 diagonal so that bishop and queen both aim at b4.
The only move that does not leave the king exposed. Black does not mind the pawn on e5: the real threat is ...Bb4, which would pin and overload the c3 knight.
The only way to stop ...Bb4: the queen on d2 now covers it.
A second pawn. Not 13...Nxe5? 14.Nb5!, which threatens Qd8 mate and the queen at once.
Again the e5 pawn is poisoned (15.Nf5 with threats of mate on d7). The queen forks the knight on e4 and the pawn on e5, and blocks the d-file.
Keeps e4 defended. 15.Qe2 would shut the bishop in for ever.
Three pawns up, but only the queen has moved. The next moves are about catching up in development before White's pieces come in.
Pins the knight on d4 against the queen and develops the bishop with tempo.
White's idea: Bd6, which will stop Black castling safely.
17...Bxd4 first leads to a very similar position. The text invites 18.c4, which leaves the queen no square, and Black has to take on d4 to free the fifth rank for her.
Now the king is safe.
The bishop attacks the exchange and takes c5 from the queen, so that queens cannot come off. With no black piece near his king, White's g4 and h4-g5 would then give a dangerous attack.

Black does not waste a tempo retreating the rook: after 21...Rd8 22.g4 Nc6 23.O-O Nde5 24.h4 the rook has to be given up anyway, and Black's pieces are still far from the kingside. The counter-punch gives back the exchange at once, but it removes the bishop that controls c5 and so makes the queen trade possible.
The knight is a nuisance, hitting b7 and f7.
Black will trade queens next, and White's attack has nothing left to attack with.

**Verdict:** good for Black. He has three pawns for the exchange, a king that is finally safe and the move that trades queens. The game this follows, Giri against Vachier-Lagrave (Paris rapid, 2019), was won by Black. The warning is the huge number of forcing moves that has to be remembered: from 11.e5 on every move for Black is a single move.
Loses a tempo.
Caruana's choice against Vachier-Lagrave in the 2021 Candidates, after a year of preparation. The pawn supports the knight on d4, so that the bishop can leave f1 for c4 without the d4 knight falling.
The novelty: the queen is lured off the d-file so that Bd6 comes with decisive force.
The only way to return material and reduce the pressure.
Black is two pawns up in the ending, but the pieces are all on the queenside and the rooks are tied up. Both sides have to be precise. Black is the one with the margin for error.
The line played in correspondence games.
Black has too many pawns, but the pieces are still at home and he has to be careful.
Defends e5, but allows the bishop to come out.
White's pieces are tied up on c3, b3 and the g1-a7 diagonal, and Black can develop freely.
Very sharp: after the capture Black's king stays in the middle for the rest of the game.
Also leaves the king stuck in the centre.
An attempt to grab the light squares round e6.
Black has won a knight outpost on e5 and the endgame is safe; the e5 knight stops White's g and c pawns from moving.
White's bishop pair is gone and Black has five pawns in the centre; White cannot break them down.
Tried in a dozen games and with poor results: White does not have the time to trap the queen.
Hits the undefended bishop on h4: if the rook goes to b1 now, ...Nxe4 wins a pawn, so White has to trade.
Material is level, but Black has the safer king and the better pawns.
The solid alternative: it defends b2 and makes Qxb2 impossible, since Na4 traps the queen.
Black ignores b2 and hits the loose bishop on h4.
The bishop retreats with tempo on b6.
The queen has lost two moves, but so has White: a3 and Bf2 are not moves White wanted to make. Third game.
A break that comes too early: the king is still in the centre and the e6 pawn is the weak point.
The standard shot against ...g5 when the king is uncastled: after the recapture the queen reaches h5 with check.

lines.name: Delayed Poisoned Pawn: 9.Qd3
lines.summary: A worse version of 9.Qd2: the queen blocks its own bishop. The pawn is taken again, and the sequence that follows is a forced one ending in an ending where Black has the better of it.

next.text: Like 9.Qd2, but the queen blocks the bishop on f1 and the c4 square, which changes how Black can recapture later. White keeps the queenside file open and hopes for f5 and Nd5 tricks against a queen on a3.
The usual try: White wants to destroy the e6 pawn and hit the light squares.
Hits the loose bishop.

Here Black may recapture with the bishop. With the queen on d2 he usually takes with the f-pawn, because White wants Bc4 to press on e6; with the queen on d3 the bishop cannot reach c4, so the bishop recapture is possible and trades off White's active knight.
White plays this before taking on b7, because 14.Rxb7 allows ...Nbd7 and Black is fine.
Black must stop the queen reaching g6, since otherwise White's attack is decisive.
Castling looks dangerous with queens and rooks on the board, but it is fine.
White wants Qg6, but at once that would let the black queen take on c3 with check, so the rook comes first.
The check comes first: with the bishop off e7 the rook on c7 can be taken without a loose piece being left behind.
If Black takes on c4, White gives perpetual check. The rook attacks the queen and keeps the bishop out of g6.
**Verdict:** a pleasant ending for Black. Black has connected passed pawns in the centre, and White's extra pawn is a doubled h-pawn. The study this follows judges it favourable for Black.

lines.name: Delayed Poisoned Pawn: 9.a3, the solid reply
lines.summary: White defends b2 and goes for a kingside attack. Black keeps the king in the centre, plays ...b5 and ...Bb7 and meets g4 with ...g5. The main line is a draw by repetition in practice.

next.text: The only real setup White has: queen to f3, long castling, g4. Kingside castling is bad because the f-pawn has already moved.
Black should not castle. Long castling is impossible with the open c-file, and short castling walks into the attack. The king stays on e8 and Black counterattacks.
The bishop attacks e4 with the rook behind it. The other move here is 13...g5, which the text reaches anyway.
Defends e4 and so keeps f5 possible.
A standard pawn sacrifice: Black wants the knight on e5, and the pawn on f4 is the price.
Prepares g5 after ...gxf4, so that the h-file opens.
The knight lands on the best square and the d7 square is free for the other knight.
Preparing ...Nf8-g6 if the rook comes down.
The king is safe on c8. The only thing to watch is g6.
Now f7 is defended and g6 is no threat.

**Verdict:** balanced. Black's knights are great on e5 and g6, White has the open h-file and some activity. Karjakin against Vachier-Lagrave (London 2017), which this follows, was won by Black in a long endgame.
The safer try.
The kingside is frozen; Black pushes ...a5 and ...b4 on the queenside.
Prevents ...g5.
Piles up on e4.
Forced; everything else loses.
The knight cannot be taken: Nxe4 dxe4 forks.
Anand against Vachier-Lagrave in 2018, drawn: the kingside is locked, White's pawns are weak and Black's king is relatively safe.

lines.name: 7...h6 8.Bxf6: the ...g5 pawn sacrifice
lines.summary: If White gives up the bishop at once, Black recaptures with the queen, plays ...Nc6 and ...g5, and gets the bishop pair and the e5 outpost for a pawn.

next.text: White has given up the bishop on f6 without making a threat. The queen develops with a threat on d4, and f4 is loose.
Threatens ...Nxd4. If White captures on c6, ...bxc6 gives Black a huge centre.
The point. Black gives a pawn to get the knight to e5 and open lines for the bishop pair.
White declines the pawn.
The knight on f3 has lost its defender.
**Verdict:** Black will get two bishops and regain the pawn with ...b5 and ...Bb7. Equal, with chances to press.
Black regains the pawn with the bishop pair.
Black wins the pawn back and is better.
Not 12.Nxg5? Bh6, which pins the knight to the queen.
The king sits on e7 for good, but White has no way to attack it without his dark-squared bishop, and Black's bishop pair is strong.

lines.name: 7...Be7 8.Qf3: Giri's 10...h6
lines.summary: Black develops and waits for White to commit his king to the queenside, then answers the g4 push with ...h6, so that the bishop must decide at once. The line is forcing and ends in an ending with opposite-coloured bishops that is about equal.

next.text: The classical move, and the one the beginner-oriented study by LeninPerez recommends. The bishop defends the knight on f6, so Bxf6 can be met by ...Bxf6 with the bishop looking at d4 and b2, and Black can still castle short, leave the king in the middle or play ...b5-b4.
The queen goes to the long diagonal, which makes ...b5 awkward unless the bishop can reach b7 at once, and prepares long castling and the pawn storm. Later Qg3 hits d6 and g7.
The knight defends f6 and e5. The other move order, 8...Qc7 9.O-O-O Nbd7, gives the same position.
The queen defends e5 and d6 and gets off the d-file, where White's rook and queen would otherwise look at her.
The standard pawn storm: g5 drives the f6 knight away and f5 follows. The older 10...b5 11.Bxf6 Nxf6 12.g5 Nd7 13.f5 is sharp enough to be a line of its own (next game).

Giri's idea. The bishop must decide at once: 11.Bh4? is met by ...g5 and the knight reaches e5, so it takes on f6, and the recapture puts Black's bishop on the long diagonal against d4 and b2, where it plays a part in the tactics later.
Black recaptures with the bishop.
White continues with g5 against whatever Black plays: slow moves are punished by ...b5, ...Bb7 and ...Nc5.
Giri's idea. The knight heads for a4 or c4, and the bishop on f6 takes on d4 at the right moment.
Keeps the tension. 13.g5 is the most testing and the study reports Giri's analysis of it as roughly equal:
Not 13...Bxd4? 14.Rxd4 Qc5 15.Rhd1, where the rook is no longer hit with tempo and the knight's trip to a4 achieves nothing.
Correct. Taking on g5 loses to Qh7.
The king leaves the centre for the queenside, and the rook on d8 will support the ...d5 break that saves the game later.
The key resource: White would be completely winning if it were not for this move. The pawn opens the d-file and the c7-h2 diagonal for the queen.
Hits the queen.
Another only move: it keeps all the black pieces working.
Black must attack White's weak pawns at once: after 25...Qe5? 26.Qh2 White trades queens up two pawns.

**Verdict:** about equal. White is a pawn up, but opposite-coloured bishops and Black's active rook make the ending very hard to win. Both sides must know the line to the end; that is the price of the Giri system.
Opens the h-file for White.
White is much better: the h-file is his and g6 follows.
Hands White the d-file without a tempo.
White gets the d-file for nothing.
Both sides have their trumps: White has more space and the pressure on d6, and Black has no weaknesses.
The older move, which has gone badly: White's Qh5 and the g6 and f5 pushes come too quickly.
The knight recapture leaves the bishop on e7 passive and the pieces uncoordinated.
Walks into ...g5.
Black is better: the knight on e5 hits g4, and the study describes the position as a bad version of a line White would like to avoid.

lines.name: 7...Be7 8.Qf3: the old main line 10...b5 11.Bxf6 Nxf6 12.g5
lines.summary: The sharpest version of the pawn storm. White lets the g5 pawn go to open the f-file and the h5 square, and the king in the middle is under fire. Each of Black's 13th moves is risky, which is why Giri's 10...h6 is preferred.

next.text: Black launches the queenside attack at once. It is a race, and Black's king is still in the centre.
The breakthrough: White lets the g5 pawn go to open the f-file and the h5 square for the queen. The study I used for this line finds all three of Black's tries below better for White.
Takes the pawn with check.
The knight blocks the e-file and hits the queen.
Pins the f-pawn and hits g5 in one move.

**Verdict:** slightly better for White, according to the study. Black controls e5, but White controls d5 and has the h-file, and Black's king stays in the centre. White's idea is to poke the bishop on g5 with h4 and break through; Black's counter is ...b4-b3 and the c-file. Black does not have to go into this line: 10...h6 is the alternative.
The modern try: Black puts the king on g8 and gets counterplay with ...b4 and ...e5.
The knight on e5 is strong, but White has the h-file and g6 ideas. The study judges White better.
After 14.f6 gxf6 15.gxf6 Bf8 16.Rg1 h5 White keeps the initiative with Rg7 and Qh5 ideas against f7.

lines.name: 7...Nbd7: the Anand variation, 9...b5
lines.summary: Black plays ...b5 at once instead of ...Be7, saving a tempo and getting the bishop to b7. The main line is a long forcing sequence in which White gets three pieces for the queen.

next.text: A more modern set-up: the knight defends f6, covers e5 and heads for c5, and the bishop stays free to go to e7 or b7.
Black saves the tempo that the main line spends on ...Be7, and the bishop can go to b7 at once. The risk is that without a bishop on e7 the e6 and d6 pawns are targets.
White develops and prepares Rhe1 and Nd5; the bishop also guards e4, so that the c3 knight is free to jump.
The source calls it the main move and a serious option: the queen leaves c7, where Nd5 and e5 break-ups would hit her, and attacks the d4 knight.
White has won the queen for two knights and a bishop, and the b5 pawn is the first target.
Black has to open the centre; otherwise 23.e5 crushes him.
Opens the e-file and the b2-h8 diagonal before Black's pieces can come back.

**Verdict:** balanced, as the study I used judges it, with active pieces on both sides and both kings a little exposed. It is a long forcing sequence and a hard one to remember. The study notes 27.Re3!? as a possible improvement for White.
Too hasty.
Opens the e-file against the king.
Black's king is stuck on d8 and White is winning.

lines.name: 7...Qb6: the immediate Poisoned Pawn
lines.summary: The older move order. It reaches the same pawn-grabbing structure, but White keeps the bishop on g5 and has extra options, which is why the delayed order with ...h6 is preferred.

next.text: The Poisoned Pawn, Fischer's weapon.
