8.Nb3 is the quiet way to guard b2; it is not covered in the studies I used.
The bishop pins the knight against the queen, which is why the rook goes to b3.

**Verdict:** Black is a pawn up with a safe-looking queen, but the king is in the middle and the pieces are far from the kingside. The studies that give this line stop here without a verdict. The point of 7...h6 first is that the bishop has to leave g5: on h4 it is loose (...Be7 hits it), and the quiet 9.Nb3 that is possible here would be met by ...Qe3+, which takes the f4 pawn.
The other main try.
Black's pawns are damaged but the centre and the f-file compensate.

lines.name: 7...b5: the Polugaevsky Variation
lines.summary: Black ignores the threat of e5 and gets the queen to e5 with check, trading a knight for the bishop and winning time. The line is razor sharp and the study I used judges it slightly better for White.

next.text: The Polugaevsky Variation. Black lets White play e5 on purpose: the knight on f6 is given up for the bishop, and the queen lands on e5 with check.
The point: the queen hits the e5 pawn and the bishop on g5 at once.
An odd-looking only move: the rook leaves the long diagonal to avoid Bf3 with tempo, and it will swing along the seventh rank.
Castling saves the king and the game: 18...Rf8? 19.c3 and White wins.

**Verdict:** slightly better for White, as the study I used judges it. White must avoid trading down into an opposite-coloured bishop ending, which would give Black a draw, but otherwise has chances to win. A line for those who want a risk, not one to rely on.
Natural but it loses to a combination on e6.
Breaks open the king.
White wins.
Wrong: the pawn move does not address the double attack on the rook and the bishop.
White wins: the rook on a8 is hit and h4 is no help.

lines.name: 7...Qc7: 8.Bxf6 gxf6, a Richter-Rauzer structure
lines.summary: Black accepts doubled f-pawns for the bishop pair and counterplay on the b-file. White tries to attack the king in the centre; the line is playable but slightly easier for White.

next.text: The queen steps off the d-file and prepares ...b5 and ...Nc6, but it allows White to wreck the pawns at once.
The Rauzer structure: doubled pawns in front of the king, but the bishop pair and the g-file. White now continues as in the Richter-Rauzer.
The rook prepares ...b4.
**Verdict:** a little better for White. Black has plenty of counterplay with the rooks on the b- and g-files, but White has Bh5+ and Rhf1 on the way and the black king is in the centre.
Loses time and the light squares.
Always an important move: it pressures e6 and the light squares.

lines.name: White's quieter 7th moves: 7.Qf3, 7.Qd3, 7.Qe2, 7.Qd2 and the bishop moves
lines.summary: If White delays f4, Black develops with ...Nbd7 and ...Qc7 and uses the tempo for ...b5. Against the queen moves the pawn storm on the queenside is faster, and against the bishop moves Black can simply castle.

next.text: It blocks the f-pawn, which looks unnatural, but the study I used calls it the strongest of the four queen moves: it does not block the bishop on f1, allows long castling and hits a8, so that ...b5 is not free.
Black answers Qg3 with ...b5 because the queen has left the long diagonal.
Stops ...b4.
Defends e4 in case the c3 knight is chased away.
White has spent a lot of tempi on queen moves, and Black can castle without fear.
Black counterattacks instead of defending.
**Verdict:** better for Black, according to the study. White has no real threats on the kingside, while Black's rooks, bishop and queen all point at the white king.
Black has a piece for three pawns; after ...Nxg3 the ending should be equal.
Not 8...Be7 and then ...Nbd7: Nc6 would take away the bishop and the right to castle, because the knight on d7 is the only guard of c6.
Unpins the knight and hits a2.
Kovalev against Bologan, Minsk 2000, which Black won. With the queen on d3 Black gives up the Poisoned Pawn, since White would castle long, and uses the tempo for ...b5-b4.
Black is a piece up and the king is safe on d7.
With the queen no longer guarding d4, Bxf6 would lose a tempo to ...Qxf6, so Black simply develops.
Black has the bishop pair; after f4 this is the fourth game of the first file.
An ordinary equal middlegame.
Equal and quiet.
This is the Fischer-Sozin structure; 10...Nc5 removes any chance of a Bxe6 sacrifice.

lines.name: English Attack: 7...Be7 8.f3 Be6 9.Qd2 h5, the main line with 10.Be2
lines.summary: Black stops g4 before it starts, and the English Attack turns from a pawn race into a manoeuvring game. White trades on d5, Black ends up with the bishop pair and a comfortable open game.

next.text: The English Attack, today White's most popular sixth move. The bishop defends d4 for good, so the knight can be challenged without any pin, and f3, Qd2, long castling and the g4-g5 and h4 pawn storm follow. It is a race: White's pawns against the black king, Black's queenside pawns against the white king on the other wing.

The principled reply. The pawn kicks the d4 knight, takes space and opens the f8 bishop; the price is the structure from the overview, a hole on d5 and a backward pawn on d6. The Scheveningen set-up 6...e6 (sixth file) keeps d5 under control but gives White a free hand with g4, and 6...Ng4 (also sixth file) is the drawing line.
The knight leaves the centre without blocking the f-pawn or the bishop. 7.Nf3 (fifth file) is the quiet alternative.
The accurate move order. 7...Be6 is the more common move, but it allows 8.f4. The text avoids that, and after 8.f3 Be6 the main line is reached either way.
Defends e4 so that the c3 knight is free, takes g4 from Black's knight and prepares the pawn storm.
The bishop guards d5 and hits the knight on b3 and c4. It is safe from f4, because White has already used a tempo on f3.
Prepares long castling and covers d5: if Black plays ...d5 now, White castles long and has the d-file.

The modern idea, used at the top level. It stops g4 for good, because g4 hxg4 fxg4 would open the h-file for Black. The old answer 9...O-O leads to the pawn race of the first game of the next file; with ...h5 White cannot attack with the g-pawn, so the game becomes positional. The cost is that castling short is no longer attractive, so the king stays in the middle for a while.
Flexible: White waits to see where Black puts his king, and prepares kingside castling. 10.Nd5 and 10.O-O-O have their own games.
Now that the b8 knight has gone to d7, nothing guards c6. White plans exchanges on d5, exd5 and Na5-c6.
The bishop leaves the attacked square and hits c2.

The study's choice; elite games mostly play 14...Qc7 (or 14...Qc8), but then the knight can sit on a5 for ever. With the queen on b8 the bishop can go to d8 and remove it, and the queen also guards d6. 14...Qc8 looks active, but 15.c3 Bd8 16.Nc4 Qb8 gives White a pressure on d6 that the text avoids.
Forces the knight to decide: Nb3 would block White's own b-pawn, and b4 is met by ...Bxa5.
Ba4 would challenge the knight on d7, which guards c5.
Challenges the c4 pawn at once. If it is taken, ...axb5 and ...Rxa2 hits a pawn.
**Verdict:** equal and comfortable for Black. The queenside is open for ...a5, ...Rc8 and ...Nc5 ideas, White's d5 pawn is a target and the black bishop on g6 eyes the whole diagonal.
Too early.
The answer to an early g4 in every English Attack: the centre opens while White's king is still in the middle.
Black regains the piece with a better position.
Black has the stronger centre and active bishops.
Hits d6 and g7 but loses time.
Black has taken the centre with ...d5 and ...d4, and White's pieces have been pushed back.
The knight on e2 blocks the bishop and the queen, and Black develops with ease.

lines.name: English Attack: 9...h5 10.O-O-O Nbd7 11.Kb1 b5
lines.summary: White castles long and waits with Kb1, and Black expands on the queenside. The critical continuations are 12.Nd5 for a quick ending, 12.h3 and 12.f4.

next.text: White castles long, as in the old main line, but g4 is not available.
Black does not castle: with the h-pawn on h5 the king is better in the centre.
The usual waiting move. It takes the king off the c-file, where ...Bxb3 and ...Qa5 ideas would be annoying, and keeps White flexible.
Black expands. The general plan is ...Qc7, ...Nb6 and ...b4 or ...Nc4; the knight on b6 also guards d5.
The most forcing: White trades off the knight on d5 and heads for a quiet position.
With the bishop, not the knight: after ...Nxd5 the recapture exd5 would hit the bishop on e6 with tempo, whereas now the knight on b6 puts more pressure on d5.
Threatens the d5 pawn, which cannot be defended by c4 because of the b5 pawn.
The only way for White not to be worse: the knight heads for c6 and a quick ending.
**Verdict:** equal. Black has more space and active rooks, and the king comes to e7.
Covers g4 so that f4 or g4 becomes possible.
Stops g4.
Black has a good game: the queen guards e5 and the knight eyes c4 and a4.
A slower way to play for g4: it stops ...h4, and h3 and g4 follow.
Black is much better: White spent too much time on the pawn moves and Black's counterplay is faster.
Avoids the complications of g4 and goes for a different pawn push.
Prepares ...Bc4 in case f5 comes.
The knight comes with tempo on the queen.
Equal: Black has ideas on both wings.
Taking on c4 would leave the knight on b3 in a bad way, so White retreats the bishop, and Black plays ...a5 and ...b4.

lines.name: English Attack: 9...h5 10.Nd5 and the exchange sacrifice on a3
lines.summary: White trades knights at once. Black recaptures with the knight, keeps the bishop pair and plays ...a5 and ...Nd7. The other recapture 10...Bxd5 allows a very different, more risky game with a sacrifice of the exchange.

next.text: White heads for kingside castling and forces the issue on d5.
If possible, Black keeps the bishop pair.
White finishes development. 12.Na5 does not work: after 12...b6 the knight cannot go to c6, because the b8 knight guards it.
Black stops Na5 for good, so that the b8 knight can come out.
Stops ...a4, which would drive the knight from b3 to an awkward square.
**Verdict:** equal. The d5 pawn is a target and the black bishops control the board, but White's pieces are well placed and the position needs care.
The other recapture is playable, with a different character.
Black has given up the exchange and a pawn for the open a-file and the white king. Objectively White is better, but it is difficult to prove with the king on b1.

lines.name: English Attack: 9...O-O and the pawn race, 11.g4 b5 12.g5 b4
lines.summary: The old main line: both kings castle on opposite wings and each side storms the other. Black sacrifices a bishop and a pawn to open the a-file and the long diagonal against the white king. With best play the game is level.

next.text: The older main line. Black castles into the attack because the counterattack on the other wing is faster than it looks.
The knight supports ...b5 and may go to b6 or c5.
The storm begins. g5 will drive the knight from f6 with tempo.
Black races. It is the only way: slow moves lose to g5 and h4-h5.
The pawn hits the c3 knight, and White cannot take on f6 first because of ...bxc3.
Moves the knight out of the pawn's way and heads for g3 and the kingside.
The knight steps out of the way and heads for c7, where it guards d5 and the queenside.
Black ignores the attack and goes on with his own: the knights will be driven from b3.
The bishop on e6 is attacked, but so is the knight on b3.
White's best: the attacked knight jumps to d4, forcing ...exd4 and then Nxd4 with a threat on e6. The captures 16.fxe6 axb3 give Black the better game.
The most beneficial way to give up the bishop: it opens the a-file against the white king.
Counter-intuitively, White's king is mostly safe: the knight goes to b5 and covers c3.

**Verdict:** equal. Svidler against Van Wely (Foros 2007) was drawn. The line is the reason ...h5 is popular: Black can still choose this pawn race if he wants it, but without ...h5 he has to know a lot of theory.
Wins a bishop, but the b-pawn queens.
Black has two open files for his rooks and White's king is open.
and the a-pawn queens.
Hands White the open lines.
The knight comes with tempo and the bishop heads for d4 and f6.
Misplaces the knight on the rim.
Opens the h-file for White's rook: the worst thing Black can do.
Black equalises: the pawn on f6 is gone and the bishop controls d5 again.
and Black wins the queen.
Playable: the knight avoids the pawn at once, White trades on d5 and the structure is that of the quieter lines.

lines.name: English Attack: 7.Nf3 Be7 8.Bc4 and 8.Nd2
lines.summary: White keeps the knight on f3, which blocks his own kingside pawns but prepares Bc4, Ng5 and kingside castling. Black plays ...O-O and ...Be6, offering a trade, and heads for an equal ending.

next.text: White blocks the f-pawn, so there is no pawn storm, but he gets quiet kingside castling, Bc4 and Ng5 ideas against f7, and b3 for the bishop if Black plays ...b5.
The bishop prevents Bg5 and Ng5 tricks and prepares castling.
With the knight on f3 it is hard for White to push the kingside pawns, so there is no hurry to run to the queenside.
Offers the trade before Ng5 can hit e6.
Black opens the f-file for the rook. The doubled pawns take d5 and f5 away from White.
The point of the exchange: Na4 controls b6 and c5.
Challenges both squares, and unblocks the bishop on e7.
Takes d5 from the black pawn.
**Verdict:** equal. The pawn structure looks odd, but Black controls d4, f4 and d5 and has the central pawns.
Not 10...Nbd7? 11.Bxe6 fxe6 12.Ng5, when e6 is hard to defend because the knight blocks the queen.
Black wins back the pawn and is fine: Kamsky against Gelfand, Candidates 2011, was drawn.
Equal: the bishop pair against two knights.
White reroutes the knight to c4 and b6 or d5 but it takes many moves.
Black has time because the knight on d2 blocks the queen.
Not 9...bxc4? 10.Nxc4 and Nb6 comes.
Black may be a pawn down with a loose structure, but he has a strong attack on the kingside and all his pieces are in play.

lines.name: English Attack: 7.Nb3 Be7 8.Qd2 Ng4, 8.h3 and 8.Be2
lines.summary: If White does not play 8.f3, Black can trade his bad knight for the bishop with ...Ng4, or go for ...Be6 with an extra tempo. 8.h3 prepares f4 without wasting a move on f3.

next.text: White saves the move f3, but now the knight on f6 is not bothered.
The bishop is attacked and the e3 bishop is needed to guard d4 and d5. Black trades it, and without the dark-squared bishop the kingside attack loses a lot of force.
Now that d5 has lost its defender White plays the knight there.
The bishop comes to g5 next, and White cannot simply attack on the kingside.
**Verdict:** equal. The position is a quiet one with Black's pawn centre solid and the knight on d2 clumsy. Giri against Swiercz (Youth Stars 2008) was drawn.
The more natural move gives White 9.O-O-O.
Theoretically level, but White has the easier game and Caruana-Ivanchuk, Bucharest 2012, ended in a draw.
Prepares f4 directly, without a tempo on f3, and g4 as well.
Castling at once would allow g4.
Not ...Nbd7, which would block a defender of d6.
Transposes to the Classical Variation, which is covered by the other chapter.

lines.name: English Attack: 6...e6, the Scheveningen set-up with ...b5 and ...Bb7
lines.summary: Black keeps d5 under control and plays ...b5, ...Bb7 and ...h6, then breaks with ...e5 and ...d5. It is a second choice: the line below is given by the study without commentary, and 7.g4 leads to the Perenyi Attack.

next.text: The Scheveningen move order. The pawn guards d5 and f5, so White's knights have no outposts, but the bishop on c8 is blocked and the pawn no longer kicks the knight from d4: White gets a free hand with the pawn storm. Black usually has to spend a tempo on ...e5 later.
The bishop takes the long diagonal at once; it will also support ...d5 later.
Takes g5 from the pawn, so that the knight on f6 is not driven away.
The pawn comes to e5 at last, with tempo on the knight, and Black's pieces now cover d5.
Hits the pawn on e4 and the knight on f5 is no longer supported by the e-pawn.

**Verdict:** playable and unclear. Black has to win back the pawn on d5 with ...Nf6 and ...Bxd5 and has the better development, but the study gives no further moves and no verdict, so the line should be treated as a second choice behind 6...e5.
The Perenyi Attack.

Everything is forced: the knights are exchanged, and after 11.exf5 both sides have shattered kingside pawns, the g-file is open and the kings are exposed. The studies I used stop at 9.g5, so this line should be checked before it is played.

lines.name: English Attack: 6...Ng4, the Anti-English
lines.summary: Black attacks the bishop at once. If White retreats with Bc1 Black can repeat; if he plays Bg5 Black gets a wild kingside pawn structure with ...h6 and ...g5 and a knight on e5.

next.text: The Anti-English. It attacks the bishop at once and makes White decide whether to give up the bishop pair or to repeat moves. The study I used says that Black can also repeat with ...Nf6 and ...Ng4 if White is happy with a draw.
White keeps the bishop and pins the e7 pawn.
Asks the bishop what it wants to do.
Black expands on the kingside early and takes the bishop's retreat squares away.
The bishop on g7 eyes d4 and the long diagonal.
Kicks the knight away.

**Verdict:** playable, though not the most common line. Black has weakened the kingside, so he cannot castle short quickly, but the knight on e5 is superb, the bishop on g7 is strong and White has no good way to attack the pawns. Care is needed with the king: it will probably go long or stay in the middle.
Hits the knight but loses material.
The knight hits the queen and the bishop at once, and the d4 knight cannot be taken.
Greedy.
Forks the king and the queen.
If White retreats, Black can repeat the moves with ...Nf6 and ...Ng4, or play the main move 6...e5 after all.
